City staff will require monthly financial oversight and clean audits while pressing DHA to address $249/month unpaid pandemic-era rent arrears.
conflicts.resolution: Item 7 remained on the June 16 agenda for formal approval after staff committed to inserting monthly financial monitoring and audit conditions.

conflicts.meeting_title: Durham City Council Work Session June 5, 2025
conflicts.issue: 505 West Chapel Hill Street Post-Peebles Direction: Immediate Parceling vs. Re-Engaging Community on Master Plan (Item 25)
conflicts.summary: After unanimously ending talks with Peebles Corp, Council split over whether to pivot immediately to parceling out the Milton Small building and building standalone affordable housing (Option 3) or pause to re-consult the broader public on the original master plan.
conflicts.side_a_position: Pursue Option 3 immediately by exploring parceling the Milton Small building for Preservation NC and advancing standalone affordable housing on city-owned land.
side_a_arguments: After seven-plus years of delay, carving out Milton Small lets historic preservation specialists handle the building while freeing the lot for 60% AMI housing.
Downturns in commercial/market-rate construction actually lower costs for publicly subsidized affordable housing.
conflicts.side_b_position: Pause for site activation and broader citywide engagement before dismantling the master-planned five-priority vision.
side_b_arguments: The original master plan reflected broad citywide engagement across Hayti artists, DDI, and businesses—not solely the advocates in chambers.
Piecemeal parceling permanently anchors the site and forfeits the ability to deliver a cohesive catalytic downtown project.
conflicts.resolution: Council directed staff to meet with Preservation NC and affordable housing developers during July recess and return in August with pro/con analysis on Option 3 and parceling implications.

conflicts.meeting_title: Durham City Council Work Session June 5, 2025
conflicts.issue: Funding Part-Time Livable Wage Adjustments & Additional $200,000 for Justice Matters IAP in FY25-26 Budget (Item 6)
conflicts.summary: Following a consensus poll to raise part-time step spreads from 3% to 5% ($270k), Council split on whether to cut other budget items immediately to add $200,000 for Justice Matters' Immigrant Advocacy Program ($470k total) or hold the balanced budget.
conflicts.side_a_position: Find $470k in cuts, delays, or carryover commitments to fund both the 3%-to-5% part-time step raise and +$200k for Justice Matters now (with Cook also favoring fuller part-time DMLW parity).
side_a_arguments: Immigrant legal defense communities face escalating federal threats, and $250k is insufficient relative to the $700M+ city budget.
43% of non-commensurate part-time workers are over age 40, and 3%-to-5% steps plus $200k can be accommodated via minor contract delays rather than a tax hike.
conflicts.side_b_position: Accept the 3%-to-5% part-time step increase ($270k) without adding a tax hike or raiding balanced budget lines, and prioritize Justice Matters in fall carryover review.
side_b_arguments: Staff advised that $470k exceeds the $150k-$250k budget margin of error and would otherwise require cutting balanced priorities or raising taxes.
Full-time compression complaints and benefits cliffs are serious risks requiring a multi-year study, while fall carryover funds can fairly weigh Justice Matters against other needs.
conflicts.resolution: Council reached informal consensus on the 3%-to-5% part-time step boost ($270k), left Justice Matters at $250k for June 16 budget adoption, and publicly committed to prioritizing it in fall carryover discussions.

conflicts.meeting_title: City Council Work Session on Budget May 28, 2025
conflicts.issue: Applying the $21.90/Hour Durham Minimum Livable Wage to Non-Commensurate Part-Time Workers
conflicts.summary: Council members clashed with staff recommendations and debated among themselves over excluding roughly 201 seasonal and non-commensurate part-time workers (earning as little as $16.85/hour) from the $21.90/hour Durham Minimum Livable Wage.
conflicts.side_a_position: Bring all part-time city workers—including seasonal youth-care and recreation staff—up to the $21.90/hour Durham Minimum Livable Wage and eliminate the 3% vs. 4-6% merit disparity.
side_a_arguments: Prior council direction in 2019 was to pay all city workers a living wage without carveouts, and paying youth-care/after-school staff $16.65-$16.85/hour undermines childcare quality.
Many part-time DPR workers are adult women of color or 10-month school employees working limited hours annually (e.g., ~366-472 hours), meaning the total budget cost is modest.
Part-time employees deserve full livable wages and equitable merit raises rather than a lower 3% cap compared to 4-6% for full-time workers.
conflicts.side_b_position: Maintain pay differentiation between non-commensurate seasonal roles and full-time/higher-responsibility positions to prevent severe compression and fiscal strain.
side_b_arguments: Paying gatekeepers or camp aides the same $21.90/hour as lifeguards, full-time recreation specialists, or degreed/skilled workers collapses pay hierarchies and creates severe compression—especially with DMLW projected near $25+/hour in FY 2027.
Expensive value mandates require growing the tax base or cutting elsewhere rather than eroding distinctions across the organizational chart.
conflicts.resolution: City Manager Bo Ferguson clarified the city can afford full DMLW for all part-timers if Council accepts the fairness trade-offs, and committed to returning on June 5 with demographic data, job titles, and cost options.

conflicts.meeting_title: City Council Work Session on Budget May 28, 2025
conflicts.issue: Long-Term Tax Funding Strategy for Fare-Free GoDurham Transit
conflicts.summary: Council agreed on continuing fare-free GoDurham service through FY 2026 but debated whether to rely on draining COVID-era transit fund balance now or prepare incrementally for future tax hikes or eventual fare reintroduction.
conflicts.side_a_position: Spend down existing transit fund balance to keep buses fare-free now without preemptively raising transit property taxes before needed.
side_a_arguments: 87% of GoDurham riders earn under $35,000 annually, making fare-free transit a critical equity, affordability, and ridership investment.
Reinstalling fareboxes and collecting fares from riders with senior/youth carveouts yields minimal net revenue while creating barriers.
conflicts.side_b_position: Plan incrementally for the FY 2027 fiscal cliff or revenue diversification rather than leaving a sudden tax increase or fare decision to a future council.
side_b_arguments: Waiting until fund balance reaches zero risks forcing a sharp transit tax hike during an economic downturn.
Expanding the tax base and non-property-tax revenues (and asking large regional employers for contributions) is necessary to sustain free transit without overburdening homeowners.
conflicts.resolution: Staff retained the revenue-neutral 2.4-cent transit tax rate for FY 2026 while flagging that FY 2027 will require additional tax revenue or service adjustments.

conflicts.meeting_title: City Council Work Session on Budget May 28, 2025
conflicts.issue: Proposed Property Tax Increase, Peripheral Growth Costs, and Missing Gun Violence / Housing Priorities
conflicts.summary: During Day 1 closing remarks, council members expressed diverging anxieties over the 5.48-cent rate increase above revenue neutral, infrastructure costs of peripheral development, housing affordability, and gun violence.
conflicts.side_a_position: Question the proposed tax rate increase amid economic strain and federal cuts while criticizing insufficient immediate action on housing insecurity and the cost of peripheral expansion.
side_a_arguments: Residents face job losses, federal funding cuts, and widening inequality, making a higher post-revaluation tax bill straining for middle- and low-income residents.
Outward suburban expansion carries underexamined long-term utility and service costs, while housing affordability lacks dedicated spotlight on the budget work-session agenda.
conflicts.side_b_position: Defend targeted rate investments above revenue neutral and argue expanding the tax base through development inside the Urban Growth Boundary—alongside stronger gun-violence and public-safety action—is essential.
side_b_arguments: Going solely revenue neutral would force deep service cuts; instead, Council should broaden eligibility for the joint Low-Income Homeowner Relief program.
Refusing development inside the Urban Growth Boundary undermines tax-base growth needed to fund progressive city services without constantly raising property taxes.
Mayor Williams separately criticized the lack of immediate gun-violence strategy items comparable to Vision Zero investments, noting Bull City United and ShotSpotter ended.
conflicts.resolution: No changes were directed on Day 1; members continued discussions on Day 2 and scheduled follow-ups for June 5.

conflicts.meeting_title: Durham City Council Meeting May 19, 2025 (with closed captioning)
conflicts.issue: Peripheral Car-Centric Land Use Pattern and Advocacy Critique on Brier Creek Multifamily (Item 26)
conflicts.summary: Although Council ultimately approved the 408-unit Brier Creek Multifamily project 7-0, Council Members Baker and Freeman voiced sharp criticisms of peripheral car-centric growth and outside advocacy framing.
conflicts.side_a_position: Critique the broader land-use pattern of building dense apartments in car-dependent peripheral areas without transit and question outside YIMBY advocacy rhetoric.
side_a_arguments: Approving high-density housing on the Wake County border far from frequent transit entrenches automobile dependency (Baker).
Outside groups claiming to champion affordability often rubber-stamp market-rate development without building substantive partnerships with local affordable housing organizations (Freeman).
conflicts.side_b_position: Praise the developer's responsive proffers (5% at 80% AMI for 30 years, $50,000 housing fund, $16,500 DPS, native plantings) and support adding multifamily housing supply near jobs and retail.
side_b_arguments: The parcel sits inside existing city boundaries adjacent to existing Brier Creek commercial retail and employment corridors.
The applicant increased school and housing commitments directly in response to neighborhood and Planning Commission feedback.
conflicts.resolution: Despite policy reservations expressed during debate, all seven members voted Aye on the zoning map change, UEA, and consistency statement (7-0).

conflicts.meeting_title: Durham City Council Meeting February 3, 2025 (audio synched with closed captioning)
conflicts.issue: Item 13: Consolidated Annexation Ordinance and Utility Extension Agreement - Moriah Ridge (M/I Homes of Raleigh LLC)
conflicts.summary: M/I Homes sought voluntary annexation and utility extension for 15 parcels totaling 168.37 acres across the Durham-Orange county line for up to 1,000 residential units and 2,500 sq ft of office space, while staff disclosed a corrected FIA reducing projected FY34 net fiscal benefit from ~$27M to $5.36M. Roughly 25 speakers strongly opposed the development for breaching the Urban Growth Boundary, splitting Orange County property taxes/schools (CHCCS) from Durham municipal infrastructure, alleging aggressive acquisition tactics toward remaining 'donut hole' homeowners, and relying on incomplete stream surveys. All five Council members agreed the project was premature and inconsistent with the UGB and comprehensive plan (though Mayor Pro Tem Middleton cautioned external state development pressures could return), and the annexation motion failed unanimously 0-5.
conflicts.side_a_position: Voted Aye (Failed 0-5)
conflicts.side_b_position: Voted Nay / Opposed
conflicts.resolution: Failed (0-5)

conflicts.meeting_title: Durham City Council Meeting January 21, 2025 (audio synched with closed captioning)
conflicts.issue: Return on Investment and Living-Wage Metrics for $250,000 Ellis D. Jones & Sons Economic Development Incentive
conflicts.summary: Council split 6-1 over whether a $250,000 Neighborhood Revitalization / Durham Legacy Business grant to Ellis D. Jones & Sons Funeral Home required stronger quantitative ROI and living-wage job justification or was warranted as an equity-centered capital preservation investment.
conflicts.side_a_position: Support the $250,000 grant as a performance-based equity and neighborhood revitalization investment in a fourth-generation Black-owned legacy institution.
side_a_arguments: Unlike corporate recruitment deals (such as Apple or Google), Neighborhood Revitalization Grants leverage roughly 3:1 private capital to preserve Black-owned legacy businesses harmed by historic systemic inequities and gentrification.
The performance-based agreement helps unlock bank lending for capital improvements and requires the renovated second floor to host community events and meetings for at least five years.
conflicts.side_b_position: Question the $250,000 public expenditure without a quantitative 'but-for' or tax-revenue ROI analysis and fuller living-wage job creation.
side_b_arguments: According to the staff jobs table, only three of five projected jobs over five years meet the city's living-wage threshold.

Staff did not perform a quantitative tax-revenue or public ROI analysis (only qualitative arguments) or a formal 'but-for' calculation demonstrating the project could not proceed without the $250,000 grant.
conflicts.resolution: Passed 6-1 (Carl Rist voting No) after Mayor Leonardo Williams noted he texted Carl Rist to continue discussing legacy-business incentive evaluation in future policy conversations.

conflicts.meeting_title: Durham City Council Dec 16 2024
conflicts.issue: Community Engagement Consultant Transition and Intellectual Property (Item 19 - WSP USA Translation)
conflicts.summary: Council Member DeDreana Freeman challenged relying on City staff and WSP USA Inc. after removing Idealisms LLC (Item 18), arguing it unfairly appropriated relationships built by community practitioners; other members and the City Attorney countered that municipal consultant work product belongs to the City and Spanish translation should proceed.
conflicts.side_a_position: Concerned that cutting Idealisms LLC while continuing staff-led engagement exploits community-based practitioners' relationships
side_a_arguments: Community engagement firms build years of local trust that City staff should not bypass or repurpose
Questioned continuing the study scope without the originally partnered community engagement firm
conflicts.side_b_position: Support approving the $7,250 WSP amendment to translate already-completed Durham Freeway Study reports into Spanish
side_b_arguments: City Attorney Kimberly Rehberg advised that deliverables produced under City contracts are work for hire owned by the City
Spanish-speaking residents need immediate translated access to existing technical reports
conflicts.resolution: Passed 7-0 after Council Member Freeman voted Aye while maintaining her process critique on the record.

conflicts.meeting_title: Durham City Council Work Session October 24, 2024
conflicts.issue: Process and Utility of Testing the EAB Sustainable Decision-Making Tool (Item 9)
conflicts.summary: Council divided over advancing an Environmental Affairs Board sustainability assessment checklist directly to a Council test case versus requiring staff vetting first and limiting bureaucratic layers.
conflicts.side_a_position: Run a collaborative test case with staff to standardize sustainability and equity metrics across all City departments.
side_a_arguments: A single standardized rubric gives non-expert policymakers consistent data instead of piecemeal departmental reports.
Piloting one item with staff will quickly show whether the tool helps or burdens workflows.
conflicts.side_b_position: Require advisory boards to collaborate directly with City staff experts before asking Council to approve or pilot an operational tool.
side_b_arguments: Bypassing department staff demoralizes professional staff and creates out-of-order policy proposals.
Existing staff already incorporate sustainability and racial equity considerations without needing extra bureaucratic checklists.
conflicts.resolution: Caballero and Cook clarified the test case meant EAB working directly with appropriate staff first; no formal vote was taken.

conflicts.meeting_title: Durham City Council Sept 3 2024
conflicts.issue: Lee Valley Consolidated Annexation, Transit-Oriented Design, and Proffer Sufficiency
conflicts.summary: Council split 4-1 on annexation/utility extension and 5-1 on the two Lee Valley rezoning ordinances, with Nate Baker dissenting over auto-oriented design in a designated Transit Opportunity Area while the majority accepted the project's affordability and sustainability proffers.
conflicts.side_a_position: Support annexation and rezoning based on improved affordability/sustainability proffers and met extension conditions.
side_a_arguments: The applicant satisfied conditions from the prior extension and added post-Planning Commission proffers, including affordability and sustainability commitments.
No active BRT or passenger rail corridor currently serves the site, and case-by-case gains should be taken rather than imposing ex-post-facto standards ahead of the UDO rewrite.
Housing diversity should be evaluated across the broader surrounding area rather than expecting every single parcel to contain every housing type.
conflicts.side_b_position: Oppose annexation and rezoning for falling short of Transit Opportunity Area design expectations.
side_b_arguments: The Future Place Type Map designates the site as a Transit Opportunity Area intended to transition Durham away from auto-centric development.
Additional transit-oriented design commitments and office/civic/commercial integration were needed despite staff guidance.
conflicts.resolution: Annexation passed 4-1 and both UDO rezoning motions passed 5-1 with Nate Baker voting no; consistency statement passed 6-0.

conflicts.meeting_title: Durham City Council Work Session August 8, 2024
conflicts.issue: 505 West Chapel Hill Street Preferred Developer Terms: Land Sale vs. Ground Lease and Affordable Unit Count (Item 7)
conflicts.summary: While all present members expressed positive views toward The Peebles Corporation's team, Council divided over voting Peebles preferred under the Base Proposal's $7.5M fee-simple sale and 92 affordable units versus requiring pre-vote modeling of a long-term ground lease and significantly more affordable units.
conflicts.side_a_position: Advance Peebles' Base Proposal largely as submitted to respect RFP fidelity, avoid stalling a third time after Fallon's collapse, and preserve historic hotel/commercial revenue.
side_a_arguments: The RFP specifically authorized land sale with restrictive covenants and set 250,000 sq ft commercial and 92-unit thresholds that Peebles met; changing core terms mid-stream risks a de facto RFP reopening and developer distrust.

Middleton argued it is legally and ethically unfair to lock in one preferred developer while altering terms that other proposers might also bid better on, while Freeman stressed getting units built after seven years of delay.
conflicts.side_b_position: Require staff and Peebles to model retaining City land ownership via long-term ground lease and increasing affordable units (toward the consortium's 175-unit ask) before locking into a binding term sheet.
side_b_arguments: Selling the City's last large downtown parcel for $7.5M surrenders long-term public wealth and leverage; a 50-99 year ground lease protects permanent affordability.

Council members should see concrete financial tradeoffs upfront (and Baker requested voluntary 5% market-rent caps, affordable retail, geothermal/solar, and protected bikeways) rather than repeating Fallon-style surprises a year later.
conflicts.resolution: City Attorney Fred Lamar confirmed no re-bid is legally required; General Services Director Stacy Poston agreed to return on August 19 with revised GBA motions adding an interim step to explore expanded affordable units and a ground-lease option alongside the base proposal.

conflicts.meeting_title: Durham City Council Work Session August 8, 2024
conflicts.issue: Council Suite Furniture Replacement Cost During a Tax-Increase Year (Other Matters)
conflicts.summary: Following Mayor Williams's request for opt-outs on budgeted Council Suite furniture replacements, multiple members objected to the overall price tag during a high-tax year.
conflicts.side_a_position: Proceed with budgeted furniture and audiovisual upgrades for the Mayor's office and common conference room while allowing individual members to opt out.
side_a_arguments: Existing furniture is outdated and funds were already budgeted; individual opt-outs substantially reduce total expenditure.
conflicts.side_b_position: Opt out of personal office furniture spending and question the overall price tag given resident tax pressures.
side_b_arguments: Spending large sums on Council furniture sends the wrong message in a year when residents face steep property-tax bills; upgrades should be narrowed to shared AV/conference needs.
conflicts.resolution: Five members publicly stated they opted out of individual office furniture; no formal vote was taken.

conflicts.meeting_title: Durham City Council Work Session June 6, 2024
conflicts.issue: UDO Rewrite Audit Transparency, Survey Demographics, and Density vs. Unit-Size Assumptions (Item 37)
conflicts.summary: Council members sharply questioned Code Studio and Planning staff over missing written audit deliverables, dropped short-term code amendments, heavily skewed online survey demographics, and whether eliminating density caps guarantees affordable family housing.
conflicts.side_a_position: Audit deliverables and survey framing are inadequate/unrepresentative, and density alone does not ensure family-sized affordability.
side_a_arguments: Council was led to expect short-term targeted UDO recommendations and a full written audit report rather than only a slide deck.
Presenting online survey results that are 82% white and >51% over $100k income as a baseline before qualitative community engagement undermines equitable engagement.

Code Studio's affordability chart relies on shrinking units to 800 sq ft for a family of four; density should be paired with affordable housing density bonuses, and inner-core lot caps of 8 units may be overly conservative vs. 12-plexes or cottage courts.
conflicts.side_b_position: Eliminating units-per-acre density caps is vital to lower rents and support transit, and early online data is only an incomplete baseline.
side_b_arguments: Removing density caps and regulating by form/height aligns land use with the Comprehensive Plan, Urban Growth Boundary, and regional transit goals.

Online surveys historically skew white and affluent nationwide, which is why Dr. Tuwana Allen's parallel in-person ambassador outreach is underway; incomplete survey numbers (214 responses) should simply be held or framed clearly.
conflicts.resolution: Informational presentation only; Planning staff confirmed the first full draft UDO will return in late fall 2024 ahead of early 2025 public review.

conflicts.meeting_title: Durham City Council Meeting April 15, 2024
conflicts.issue: Item 27 (Wake Olive Apartments): Approve Annexation Ordinance and Utility Extension Agreement
conflicts.summary: Wake Olive Apartments proposed annexing and rezoning 12.16 acres on NC 98 (Wake Forest Highway) from RR/RS-20 to PDR 17.92 for 218 apartments, following a unanimous 10-0 denial vote from the Planning Commission. Thirteen nearby residents opposed the project due to extreme traffic congestion along two-lane Wake Forest Highway, auto-dependent separation from services and transit, and potential watershed impacts on Lick Creek. Although the developer proffered 13 income-restricted units (7 at 60% AMI, 6 at 80% AMI) for 30 years, EV chargers, native landscaping, and a 10-foot path, opponents on Council criticized post-Planning Commission proffers, lack of mixed commercial/civic uses, and far-flung sprawl outside established infrastructure corridors. After Chelsea Cook withdrew a motion to return the case to Planning Commission and the applicant's request for staff referral lacked consensus, Mayor Williams and Mark-Anthony Middleton voted aye while Caballero, Baker, Rist, Freeman, and Cook voted nay, defeating the annexation 2-5 and rendering the companion zoning and consistency votes moot.
conflicts.side_a_position: Voted Aye (Failed 2-5)
conflicts.side_b_position: Voted Nay / Opposed
conflicts.resolution: Failed (2-5)

conflicts.meeting_title: Durham City Council March 4, 2024
conflicts.issue: Olive Branch Reserve North Annexation and Density vs. Environmental & Infrastructure Impacts (Item 25)
conflicts.summary: Council split 4-2 on annexing and extending utilities to an 87.7-acre Mill Creek Residential townhome/duplex project on Olive Branch Road after a 10-0 Planning Commission recommendation for denial and heavy opposition from Preserve Rural Durham and the Neuse Riverkeeper.
conflicts.side_a_position: Approve annexation and rezoning to secure environmental protections, 17 income-restricted rentals, roadway upgrades, and duplex/townhome housing diversity.
side_a_arguments: The proposal meets 22 of 25 Comprehensive Plan policies, preserves 45% of the site (300-ft wildlife corridor and 100-ft stream buffers), and will be governed by Durham's stricter 2023 UDO erosion/mass-grading rules.
Denying the rezoning invites by-right development of 129 expensive single-family homes ($600K-$800K+) on wells and septic with fewer protections and no developer-funded NCDOT road improvements.
The developer increased its proffer at the hearing to 6% (17 units) income-restricted for 30 years (3% at 80% AMI, 3% at 100% AMI) plus $23,000 for DPS without city subsidy.
conflicts.side_b_position: Deny the annexation and rezoning due to Comprehensive Plan inconsistency, severe sedimentation in Martin Branch Creek, and unmitigated car-centric sprawl.
side_b_arguments: The Planning Commission voted unanimously (10-0) to recommend denial because the single-use development is miles from groceries/transit and entrenches auto-dependent sprawl.

Martin Branch Creek is already severely impaired (measured at 40x state turbidity limits), and Southeast Durham faces cumulative impacts from 41 active developments, blasting damage, overcrowded schools, and 13-minute EMS response times.
100% AMI units do not meet the Comprehensive Plan's affordable housing target (30-80% AMI) and are insufficient to offset the environmental and infrastructure costs.
conflicts.resolution: Annexation and utility extension agreement passed 4-2; Council then voted 6-0 on the companion zoning ordinance and consistency statement.

conflicts.meeting_title: City Council Budget Retreat - March 1, 2024 - 9:00 a.m.
conflicts.issue: Timing of a 2024 General Obligation Bond Referendum Amid Pay-Study Tax Pressures
conflicts.summary: Council members expressed differing views on whether to place a major GO Bond package (~$300M-$610M across sidewalks, parks, sustainability, and potentially a Convention Center) on the November 2024 ballot given concurrent tax increases needed for employee pay.
conflicts.side_a_position: Defer the GO Bond referendum to 2025 or later to prioritize employee compensation and avoid stacking multiple tax increases in 2024.
side_a_arguments: Funding the employee pay study will already require a substantial property tax increase in FY25, making it difficult to ask voters for bond debt simultaneously.
More time is needed to mount a public education campaign and evaluate whether borrowing substantially accelerates project delivery beyond current CIP pacing.
conflicts.side_b_position: Continue evaluating a 2024 GO Bond package (and public-private/county partnerships for the Convention Center) to address urgent sidewalk, park, and climate backlogs.
side_b_arguments: Sidewalks, safer streets, affordable housing, and neighborhood parks are top resident priorities, and current 2.5 miles/year sidewalk pacing would take 170 years without bond acceleration.
A Convention Center and headquarters hotel partnership with the County and private sector could expand sales and occupancy tax capacity, provided jobs meet living-wage or union standards.
conflicts.resolution: Staff noted that final project selections and a Council resolution would be needed by June 2024 for LGC approval if pursuing a November 2024 ballot referendum; no decision was finalized.

conflicts.meeting_title: Durham City Council Work Session October 23, 2025
conflicts.issue: Paragrin Technologies Software Contract (Item 25) for DPD Operations / Real Time Crime Center
conflicts.summary: Public speakers and council members pushed back against fast-tracking a priority contract with Paragrin Technologies, demanding public education and written privacy, AI, and ICE data-sharing guardrails before any vote.
conflicts.side_a_position: Hold the contract for community town halls, written answers on data access/AI/immigration risk, and full transparency before council action.
side_a_arguments: Surveillance and data-integration tools require transparent public dialogue rather than a single priority work-session cycle.
Residents need ironclad, written guarantees prohibiting third-party data harvesting, Palantir/ICE leakage, and unchecked AI analytics.
conflicts.side_b_position: Advance the software tool as an internal search upgrade over existing DPD CAD/RMS data without new surveillance hardware.
side_b_arguments: Police Chief Patrice Andrews, City Manager Bo Ferguson, and Paragrin explained the platform only queries data DPD already possesses, with zero Palantir affiliation or ICE sharing.
Improving internal search speeds officer investigations without expanding external camera or sensor networks.
conflicts.resolution: City Manager Bo Ferguson agreed to refer Item 25 back to staff rather than place it on the November 3 agenda so DPD could host public outreach and provide written responses.

conflicts.meeting_title: Durham City Council October 20, 2025
conflicts.issue: Tenant Protection Ordinance (§10-241(f)): Unamended Passage vs. Preemption Caveat and Code Cross-Reference Amendment
conflicts.summary: Council members split over whether to add the City Attorney's proposed state-preemption disclaimer and local code enumerations to §10-241(f) before passing the rent-collection prohibition.
conflicts.side_a_position: Adopt §10-241(f) immediately without adding a preemption caveat or altering the cure-period structure.
side_a_arguments: Inserting 'unless otherwise preempted by state or federal law' undermines enforceability and gives landlords a ready-made pretext to ignore the ordinance.
Existing housing code already incorporates a 72-hour cure framework for imminently dangerous conditions, so tenants need clear protection effective immediately.
conflicts.side_b_position: Attach legal preemption caveats and specific Durham code enumerations to mitigate litigation risk raised by the City Attorney's office.
side_b_arguments: Senior Deputy City Attorney Fred Lamar warned that state landlord-tenant statutes likely preempt municipal restrictions on rent collection.
Tailoring language and cure references could lower legal exposure while preserving neighborhood inspection triggers.
conflicts.resolution: Mark-Anthony Middleton withdrew the preemption amendment at 03:22:40 and backed the unamended ordinance, which passed 7-0.

conflicts.meeting_title: Durham City Council October 20, 2025
conflicts.issue: Structure, Affordability Targeting, and Oversight of the $1.75M Affordable ADU Loan Pilot (Item 16)
conflicts.summary: Council members scrutinized the Quorum Houses LLC ADU pilot's 80% AMI threshold, single-bidder procurement, loan forgiveness, and compliance risks while ultimately voting yes.
conflicts.side_a_position: Question 80% AMI targeting, single-bidder risk, Airbnb/lease-up enforcement, and oppose loan forgiveness.
side_a_arguments: 80% AMI rents and an ~$80,000 average city loan per unit yield modest affordability depth relative to multifamily subsidies.
Allowing loans to become forgivable turns scarce revolving housing funds into grants, while homeowners acting as landlords require strict Airbnb bans and lease-up monitoring.
conflicts.side_b_position: Launch the 20-unit pilot with Quorum Houses LLC to fill a private lending void and evaluate scalability.
side_b_arguments: Commercial banks and mission lenders have struggled to underwrite small ADU construction loans, so direct city lending fills a real market gap.
Forever Home Durham promised an ADU pilot, and Quorum Houses was the sole qualified respondent with hands-on ADU construction capacity.
conflicts.resolution: Council unanimously passed the $1.75 million pilot 7-0 with expectations of compliance enforcement and program evaluation.

conflicts.meeting_title: Durham City Council Work Session October 9, 2025
conflicts.issue: Wildlife Feeding Prohibition Ordinance (Item 14): Citywide Misdemeanor vs. Chapter 26 Nuisance Code / County Enforcement
conflicts.summary: After competing public testimony from animal-care advocates and Trotter Ridge homeowners suffering up to $10,000 in squirrel damage, council members resisted adopting a citywide misdemeanor ordinance in Chapter 6.
conflicts.side_a_position: Explore placing targeted nuisance language in Chapter 26 (Property Nuisances) or rely on County animal-nuisance law, HOA remedies, and education.
side_a_arguments: Creating a citywide misdemeanor in Chapter 6 risks overly broad enforcement against backyard bird feeders or feral-cat TNVR caretakers for what appears to be a localized neighborhood dispute.

Deputy City Attorney Hernandez noted Durham County's existing animal-nuisance ordinance already covers willful creation of wildlife property nuisances, and Chapter 26 handles grass/porch nuisances without new misdemeanor language.
conflicts.side_b_position: Provide residents with an enforceable local prohibition after severe property damage caused by concentrated wildlife feeding.
side_b_arguments: Trotter Ridge neighbors documented $2,000 to $10,000 in vehicle wiring, chimney, and property damage and deer attacks without effective county relief.
Staff noted education-only ordinances without enforcement authority leave code inspectors powerless when neighbors refuse voluntary compliance.
conflicts.resolution: Council referred Item 14 back to staff to analyze Chapter 26 nuisance-code placement and county coordination rather than advancing the Chapter 6 ordinance to October 20.

conflicts.meeting_title: Durham City Council Work Session October 9, 2025
conflicts.issue: Anti-Displacement / Wealth Recapture Alongside Trail Investments (Item 9) & ADU Loan Pilot Structure (Item 16)
conflicts.summary: During the Rail Trail and ADU Loan Pilot presentations, council members differed over the urgency and feasibility of pairing major infrastructure with anti-displacement policy and structuring direct city ADU lending.
conflicts.side_a_position: Commission targeted anti-displacement/wealth-recapture policy research alongside Rail Trail delivery and scrutinize ADU direct-lending ROI.
side_a_arguments: Major public amenities drive gentrification; Durham should study creative anti-displacement models allowed under NC law alongside construction through 2028 rather than repeating past displacement (Chelsea Cook).

In Item 16, fronting $1.75M in full city loans rather than interest buy-downs limits scale, and making ADU loans forgivable reduces units-per-dollar return (Chelsea Cook; Nate Baker earlier absent during Item 16).
conflicts.side_b_position: Deliver the Rail Trail and launch the city-backed ADU loan pilot pragmatically without stalling construction or waiting on absent private banks.
side_b_arguments: Equitable engagement along the Rail Trail began in 2019 (including Stagville Memorial Plaza), much land turnover already occurred, and further study shouldn't delay project delivery (Mark-Anthony Middleton, Leonardo Williams).
Because no commercial bank or CDFI currently lends for backyard ADUs, direct city gap financing with Quorum Houses LLC is necessary to test feasibility (Carl Rist, staff).
conflicts.resolution: Informational presentations; Council advanced Item 16 to the October 20 Consent Agenda (later pulled for vote) and noted Item 9 enhancements while asking staff to track ADU pilot metrics.

conflicts.meeting_title: Durham City Council October 6, 2025
conflicts.issue: Unprinted $47,000 Floor Amendment for Museum of Durham History
conflicts.summary: Members clashed over budget transparency when a $47,000 fund-balance appropriation for the Museum of Durham History was introduced on the floor without advance written documentation.
conflicts.side_a_position: Approve the $47,000 match immediately from fund balance to support the museum's county-matched operational need.
side_a_arguments: Durham County was reviewing the matching share of a $93,145 request, and delaying could disrupt museum operations.
The item had been previewed during the September 18 work session carryover discussion.
conflicts.side_b_position: Criticize the lack of printed ordinance text, budget office review, and fair access for other nonprofits before final adoption.
side_b_arguments: Council members should not be asked to vote on unprinted mid-meeting fund-balance expenditures without formal staff memos.
Ad-hoc floor awards bypass competitive grant processes used for peer cultural nonprofits.
conflicts.resolution: Despite procedural objections, all seven members voted Aye on the amended budget ordinance (7-0).

conflicts.meeting_title: Durham City Council Work Session September 18, 2025
conflicts.issue: City Manager Contract Approval Authority Thresholds
conflicts.summary: Council split during the work-session preview on whether raising the Manager's services contract signing limit to $500,000 overly curtails Council transparency.
conflicts.side_a_position: Raise delegated authority across goods, construction, utilities, and services to reduce agenda friction.
side_a_arguments: Outdated $50,000 limits force routine operational renewals and minor change orders onto Council agendas.
Peer North Carolina cities grant higher administrative procurement authority to city managers.
conflicts.side_b_position: Keep professional services contracts capped lower (around $100,000-$250,000) to preserve public visibility.
side_b_arguments: High-dollar consulting and services contracts raise policy questions that residents expect elected officials to review in public.
Goods and construction bids are more standardized than discretionary service contracts.
conflicts.resolution: Placed on the October 6 General Business Agenda for formal vote (ultimately settled at a $250,000 services cap).

conflicts.meeting_title: Durham City Council Work Session - Strategic Plan Visioning Workshop September 18, 2025
conflicts.issue: Standalone Affordable Housing and Climate Goals vs. Existing Five-Goal Structure
conflicts.summary: Council members diverged on whether affordable housing and climate change should become standalone top-level strategic plan goals or remain distinct priorities within a concise five-goal framework.
conflicts.side_a_position: Elevate Affordable Housing (and environmental/climate goals) to standalone top-level strategic goals.
side_a_arguments: Durham's housing affordability crisis is Council's foremost public priority and deserves explicit top-line visibility rather than sitting inside a broad built-environment goal.
Elevating housing makes performance metrics and budget alignment clearer to residents.
conflicts.side_b_position: Keep the concise five-goal structure while establishing Affordable Housing as a prominent priority under 'Vibrant Built and Natural Environment.'
side_b_arguments: Expanding beyond five top-level goals dilutes strategic focus and fragments cross-cutting linkages between land use, transit, and housing.
Maintaining housing alongside climate and infrastructure inside a single built-environment goal mirrors comprehensive planning.
conflicts.resolution: No formal vote taken; consultants and staff were directed to draft synthesized options for a follow-up session.

conflicts.meeting_title: Durham City Council Work Session September 4, 2025
conflicts.issue: 505 W. Chapel Hill Street Master Planning vs. Early Affordable Housing Partition
conflicts.summary: Council disagreed over Chelsea Cook's request to pull forward an October 9 interim report aimed at partitioning 505 W. Chapel Hill Street for affordable housing versus waiting for staff's November 20 comprehensive update.
conflicts.side_a_position: Hold an October 9 interim update to explore carving out land at 505 W. Chapel Hill St. quickly for affordable housing.
side_a_arguments: Delaying until late November wastes months during a severe affordable housing shortage.
An early check-in lets Council gauge whether part of the former police site can be split off immediately.
conflicts.side_b_position: Maintain the November 20 comprehensive staff briefing before partitioning the parcel.
side_b_arguments: Staff need until November 20 to deliver thorough site master-planning, environmental remediation context, and Preservation NC coordination on historic structures.
Piecemeal partitioning prematurely risks foreclosing a cohesive mixed-use or civic redevelopment strategy.
conflicts.resolution: Kept the November 20 briefing schedule without adding an October 9 interim agenda item.

conflicts.meeting_title: Durham Joint City County Planning Committee (JCCPC) - September 3, 2025
conflicts.issue: New UDO Affordable Housing Density Bonus Design (Deep 30% AMI Subsidies vs. Broader 70%-80% AMI By-Right Bonuses)
conflicts.summary: JCCPC members debated how the New UDO's affordable housing density bonus should balance modest by-right incentives at 70%-80% AMI against deeper affordability targets at 30% AMI that typically require direct public subsidy.
conflicts.side_a_position: Focus zoning bonuses on feasible market-driven thresholds (e.g., 60%-80% AMI or Austin-style 100% affordable by-right deregulation) paired with fee-in-lieu flexibility.
side_a_arguments: By-right zoning bonuses cannot mathematically cross-subsidize 30% AMI units without LIHTC or local bond dollars, so overly steep rules go unused.
Austin's 'Affordability Unlocked' model proves stripping height, parking, and setback barriers unlocks significantly more subsidized supply.
conflicts.side_b_position: Guard against eroding resident leverage and ensure density bonuses deliver meaningful deeply affordable units and neighborhood benefits.
side_b_arguments: Durham's greatest unmet shortage is for households at 30%-50% AMI, which developers routinely skip when bonuses stop at 80% AMI.
Giving away extra height and density by-right without calibrated requirements risks upzoning land values without proportionate community benefit.
conflicts.resolution: Informational workshop only; consultants and planning staff recorded committee feedback to calibrate draft UDO housing incentives.

conflicts.meeting_title: Durham City Council Work Session August 21, 2025
conflicts.issue: Recurring Non-Competitive Nonprofit Contracts vs. Competitive Grant Equity (El Centro Hispano)
conflicts.summary: Council members debated whether continuing recurring annual contracts for organizations added via prior budget amendments (such as El Centro Hispano) undermines fairness for nonprofits competing in open RFP cycles.
conflicts.side_a_position: Scrutinize recurring direct-award nonprofit contracts and transition toward transparent competitive funding criteria.
side_a_arguments: Rolling over past council-earmarked awards year after year creates an uneven playing field against peer community organizations.
Council needs a comprehensive inventory of all recurring nonprofit contracts to ensure equitable evaluation.
conflicts.side_b_position: Maintain continuity for established core service partners that deliver critical bilingual and community navigation services.
side_b_arguments: El Centro Hispano's contract funds essential front-line municipal partnership staffing originally requested by Council in 2022.
Sudden funding cuts disrupt vital services for vulnerable residents before alternative grant mechanisms exist.
conflicts.resolution: Kept Item 7 on the September 2 Consent Agenda while directing Budget Director Christina Reirden to compile a complete inventory of city-funded nonprofits.

conflicts.meeting_title: Durham City Council Work Session August 21, 2025
conflicts.issue: Timing of the December 2025 Post-Election Organizational Meeting
conflicts.summary: Facilitated by Mary Grace Stone King, Council weighed holding the December 2025 swearing-in on December 1 versus December 4 or 15 amid post-canvass election certification timelines.
conflicts.side_a_position: Swear in newly elected or re-elected members as early as legally certified on December 1 or December 4.
side_a_arguments: Prompt seating respects voters' mandate and avoids lame-duck votes after the municipal election.
Standard early-December organizational meetings align with longstanding Council calendar traditions.
conflicts.side_b_position: Delay until December 15 or verify statutory canvass/recount windows before setting a binding date.
side_b_arguments: Close municipal races, provisional ballots, or recount windows can delay official Board of Elections certification past December 1.
Locking a date without City Attorney verification risks scheduling conflicts with statutory certification rules.
conflicts.resolution: No consensus reached; deferred to the next work session pending City Attorney verification of election certification deadlines.

conflicts.meeting_title: Durham City Council August 18, 2025
conflicts.issue: Walltown Small Area Plan Floor Amendment Locking Current Northgate Mall Zoning Limits
conflicts.summary: Council debated a floor amendment introduced by Nate Baker (from Walltown Community Association testimony) advising that Northgate Mall's existing height and research-and-development limits stay locked until a rezoning application, despite the pending New UDO rewrite.
conflicts.side_a_position: Insert explicit plan language protecting current Northgate Mall height and use restrictions so the New UDO does not grant by-right upzoning without community negotiation.
side_a_arguments: Upzoning Northgate to CX-5 by right in the New UDO strips Walltown residents of leverage to negotiate affordable housing and community benefits.
Neighborhood-specific small area guidance is the proper place to protect historical community organizing.
conflicts.side_b_position: Reject inserting late regulatory zoning locks into an advisory Comprehensive Plan document without JCCPC/County review.
side_b_arguments: Comprehensive and small area plans are advisory rather than regulatory, and New UDO district conversions do not map one-for-one to old districts.
Major late edits to a joint City-County planning document should go through the New UDO rewrite and JCCPC review process.
conflicts.resolution: Nate Baker withdrew the floor amendment before final voting, and Council adopted the Walltown Small Area Plan and Place Type Map Amendment unanimously 6-0.

conflicts.meeting_title: Durham City Council June 2, 2025
conflicts.issue: Naming Amazon and RDU 1 Directly in Workers' Rights Resolution (Item 38)
conflicts.summary: Council debated whether to retain the Workers' Rights Commission's specific accusation of retaliation against Amazon or generalize the condemnation clause.
conflicts.side_a_position: Strike language accusing Amazon of retaliation and remove specific 'RDU 1' facility references from the official municipal resolution.
side_a_arguments: An official City Council resolution bearing the City's seal should not endorse uninvestigated accusations against a named corporate citizen.
Condemning anti-union retaliation universally without naming Amazon/RDU 1 makes the resolution stronger and avoids legal/procedural scrutiny.
conflicts.side_b_position: Retain worker-drafted condemnation of retaliation against Amazon organizing (or specify RDU 1) unless majority consensus favors removing it.
side_b_arguments: Amazon retaliation claims are widely reported and Workers' Rights Commission members organizing at Amazon drafted the language intentionally.
Targeted solidarity language matters in a state with anti-union preemption and low union density.
conflicts.resolution: Cook proposed replacing the clause to condemn retaliation at RDU 1 and then accepted a friendly edit removing 'RDU 1'; Council passed the amended resolution 7-0 after Baker corrected his initial vote.

conflicts.meeting_title: City Council Work Session on Budget May 29, 2025
conflicts.issue: Immediate Day Shelter and Non-Congregate Shelter Funding vs. Waiting for Homelessness Strategic Plan
conflicts.summary: Council divided over whether to add immediate short-term funding for a day shelter and low-barrier non-congregate sheltering in the FY 2025-26 budget or wait for Community Safety's homelessness strategic plan before making new financial commitments.
conflicts.side_a_position: Allocate immediate short-term funding (such as ~$50,000 for a day shelter or pallet/safe-sleeping pilots) in FY 2025-26 rather than waiting a year for a strategic plan.
side_a_arguments: The 2025 point-in-time count showed chronic homelessness nearly doubled even as overall numbers dipped, and 111 individuals plus 62 families remain on shelter waitlists.
Without a day shelter, unhoused residents remain exposed to the elements and rely on public spaces like the downtown library during daytime hours.
A ~$50,000 day shelter investment was among Council's top budget retreat priorities and is small relative to a $722 million total budget.
conflicts.side_b_position: Complete the homelessness strategic plan and establish clear operational partnerships and RFPs before appropriating new shelter funds.
side_b_arguments: No clear operator, scope, or implementation plan currently exists for a $50,000 day shelter allocation, risking symbolic spending without measurable results.
Council opted against increasing the dedicated housing tax rate at the budget retreat, leaving limited capacity for unvetted pilots.
Waiting on the strategic plan allows Community Safety to align street outreach, housing unit matchmaking, and Continuum of Care investments systematically.
conflicts.resolution: No budget amendment was finalized; Council Member Cook indicated she may revisit day shelter funding at the June 5 work session pending Durham County's budget decisions.

conflicts.meeting_title: Durham City Council Work Session March 6, 2025 (livestream)
conflicts.issue: Allowing Resident Petition Opt-Outs from City Gravel Street Paving
conflicts.summary: Council debated whether residents living on unpaved gravel streets should be permitted to petition to opt out of City street paving, weighing neighborhood traffic-calming preferences against equity and public infrastructure standards.
conflicts.side_a_position: Explore an opt-out petition option where street residents prefer keeping unpaved streets.
side_a_arguments: Unpaved streets can serve as natural traffic calming and reflect some residents' desire to avoid paving assessments or faster cut-through traffic.
A transparent petition mechanism could respect strong neighborhood consensus on specific low-volume streets.
conflicts.side_b_position: Maintain City paving of gravel streets without an opt-out option.
side_b_arguments: Unpaved streets in Durham carry a painful racial and economic legacy ('other side of the tracks' disinvestment) and should be brought to uniform city standards.
Gravel streets impair emergency vehicle access, generate dust and stormwater runoff, and shift ongoing maintenance burdens back onto the City.
Chelsea Cook, who initially raised the inquiry, concluded she opposed an opt-out after hearing colleagues' equity and infrastructure arguments.
conflicts.resolution: Staff received consensus guidance not to pursue a resident opt-out mechanism and to proceed with planned paving.

conflicts.meeting_title: Durham City Council Budget Retreat - Feb 28, 2025 (livestream)
conflicts.issue: Maintaining 100% Battery-Electric Bus Procurement Versus Temporary Diesel Bus Purchases Amid Loss of Federal Grants
conflicts.summary: Council members split over whether GoDurham should purchase diesel buses when federal zero-emission grants are unavailable (~$600k cheaper per bus) or maintain its 2035 100% electric-fleet commitment using local tax dollars.
conflicts.side_a_position: Temporarily revert to diesel buses unless federal grants cover the electric price premium, prioritizing fare-free service and avoiding local tax spikes.
side_a_arguments: Battery-electric buses cost roughly $600,000 more per vehicle than diesel buses and federal FTA zero-emission grants are being reduced or eliminated.
Transit ridership itself cuts greenhouse gases far more than private cars, so preserving fare-free frequency with diesel buses advances community sustainability more affordably.
City taxpayers alone cannot absorb federal climate-policy reversals in a southern auto-oriented state.
conflicts.side_b_position: Maintain full commitment to electric buses and Carbon Neutrality Plan targets, funding clean transit through long-term local property taxes.
side_b_arguments: Diesel combustion is one of the dirtiest vehicle emissions sources and shifting back to diesel feels like going backward on Durham's 2035 climate commitment.
Local residents strongly value climate goals alongside fair wages and fare-free transit, and Council should build a sustainable city for the future rather than only tomorrow.
conflicts.resolution: City Manager Bo Ferguson summarized a majority willingness to consider diesel bus purchases when federal grant funding is absent to control Transit Fund costs while preserving fare-free service.

conflicts.meeting_title: Durham City Council Budget Retreat - Feb 28, 2025 (livestream)
conflicts.issue: Retaining Earmarked Tax Rates (Half Penny for Parks & Two Cents for Housing) Versus Revenue-Neutral Caps Post-Revaluation
conflicts.summary: During Budget Guidelines polling, Council members split on whether keeping fixed penny earmarks after a 74% property revaluation windfall represents an unjustified tax hike without vetted spending plans.
conflicts.side_a_position: Keep the full Half Penny for Parks (0.50c) and consider rates above revenue-neutral on Dedicated Housing and Solid Waste to capture growth for core amenities and housing.
side_a_arguments: Parks and trails are Durham's most egalitarian public spaces and need investment to correct disparities across neighborhoods.
Housing loses ARPA construction-overrun backfill funds and needs capacity for the Affordable Housing Loan Fund and City-County-Schools recommendations.
conflicts.side_b_position: Hold revenue-neutral or balancing caps (Option A) on Parks, Solid Waste, or Housing unless specific vetted expenditure plans justify higher rates.
side_b_arguments: Holding a 0.50-cent parks earmark after revaluation acts as a 0.17-cent tax increase without a finalized Parks Master Plan project list.
With dozens of competing priorities and major tax bill impacts on homeowners, agencies like Solid Waste and Parks should show operational efficiencies before exceeding balancing rates.
conflicts.resolution: Show-of-hands polls gave staff Option B flexibility on Parks, Housing, and Solid Waste, with Council scheduling follow-up budget workshops to scrutinize exact proposed expenditures.

conflicts.meeting_title: Durham City Council Work Session February 6, 2025
conflicts.issue: Durham Homeless Services Advisory Committee (HSAC) Non-Profit Appointment Split
conflicts.summary: Council tied on the HSAC non-profit seat between Tasha D. Melvin and Drew Wooten with two members absent, sending the appointment to the General Business Agenda.
conflicts.side_a_position: Appoint Tasha D. Melvin to the HSAC Non-Profit Organization seat.
side_a_arguments: Supporters cited Melvin's qualifications and community background for the non-profit seat.
conflicts.side_b_position: Support Drew Wooten for the HSAC Non-Profit Organization seat (with remaining absent votes uncast).
side_b_arguments: Remaining votes favored Drew Wooten, creating an impasse with Freeman and Caballero absent.
conflicts.resolution: Placed on the February 17 General Business Agenda as Item 2; Clerk subsequently polled full Council and Melvin won a majority.

conflicts.meeting_title: Durham City Council Meeting February 3, 2025 (audio synched with closed captioning)
conflicts.issue: Item 11 (Picket Apartments) Immediate Vote vs. Continuance for Bird-Friendly Design & Sidewalk Connectivity
conflicts.summary: Council debated whether to vote immediately on Picket Apartments (140 units, 10% affordable adjacent to Sandy Creek Park) or continue the public hearing to pursue bird-safe glazing/lighting and a multi-agency Durham Academy sidewalk partnership.
conflicts.side_a_position: Continue the public hearing to March 17, 2025 to refine bird-friendly building/lighting commitments and explore sidewalk funding coordination with Durham Academy.
side_a_arguments: Neighbors and bird conservationists documented 185 bird species at Sandy Creek Park and requested clearer window-treatment and dark-sky lighting commitments rather than ambiguous menus.
Continuing gives Ascension time to meet good-faith community stakeholders and explore off-site sidewalk partnership options alongside LEED/green building inquiries.
conflicts.side_b_position: Vote on the rezoning immediately rather than continuing when the developer already stated it cannot commit to building the full sidewalk culvert connection.
side_b_arguments: Applicant attorney Neil Ghosh clearly stated the project cannot financially absorb or timeline-guarantee triple-culvert wetland sidewalk construction beyond its $300,000 contribution.
With 10% affordable apartments near transit and services, the project's benefits already outweighed its drawbacks without risking moved goalposts.
conflicts.resolution: Mayor Williams yielded to Council consensus, reopened the public hearing, and continued it to a date certain of March 17, 2025.

conflicts.meeting_title: Durham City Council Work Session January 23, 2025 (livestream)
conflicts.issue: Cost, Duration, and Outsourcing of City Community Engagement Under the 2018 Equitable Engagement Blueprint
conflicts.summary: Debate sparked by the ~$80,000 public-outreach component of the Algal Floway contract pitted Council members criticizing expensive, multi-year third-party consulting against members defending deep, culturally responsive outreach.
conflicts.side_a_position: Audit and curb outsourced community engagement contracts (~$80k-$100k per project) and return closer to the original 90-day timeline or build internal city capacity.
side_a_arguments: Paying private consultants $80,000-$100,000 per project has spawned an expensive 'cottage industry' where engagement drags on for years while residents still complain they were not reached.
Elected officials and internal NIS staff should lead engagement while directing scarce public dollars toward housing and core delivery.
conflicts.side_b_position: Maintain multi-round, linguistically accessible, community-centered outreach even if it costs ~10% of project budgets and adapts as sites evolve.
side_b_arguments: The 2018 Equitable Engagement Blueprint was created because projects like the Durham Beltline and Third Fork Creek proceeded without reaching renters and marginalized residents.
Ten percent of a $1M project is reasonable for mailings to renters, translation, and iterative outreach whenever project locations change over multi-year timelines.
conflicts.resolution: Council agreed to schedule a dedicated future work-session policy review of the 2018 Equitable Engagement Blueprint.

conflicts.meeting_title: Durham City Council January 6, 2025 (audio synched with closed captioning)
conflicts.issue: Procedural Handling of Item 5: Vote Down Bow-Hunting Ordinance First vs. Substitute Motion to Refer to Environmental Affairs Board (EAB)
conflicts.summary: While all seven Council members agreed against adopting the citywide Section 6-3 bow-hunting reduction as written, Council Member Freeman attempted a substitute motion/friendly amendment to refer the matter to the EAB rather than voting it down, whereas Mayor Williams, Mayor Pro Tem Middleton, and Council Member Cook insisted on voting on the active main motion first.
conflicts.side_a_position: Vote directly on the already-seconded main motion to defeat the proposed Section 6-3 ordinance and decide independently afterward whether and where to refer wildlife-management alternatives.
side_a_arguments: Once a main motion is moved and seconded, Council must act on that motion to establish a clear legislative record.
It is not yet clear whether EAB is the right body to study broader wildlife, feeding, or non-lethal policies across other Durham neighborhoods.
conflicts.side_b_position: Offer a substitute motion/friendly amendment referring the item to the Environmental Affairs Board instead of delivering an outright rejection.
side_b_arguments: Referring the issue to EAB provides a constructive, collaborative pathway for Treyburn and other neighborhoods experiencing deer or wildlife conflicts rather than leaving residents empty-handed.
conflicts.resolution: Middleton declined to withdraw his main motion and Cook maintained her second; the main motion was voted down 0-7, leaving future referral to EAB or staff alternatives open.

conflicts.meeting_title: Durham City Council Work Session December 19, 2024
conflicts.issue: Authority and Safety of Lifting the Administrative Pause on City Tent Distribution to Unsheltered Residents
conflicts.summary: Council members clashed over whether to direct staff during a work session to lift an administrative pause prohibiting HEART and other city staff from distributing tents while HSAC finalizes a countywide policy.
conflicts.side_a_position: Lift the administrative pause immediately so outreach workers can distribute tents during freezing rain without risking disciplinary retaliation.
side_a_arguments: Freezing rain and cold winter nights pose immediate danger to unsheltered residents before a formal HSAC policy is finished.
Staff such as HEART responders should not face write-ups or uncertainty for providing emergency shelter gear.
conflicts.side_b_position: Do not issue unagendized work-session directives or endorse tents as winter shelter in below-freezing weather; defer to formal policy channels and indoor shelter options.
side_b_arguments: Council cannot govern by ad hoc work-session fiat without an agendized item, staff cost data, or formal vote.
Tents are unsafe in sub-freezing temperatures; the City should explore indoor facilities such as vacant City real estate or Durham Public Schools gyms and align with HSAC.
conflicts.resolution: No formal vote was taken; Mayor Williams declined to suspend the rules and instructed City Manager Wanda Page, incoming Manager Bo Ferguson, Deputy Manager Keith Chadwell, and Community Safety Director Ryan Smith to develop an urgent response.

conflicts.meeting_title: Durham City Council Dec 16 2024
conflicts.issue: City Manager Appointment Process, Transparency, and Vote Timing (Bo Ferguson)
conflicts.summary: Following a closed session, a surprise open-session motion to appoint Deputy City Manager Bo Ferguson was declared unanimously passed, sparking sharp disagreement over procedural fairness, lack of an open national search, closed-session division, and Chelsea Cook not having a chance to cast her vote.
conflicts.side_a_position: Objected to the un-agendized motion, rushed vote without discussion, and closed-door hiring process lacking a public search
side_a_arguments: Cook stated she had her hand raised to speak, did not know a final vote was closing, and never cast a ballot
Freeman cited prior closed-session disagreement (4-3 or 5-2) and criticized skipping an open search for Durham's highest-paid executive
Caballero emphasized public transparency expectations for major executive appointments and voicemail/communication delays
conflicts.side_b_position: Defended appointing internal Deputy City Manager Bo Ferguson through the same council appointment mechanism used previously
side_b_arguments: Williams and Middleton highlighted Ferguson's institutional continuity and leadership during major crises such as the 2019 gas explosion
Asserted the appointment followed the same precedent used to appoint outgoing City Manager Wanda Page
conflicts.resolution: Appointment stood as declared at 02:34:12 without a revote; Cook stated for the record she did not vote during the tally though she supported Ferguson personally.

conflicts.meeting_title: Durham City Council Work Session October 24, 2024
conflicts.issue: Deployment of Remaining $249,000 in Unobligated ARPA Funds (Item 10)
conflicts.summary: While Council rejected staff's recommendation to keep $249,000 internally for administrative salaries, members differed on whether to seed universal kindergarten baby bonds or fund existing nonprofits.
conflicts.side_a_position: Use the $249,000 as seed money—paired with corporate matches and Latino Credit Union/DPS Foundation partnerships—to launch kindergarten baby bonds / youth savings accounts.
side_a_arguments: Starting accounts (~$25 per student for ~2,000 kindergarteners born during the pandemic) creates long-term generational wealth and leverages corporate matching from firms like Wells Fargo.
Means-testing City revenue-replacement dollars complies with state law while private funds cover universal access.
conflicts.side_b_position: Prioritize already-vetted nonprofits or existing ARPA partners (such as El Futuro, Book Harvest, or Knox Street) due to extreme December 31 contracting and legal constraints.
side_b_arguments: Legal and staff capacity constraints make negotiating a brand-new subrecipient agreement and means-tested bond structure by December 31 high risk.
Existing nonprofits such as El Futuro or homelessness/food organizations already have vetted scopes ready to deploy funds without risking federal clawback.
conflicts.resolution: Council directed staff to pursue baby bonds feasibility via existing partners such as United Way/LCCCU/DPS Foundation while preparing fallback options among existing youth-serving ARPA grantees.

conflicts.meeting_title: Durham City Council Work Session October 10, 2024
conflicts.issue: Legal Effect of Adopting NACTO Urban Street and Bikeway Design Guides by Resolution (Item 31)
conflicts.summary: Council debated whether adopting NACTO design guides as 'official' guidelines via resolution prematurely locks staff into inflexible legal standards prior to the UDO rewrite.
conflicts.side_a_position: Adopt NACTO and ITE guides now as official reference guidelines to unlock federal Bipartisan Infrastructure Law flexibility and inform the UDO and Reference Guide updates.
side_a_arguments: Guidelines remain flexible reference documents rather than rigid cross-section construction standards.
Official adoption empowers Durham under the federal Bipartisan Infrastructure Law on federally funded city street projects.
conflicts.side_b_position: Avoid resolution language with mandatory legal force ahead of the UDO rewrite and require City Attorney review of the revised draft before any vote.
side_b_arguments: Using words like 'official' and 'adopt' in a resolution creates quasi-legal force that can cause disputes when field exceptions are warranted.
Staff had not finalized City Attorney review of the second draft and must ensure the UDO rewrite schedule is not delayed.
conflicts.resolution: Cook requested moving Item 31 to the General Business Agenda so the City Attorney's Office could complete review of the revised resolution before the October 21 vote.

conflicts.meeting_title: Durham City Council Work Session September 19, 2024 (Live Stream)
conflicts.issue: Durham Convention Center & 500-Key HQ Hotel Feasibility ($540M New vs. $93M Expansion)
conflicts.summary: Council divided over pursuing a $540 million new convention center and 500-key headquarters hotel, weighing hospitality tax limits and economic upside against public-spending priorities and labor protections.
conflicts.side_a_position: Question $540M public-private hospitality outlay and insist on strict community benefits, union neutrality, and core-service comparisons
side_a_arguments: Raised opportunity costs relative to affordable housing, childcare, and street/transit maintenance
Cook and Rist pressed for enforceable community benefit agreements, living wages, and union protections for hotel workers
conflicts.side_b_position: Continue evaluating downtown Convention Center competitiveness using restricted hospitality revenues
side_b_arguments: State law restricts occupancy and prepared-food tax proceeds to tourism-related projects rather than general operating services
Modernizing or replacing aging convention infrastructure prevents Durham from losing major regional events
conflicts.resolution: Informational study briefing; no funding commitment voted upon.

conflicts.meeting_title: Durham City Council Work Session September 5, 2024
conflicts.issue: Attribution of DPS School Overcrowding to City Rezonings vs. State Funding and Capital Planning (Item 25)
conflicts.summary: During a briefing projecting +5,000 Durham Public Schools students at roughly $100,000 per seat, Council pushed back firmly against tying City housing approvals to school overcrowding.
conflicts.side_a_position: Reject linking City rezonings to school capacity deficits; attribute crowding to state funding gaps and DPS planning
side_a_arguments: North Carolina law bars cities from imposing mandatory adequate-public-facilities school impact moratoriums or full-cost fees
State underfunding, charter/voucher enrollment dynamics, and County/DPS bond timing—not housing growth alone—drive classroom shortages
Requested better joint seat-generation forecasting without pitting housing supply against public schools
conflicts.side_b_position: Staff/DPS capacity framing emphasizing rapid residential rezoning student-yield pressures (+5,000 projected seats)
side_b_arguments: High-volume new residential entitlements accelerate enrollment spikes beyond current school facility capital budgets (~$100,000 per seat)
conflicts.resolution: Informational briefing concluded with Council directing better intergovernmental data sharing ahead of future growth coordination.

conflicts.meeting_title: Durham City Council Aug 19 2024
conflicts.issue: Duke Central Campus Addition University College (UC) Rezoning Without Specific Development Plan
conflicts.summary: Council members disagreed on whether to evaluate Duke's Central Campus UC rezoning without specific development plans and broader institutional commitments before deciding to continue the case to October 7, 2024.
conflicts.side_a_position: Delay/require clearer master plan, development intentions, sustainability, housing, and transportation timing commitments before voting.
side_a_arguments: Duke has no concrete development plans for parcels acquired over decades, leaving Council without control once broad UC zoning is granted.
The ordinance states a master plan shall be submitted, yet lacks clarity on what a master plan must contain compared to NCCU's publicly available plan.
Duke's transportation commitment for a 10-foot side path lacked a binding timing component, and community/council distrust of the county's largest private landowner warrants deeper due diligence.
conflicts.side_b_position: Evaluate the UC rezoning on standard land-use grounds without litigating broader disputes with Duke.
side_b_arguments: Council has previously approved rezonings without detailed development plans by relying on lists of prohibited uses, and UC zoning is designed to provide flexibility for universities.
Broader institutional conversations and grievances with Duke should be addressed in separate forums rather than prosecuted through this land-use case.
conflicts.resolution: Council polled unanimous consent at 03:26:22 to hold the public hearing open and continue the case to October 7, 2024.

conflicts.meeting_title: 7. Update on the Redevelopment of 505 W. Chapel Hill St. fr. 8/19/24 Council Meeting
conflicts.issue: Duke Central Campus Addition University College (UC) Rezoning Without Specific Development Plan
conflicts.summary: Council debated whether to approve broad UC zoning for Duke's Central Campus parcels without a concrete development plan, clear master plan standards, or binding transportation timelines.
conflicts.side_a_position: Continue the case to obtain clearer development, master plan, sustainability, housing, and side-path timing commitments.
side_a_arguments: Granting broad UC zoning without a development plan surrenders future oversight over parcels Duke has held for decades.
The ordinance's master plan requirement is poorly defined, and the 10-foot transportation side path lacked any timeline trigger.
conflicts.side_b_position: Treat the UC rezoning within standard flexible university zoning practice without prosecuting broader Duke disputes.
side_b_arguments: Council has previously approved rezonings without full development plans using prohibited-use lists, and UC zoning is meant to give universities flexibility.
Broader disagreements with Duke belong in separate discussions rather than this rezoning hearing.
conflicts.resolution: Continued by unanimous consent at 03:02:25 to October 7, 2024.

conflicts.meeting_title: Durham City Council Work Session May 23, 2024
conflicts.issue: Addressing Downtown Business Disruptions: UDO Rewrite vs. Administrative Action and Citywide Equity (Item 34)
conflicts.summary: Following DDI's urgent letter from 260 downtown businesses, Council members and DDI diverged over whether construction/streetscape reforms belong in the UDO rewrite or immediate administrative operations, and whether grants and support should extend citywide beyond downtown.
conflicts.side_a_position: Address construction communication, ADA compliance, and public goods through UDO standards, and ensure small-business support extends beyond downtown.
side_a_arguments: Large out-of-town corporate developers should have communication, sidewalk, and utility/trash allocation standards baked into the UDO rewrite and targeted amendments.
Small businesses in neighborhoods outside downtown—such as Ninth Street and Driver Street—also suffer from utility shutoffs and lack a DDI-style organization to advocate for them.
conflicts.side_b_position: Focus on immediate City operational fixes (employee parking, alert systems, fines for bad actors) without tying them to the UDO.
side_b_arguments: DDI's letter seeks pre-development meetings, enforcement of existing closure plans, employee parking relief by September, and administrative coordination rather than waiting on the UDO.
Council should stay focused on actionable operational fixes and activating the existing small business fund rather than letting out-of-town developer critiques hijack the discussion.
conflicts.resolution: No formal vote; Council asked Deputy City Manager Bo Ferguson to consult City Manager Wanda Page and return with a timeline of immediate vs. FY26 budgetary actions.

conflicts.meeting_title: Durham City Council Work Session May 9, 2024
conflicts.issue: Surplus City Land Disposition and Permanent Affordability Terms
conflicts.summary: Members differed on how aggressively the City should mandate permanent affordability covenants and community land trust transfers versus flexible RFP/upset-bid disposition on 10 surplus city-owned sites.
conflicts.side_a_position: Prioritize permanent affordability and community land trust stewardship over time-limited deed restrictions or open market upset bids.
side_a_arguments: Publicly owned land represents an irreplaceable asset that should stay permanently affordable beyond 30-year windows.
Conveyances to nonprofits or land trusts avoid speculative turnover on small infill lots.
conflicts.side_b_position: Maintain flexible disposition pathways including upset-bid and negotiated RFP authority under NC law so parcels actually get developed quickly.
side_b_arguments: State disposition statutes constrain direct transfers unless specific statutory affordable housing or nonprofit channels apply.
Overly rigid requirements can stall small, scattered-site projects identified in the HR&A inventory.
conflicts.resolution: Staff advanced Item 19 to the May 20 Consent Agenda as an initial intent-to-declare-surplus step while committing to return with disposition structure details for each parcel.

conflicts.meeting_title: Durham City Council Work Session April 18, 2024
conflicts.issue: 2024 General Obligation Bond Package Scope and Sustainability Inclusion
conflicts.summary: Council Member DeDreana Freeman questioned excluding dedicated green/climate sustainability components from the $200M Parks and Streets GO Bond package favored by the majority.
conflicts.side_a_position: Include explicit green infrastructure or sustainability investments within the 2024 GO Bond referendum rather than deferring them.
side_a_arguments: Earlier bond planning discussions contemplated green and climate resilience priorities that disappeared from the final $200M split.
Addressing climate infrastructure alongside aquatics and paving aligns with City sustainability commitments.
conflicts.side_b_position: Keep the $200M bond tightly focused on $85M in aquatic/park facilities and $115M in streets and sidewalks within manageable tax impacts.
side_b_arguments: Residents prioritized sidewalk construction, road paving, unpaved street upgrades, Wheels Aquatic Center, and East End/Long Meadow pools.
Expanding bond categories further would raise the projected 2.51-cent average / 3.45-cent peak tax rate impact.
conflicts.resolution: A Council majority gave thumbs-up to advance the $200M Parks ($85M) and Streets/Sidewalks ($115M) bond package toward the May 20 Council meeting.

conflicts.meeting_title: Durham City Council Meeting April 1, 2024
conflicts.issue: Lee Valley Rezoning Transit-Oriented Area Compliance and Collector Street Design (Item 21)
conflicts.summary: A majority of Council members questioned Lee Valley's omission of commercial/civic space, private streets, and an isolated Wendell Road collector segment, contrasting with Mark-Anthony Middleton's support for advancing East Durham housing.
conflicts.side_a_position: Require Transit-Oriented Area (TOA) projects to deliver real mixed commercial/civic uses, public street grids, and coherent Wendell Road collector alignment.
side_a_arguments: The Comprehensive Plan's TOA place type expects neighborhood-serving commercial/civic elements rather than pure residential sprawl.
Private streets and a disconnected collector-road island along Wendell Road fall short of multimodal connectivity standards.
conflicts.side_b_position: Recognize the 8-5 Planning Commission approval, affordability proffers, and DPS contribution as sufficient grounds to support needed East Durham housing.
