meetings.title: Durham City Council October 6, 2025
meetings.executive_summary: Durham City Council held its regular meeting with all seven members present, approving FY25-26 carryover budget and capital project ordinances—including $200,000 for Justice Matters and a $47,000 floor amendment for the Museum of Durham History—alongside a compromise raising the City Manager's services contract threshold to $250,000. Council unanimously designated The Chicken Hut as a Local Historic Landmark, heard informational updates on a potential wildlife feeding ordinance, and approved the 117-townhome Hartland Park annexation and rezoning in a 4-3 split vote after extended debate over watershed runoff and housing affordability.

agenda_items.title: Ceremonial Proclamations (MED Week, Imagine a Day Without Water, Customer Service Week, Digital Inclusion Week, Arts & Humanities Month, Hispanic Heritage Month)
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Mayor Leonardo Williams and Council members presented six ceremonial proclamations recognizing Minority Enterprise Development Week, Imagine a Day Without Water, Customer Service Week, Digital Inclusion Week, National Arts and Humanities Month, and Hispanic Heritage Month. Staff and community representatives from Finance, Water Management, Durham One Call, Digital Inclusion, Durham Arts Council, and El Centro Hispano offered brief remarks.

agenda_items.title: Excuse Council Member DeDreana Freeman from October 9, 2025 Work Session
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Council addressed an administrative request to excuse Council Member DeDreana Freeman from the upcoming October 9, 2025 work session. Council Member Chelsea Cook noted her electronic voting screen lagged and verbally asked to be recorded as voting yes.

agenda_items.title: Consent Agenda (Items 1, 2, 4-8, 10-12, 14-16, 21)
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Council adopted the modified Consent Agenda after pulling Items 3 and 19 for separate discussion, moving Item 9 to General Business Agenda, and keeping Public Hearings 17 and 18 on the regular docket. Included items covered the Purdue Pharma opioid settlement authorization, Merrick Moore heritage designation, an NCDOT Triangle rail study agreement, and a Durham County affordable housing interlocal agreement.

agenda_items.title: FY25-26 Budget Ordinance Amendment (#16514) and Companion CIP Ordinances
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Council considered five carryover budget and capital project ordinances plus an internal service fund plan, incorporating $200,000 for Justice Matters immigrant legal defense flagged by Javiera Caballero. Mark-Anthony Middleton offered a floor amendment adding $47,000 from fund balance as a roughly 50 percent match for the Museum of Durham History. DeDreana Freeman, Chelsea Cook, and Nate Baker expressed process concerns about voting on unprinted floor additions without prior budget review, though all members voted in favor.

agenda_items.title: Wildlife Feeding Report
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Council received an informational report on wildlife feeding prompted by neighborhood nuisance complaints over squirrel feeding. Public commenters Madeline Jones and Jean Money urged protecting trap-neuter-return (TNR) community cat feeders and backyard bird feeders, respectively, and Chelsea Cook clarified a draft ordinance would be discussed at the October 9 work session.

agenda_items.title: City Manager Contract Approval Thresholds Resolution (Superseding Resolution #9673)
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Following a September 18 work session referral, Council debated raising the City Manager's delegated contract execution thresholds across goods, construction/repair, services, and electric utility purchases. After Baker and Cook pushed to keep services at $100,000 and Mayor Williams urged $500,000 to avoid administrative bottlenecks, Council converged on a $250,000 services cap while raising the other categories to $500,000.

agenda_items.title: Local Historic Landmark Designation: The Chicken Hut (3019 Fayetteville Street)
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Planning staff Karla Rosenberg presented the Historic Preservation Commission's unanimous recommendation to designate The Chicken Hut, a historic Black-owned Durham restaurant and community gathering place, as a Local Historic Landmark. Public speakers including owner Travis Tapp and preservation advocates spoke passionately in support before Council adopted the designation ordinance.

agenda_items.title: Annexation and Zoning Map Change: Hartland Park (1021, 1105, 1213 Doc Nichols Road)
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Council held a lengthy public hearing on Ardent Building LLC's request to annex 12.999 acres and rezone from Rural Residential/Falls Jordan B to Planned Development Residential 9.001 for up to 117 townhomes inside the Urban Growth Boundary. Opponents cited Triassic clay runoff into Lick Creek and traffic congestion, while the applicant increased its affordable housing proffer from 5% to 7% (eight units at 80% AMI for 30 years) and committed to seven-day soil stabilization; the annexation and rezoning passed 4-3.

votes.item_title: Excuse Council Member DeDreana Freeman from October 9, 2025 Work Session
votes.notes: Chelsea Cook stated her voting screen lagged and verbally confirmed her Aye vote for the record.
votes.discussion_detail: Council considered a procedural priority motion to excuse Council Member DeDreana Freeman's planned absence from the October 9, 2025 work session. No objections or debate were raised on the dais regarding the request. During the electronic vote, Chelsea Cook experienced a display lag on her voting interface and explicitly asked the City Clerk to record her vote as an Aye, resulting in a unanimous 7-0 approval.

votes.item_title: Item 3A: FY25-26 Budget Ordinance Amendment (#16514) with $47,000 Museum of Durham History Floor Amendment
votes.notes: Included FY24-25 carryovers and $200,000 for Justice Matters immigrant legal defense.
votes.discussion_detail: Staff presented the annual FY24-25 carryover budget ordinance amendment along with $200,000 allocated to Justice Matters for immigrant legal defense, which Javiera Caballero had championed. Mark-Anthony Middleton moved to amend the ordinance from the floor to add $47,000 from fund balance for the Museum of Durham History, noting it represented half of the museum's $93,145 request alongside Durham County. DeDreana Freeman, Chelsea Cook, and Nate Baker voiced discomfort with adding unprinted floor appropriations without budget office documentation or standard competitive scrutiny, though all seven council members ultimately voted Aye.

votes.item_title: Item 3B: General Capital Improvement Project Ordinance FY24-25 (#16338) Carryover Amendment
votes.notes: Companion carryover capital ordinance to Item 3.
votes.discussion_detail: Immediately following the main FY25-26 operating carryover vote, Council voted on the companion FY24-25 General Capital Improvement Project Ordinance amendment (#16338). Budget staff had summarized the technical carryover accounting during the September 18 work session to align multi-year capital encumbrances. Without further debate on the dais, Council approved the ordinance unanimously 7-0.

votes.item_title: Item 3C: Equitable Greening Infrastructure (EGI) Capital Improvement Project Ordinance FY25-26
votes.notes: Companion carryover capital ordinance to Item 3.
votes.discussion_detail: Council took up the companion FY25-26 Equitable Greening Infrastructure Capital Improvement Project Ordinance as part of the Item 3 carryover package. No separate amendments or objections were raised after the main budget amendment passed. Council adopted the EGI CIP ordinance unanimously on a 7-0 electronic vote.

votes.item_title: Item 3D: Housing Capital Improvement Project Ordinance FY25-26
votes.notes: Companion housing carryover CIP ordinance to Item 3.
votes.discussion_detail: Council voted on the Housing Capital Improvement Project Ordinance for FY25-26, continuing carryover appropriations for housing capital initiatives. No members requested further discussion beyond the comments already registered under the main budget carryover item. The ordinance passed unanimously 7-0.

votes.item_title: Item 3E: Resolution Superseding #10389 Amending Internal Service Funds Financial Plan for FY25-26
votes.notes: Final companion resolution under Item 3 carryover package.
votes.discussion_detail: Council concluded its Item 3 financial actions by considering the resolution superseding Resolution #10389 to adjust Internal Service Funds financial plans for FY25-26. The measure reflected year-end carryovers for internal city operations and fleet/risk funds. It passed without objection by a unanimous 7-0 vote.

votes.item_title: Item 9: Resolution Superseding #9673 Designating City Manager Contract Approval Authority
votes.notes: After an informal 5-2 straw poll for the $250,000 services cap, all seven members voted Aye on final adoption.
votes.discussion_detail: Council debated staff's proposal to raise the City Manager's delegated contract approval limits to $500,000 across goods, construction/repair, services, and electric utility purchases, up from $300,000, $300,000, $50,000, and $100,000 respectively. Nate Baker and Chelsea Cook argued that a $500,000 services threshold would shield high-profile consulting, lobbying, and software contracts from public Council oversight, favoring $100,000 instead. Mayor Leonardo Williams countered that low thresholds bogged down agendas with routine operational extensions, while Javiera Caballero, DeDreana Freeman, and Carl Rist brokered a $250,000 compromise on services after an informal 5-2 straw poll. All seven members then voted Aye on the revised resolution.

votes.item_title: Item 17: Ordinance Designating The Chicken Hut (3019 Fayetteville Street) as a Local Historic Landmark
votes.notes: Recommended unanimously by the Historic Preservation Commission and supported by owner Travis Tapp.
votes.discussion_detail: Planning staff Karla Rosenberg presented the Historic Preservation Commission's unanimous recommendation to designate The Chicken Hut, a 0.17-acre family-owned landmark on Fayetteville Street operated since the civil rights era, as a Local Historic Landmark. Owner Travis Tapp and multiple community leaders testified about the restaurant's historic role as a Black-owned gathering hub for civic organizing, N.C. Central students, and families. Council members uniformly praised the Tapp family's legacy and historic preservation staff's work before voting 7-0 to adopt the landmark designation ordinance.

votes.item_title: Item 18A: Hartland Park Annexation Ordinance and Utility Extension Agreement (1021, 1105, 1213 Doc Nichols Road)
votes.notes: 12.999-acre site inside the Urban Growth Boundary for up to 117 townhomes by Ardent Building LLC.
votes.discussion_detail: Council held a contested public hearing on Ardent Building LLC's annexation and Utility Extension Agreement for 12.999 acres along Doc Nichols Road to construct up to 117 townhomes. Nearby residents and environmental advocates warned that steep slopes and Triassic clay soils would worsen sediment runoff into Lick Creek and Falls Lake and exacerbate traffic along Doc Nichols Road, while the developer noted the parcel sits inside the Urban Growth Boundary and raised its affordable proffer during the hearing from 5% to 7% (8 units at 80% AMI for 30 years) alongside 7-day seeding commitments. Opponents Nate Baker, DeDreana Freeman, and Chelsea Cook criticized suburban sprawl, water-quality risks, and insufficient transit connectivity, while supporters Leonardo Williams, Mark-Anthony Middleton, Javiera Caballero, and Carl Rist cited below-median-priced townhomes and infill proximity to existing utilities in passing the annexation 4-3.

votes.item_title: Item 18B: Hartland Park Zoning Map Change Ordinance (Rural Residential / Falls Jordan B to PDR 9.001)
votes.notes: Rezones 12.999 acres at 1021, 1105, and 1213 Doc Nichols Road to Planned Development Residential 9.001 Falls/Jordan District B.
votes.discussion_detail: Following passage of the Hartland Park annexation, Council voted on the companion rezoning ordinance converting the Doc Nichols Road parcels from county Rural Residential to City Planned Development Residential 9.001 within the Falls/Jordan B watershed overlay. Dissenting members Baker, Freeman, and Cook maintained that the density and clearing on erodible soils conflicted with environmental protection goals despite the applicant's 7% affordability proffer. The majority coalition of Williams, Middleton, Caballero, and Rist voted in favor, adopting the rezoning 4-3.

votes.item_title: Item 18C: Hartland Park Consistency Statement (NCGS 160D-605)
votes.notes: Statutory consistency finding required after zoning map adoption.
votes.discussion_detail: After adopting the Hartland Park zoning map amendment, Council voted on the statutory consistency statement under NCGS 160D-605 finding the rezoning aligned with the Comprehensive Plan's place type designation inside the Urban Growth Boundary. Although three members opposed the project on policy and environmental grounds, all seven members voted to adopt the consistency statement 7-0.

disagreements.meeting_title: Durham City Council October 6, 2025
disagreements.issue: Hartland Park Annexation and Rezoning (117 Townhomes on Doc Nichols Road)
disagreements.summary: Council split 4-3 over whether to annex and rezone 12.999 acres of rural-zoned Triassic clay land along Doc Nichols Road for a 117-unit townhome development.
disagreements.side_a_position: Approve Hartland Park inside the Urban Growth Boundary to deliver below-median townhomes and 7% income-restricted units.
side_a_arguments: The site sits inside the Urban Growth Boundary adjacent to existing water/sewer infrastructure and approved growth corridors.
The developer increased its proffer during the hearing from 5% to 7% (eight units at 80% AMI for 30 years) and committed to 7-day seeding.
disagreements.side_b_position: Deny the rezoning due to Lick Creek/Falls Lake watershed runoff risks, steep slopes, and auto-dependent edge expansion.
side_b_arguments: Clearing erodible Triassic basin soils risks damaging Lick Creek and downstream Falls Lake drinking water quality.
The location lacks walkable transit access and worsens traffic and infrastructure strain on Doc Nichols Road.
disagreements.resolution: Annexation and rezoning passed 4-3; consistency statement passed 7-0.

disagreements.meeting_title: Durham City Council October 6, 2025
disagreements.issue: City Manager Contract Approval Threshold for Services
disagreements.summary: Council debated how high to raise the City Manager's unilateral contract approval limit for professional services before settling on a $250,000 compromise.
disagreements.side_a_position: Raise delegated authority toward $500,000 or settle at a $250,000 compromise to improve operational efficiency.
side_a_arguments: Raising thresholds from $50,000 reflects inflation and keeps routine contract renewals from clogging regular Council agendas.
Setting services at $250,000 balances administrative speed with public oversight while raising goods and construction to $500,000.
disagreements.side_b_position: Keep the services contract approval threshold capped at $100,000 to preserve public Council scrutiny.
side_b_arguments: Services contracts often involve discretionary consultants, software, and policy vendors that warrant Council review above $100,000.
Bundling routine amendments on consent already handles administrative speed without surrendering oversight.
disagreements.resolution: After a 5-2 informal consensus for $250,000 on services, all seven members voted 7-0 to adopt the revised resolution.

disagreements.meeting_title: Durham City Council October 6, 2025
disagreements.issue: Unprinted $47,000 Floor Amendment for Museum of Durham History
disagreements.summary: Members clashed over budget transparency when a $47,000 fund-balance appropriation for the Museum of Durham History was introduced on the floor without advance written documentation.
disagreements.side_a_position: Approve the $47,000 match immediately from fund balance to support the museum's county-matched operational need.
side_a_arguments: Durham County was reviewing the matching share of a $93,145 request, and delaying could disrupt museum operations.
The item had been previewed during the September 18 work session carryover discussion.
disagreements.side_b_position: Criticize the lack of printed ordinance text, budget office review, and fair access for other nonprofits before final adoption.
side_b_arguments: Council members should not be asked to vote on unprinted mid-meeting fund-balance expenditures without formal staff memos.
Ad-hoc floor awards bypass competitive grant processes used for peer cultural nonprofits.
disagreements.resolution: Despite procedural objections, all seven members voted Aye on the amended budget ordinance (7-0).

meetings.title: Durham Joint City County Planning Committee (JCCPC) - October 1, 2025
meetings.executive_summary: The Joint City-County Planning Committee met under Chair Wendy Jacobs with City Council members Nate Baker, Mark-Anthony Middleton, and Javiera Caballero participating, unanimously approving prior minutes, the 2026 meeting schedule, and an excused absence for Commissioner Valentine. Staff presented the Comprehensive Plan Community Goals and Objectives Report Card, 78 Evaluation and Appraisal Report (EAR) policy and place-type map amendments, and draft New UDO public art incentives and Module 3 environmental/street standards, while postponing the Housing Initiative Task Force report to November.

agenda_items.title: Procedural Opening and Approval of September 3, 2025 Minutes
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Chair Wendy Jacobs called the meeting to order and announced that Item 5 (Durham Housing Initiative Task Force Report) was postponed to November due to a scheduling conflict. The committee approved the September 3, 2025 minutes unanimously on a motion by Nate Baker and second by Mark-Anthony Middleton.

agenda_items.title: Comprehensive Plan Community Goals and Objectives Report Card
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Planning staff presented the annual Comprehensive Plan Report Card tracking eight equity-oriented indicators across housing, transportation, tree canopy, and community engagement, noting a new collaboration with Durham Public Schools to track school capacity indicators. Javiera Caballero joined the meeting early during the presentation, and members discussed how indicator data informs capital priorities and UDO drafting.

agenda_items.title: Comprehensive Plan Evaluation and Appraisal Report (EAR): Place Type Map and 78 Policy Amendments
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Staff reviewed proposed updates to the Place Type Map and 78 Comprehensive Plan policy edits arising from the annual EAR review. Committee members scrutinized the implications of designating privately owned parcels as Open Space and flagged preemption risks in phrasing that merely 'encourages' rather than incentivizes environmental or affordable-housing outcomes.

agenda_items.title: New Unified Development Ordinance (UDO): Public Art Regulations and Incentives
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Planning and Cultural & Public Art staff presented proposed New UDO public art standards and density/design incentives for private developments. Committee members asked how public art commitments would be maintained over time and coordinated with neighborhood character.

agenda_items.title: New Unified Development Ordinance (UDO) Module 3: Natural Resources, Streets, and Open Space
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Staff and consultants walked through New UDO Module 3 standards covering NACTO street cross-sections, Neuse and Jordan riparian buffer protections, 3:1 steep-slope stabilization rules for Triassic clay soils, Piedmont Prairie preservation, 7% to 22% tree coverage tiers, and 30% open space standards. Members probed potential overlaps between tree protection, open space, and transit corridor density.

agenda_items.title: 2026 JCCPC Meeting Schedule, Excused Absence, and RV Parking Text Amendment Discussion
agenda_items.discussion_summary: The committee adopted its 2026 meeting calendar (omitting July) and formally excused Commissioner Valentine's absence. At the close of the meeting, members held a brief informational discussion regarding a potential recreational vehicle (RV) parking text amendment.
agenda_items.vote_summary: 2026 Schedule and Excused Absence Approved unanimously (Voice Votes)

votes.item_title: Approve September 3, 2025 JCCPC Meeting Minutes
votes.notes: Javiera Caballero joined shortly after opening during Item 6; Commissioner Valentine was absent.
votes.discussion_detail: Chair Wendy Jacobs opened the October 1 JCCPC meeting and noted that the Durham Housing Initiative Task Force presentation would move to the November agenda. Council Member and JCCPC Vice Chair Nate Baker moved to approve the September 3, 2025 meeting minutes, seconded by Mark-Anthony Middleton. With no corrections requested, the committee approved the minutes unanimously by voice vote.

votes.item_title: Adopt 2026 JCCPC Meeting Schedule (Omitting July)
votes.notes: Calendar keeps regular monthly JCCPC meetings while omitting a July 2026 session.
votes.discussion_detail: Staff presented the proposed 2026 Joint City-County Planning Committee meeting schedule, retaining monthly meetings with a summer recess in July consistent with Council and County Board schedules. Mark-Anthony Middleton moved to adopt the 2026 schedule, and Javiera Caballero seconded the motion. The committee adopted the schedule unanimously by voice vote without objection.

votes.item_title: Excuse Commissioner Valentine from October 1, 2025 JCCPC Meeting
votes.notes: Procedural motion excusing Durham County Commissioner Valentine's absence.
votes.discussion_detail: Before concluding the meeting, Chair Wendy Jacobs invited a motion to formally excuse Commissioner Valentine's absence from the October 1 JCCPC session. Javiera Caballero moved to excuse Commissioner Valentine and Mark-Anthony Middleton seconded. The motion passed unanimously by voice vote.

meetings.title: Durham City Council Work Session September 18, 2025
meetings.executive_summary: Presided over initially by Mayor Pro Tem Mark-Anthony Middleton before Mayor Leonardo Williams arrived, Council suspended rules to approve a $52,202.50 Box.com digital plan review contract and finalized the October 6 regular meeting agenda. Major substantive debates centered on raising City Manager contract approval limits (referred to GBA for October 6), developing a wildlife feeding ordinance, and Council Member Chelsea Cook's proposed tenant rent-withholding ordinance for unfit housing, which City Attorney Kim Rehberg warned faces state statutory preemption.

agenda_items.title: Suspend Rules and Approve Service Contract with Box, Inc. for Digital Plan Review
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Planning and Technology staff requested immediate work-session action to avoid a lapse in Box.com cloud file-sharing licenses used for digital development plan submittals before moving to a new permitting system. Council voted unanimously to suspend the rules and authorize the one-year $52,202.50 contract.
agenda_items.vote_summary: Rules Suspended unanimously; Contract Approved unanimously

agenda_items.title: FY24-25 Carryovers and FY25-26 Budget Ordinance Amendment Review
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Budget staff previewed FY24-25 carryover appropriations for the October 6 regular agenda, including $200,000 for Justice Matters immigrant legal representation and an anticipated ~$50,000 request for the Museum of Durham History. Council members asked clarifying questions about carryover balances and nonprofit funding requests.

agenda_items.title: City Manager Contract Approval Authority Thresholds
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Council debated staff's draft resolution raising the City Manager's contract approval authority to $500,000 across goods, construction, services, and utilities. Members disagreed over whether services contracts should stay capped at $100,000-$250,000 and placed Item 9 on the October 6 General Business Agenda for formal action.
agenda_items.vote_summary: Moved to October 6 General Business Agenda

agenda_items.title: Wildlife Feeding Staff Report and Draft Ordinance Direction
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Neighborhood Improvement Services presented options regarding nuisance wildlife feeding complaints originating from Trotter Ridge. Council directed staff to draft a tailored ordinance for October 9 discussion while avoiding unintended penalties on songbird feeders and managed community cat caretakers.
agenda_items.vote_summary: Directed staff to prepare draft ordinance

agenda_items.title: Proposed Unfit Housing / Tenant Rent Withholding Ordinance (Sec. 10-241)
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Chelsea Cook presented a draft tenant protection ordinance modeled on Charlotte's Section 11-45 prohibiting landlords from collecting rent on code-violating unfit dwellings, drawing strong support from Riverside High School students, Legal Aid advocate Jack Holtzman, and Durham tenants. City Attorney Kim Rehberg and Assistant City Attorney Sophia Hernandez warned that North Carolina's Landlord-Tenant Act likely preempts municipal rent withholding and offered two legally defensible enforcement alternatives, prompting a sharp procedural split over pausing until the next work session.
agenda_items.vote_summary: Continued to next Work Session for alternative legal drafts

agenda_items.title: South Ellerbe Creek Wetland Restoration Project Update
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Stormwater staff briefed Council on the $41 million South Ellerbe wetland project, explaining plans to split construction into Phases 3A and 3B toward an anticipated 2028 completion. Members reviewed soil remediation costs and flood-reduction milestones.

agenda_items.title: Settle October 6, 2025 Regular City Council Meeting Agenda
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Council settled the October 6 regular agenda, placing Items 1-8, 10-12, 14-16, 19, and 21 on Consent, moving Item 9 (City Manager contract limits) to the General Business Agenda, and confirming Public Hearings for Items 17 and 18.

votes.item_title: Suspend Rules to Take Immediate Action on Item 13 (Box.com Digital Plan Review Contract)
votes.notes: DeDreana Freeman and Mayor Leonardo Williams arrived later in the work session.
votes.discussion_detail: At the start of the work session, staff requested urgent action on Item 13 so digital plan review file-sharing subscriptions with Box, Inc. would not expire before the October 6 regular meeting. Under Council rules, taking final contractual action at a work session requires suspending the rules. With Mayor Leonardo Williams and DeDreana Freeman not yet arrived, the five seated members voted unanimously by voice vote to suspend the rules.

votes.item_title: Item 13: Authorize One-Year Service Contract with Box, Inc. (NTE $52,202.50)
votes.notes: Maintains digital development plan intake and review workflow during software transition.
votes.discussion_detail: Staff explained that the $52,202.50 one-year contract with Box, Inc. covers essential cloud storage and plan-review intake licenses while the City transitions toward an integrated permitting platform. Council members confirmed the short duration avoided multi-year lock-in and asked brief operational questions about file migration timelines. The five present members voted unanimously by voice vote to authorize the contract.

votes.item_title: Settle October 6, 2025 Regular City Council Meeting Agenda
votes.notes: Consent: Items 1-8, 10-12, 14-16, 19, 21; General Business Agenda: Item 9; Public Hearings: Items 17 and 18.
votes.discussion_detail: After completing presentations and discussion on Item 20, the Mayor and full Council finalized the agenda structure for the October 6, 2025 regular meeting. Members agreed to move Item 9 (City Manager contract thresholds) to the General Business Agenda for public debate and final vote while placing the remaining routine items on Consent and retaining Items 17 and 18 as Public Hearings. The settled agenda passed unanimously by voice vote.

disagreements.meeting_title: Durham City Council Work Session September 18, 2025
disagreements.issue: Proposed Unfit Housing Rent-Withholding Ordinance (Sec. 10-241)
disagreements.summary: Council divided over advancing Chelsea Cook's Charlotte-modeled rent-withholding ordinance immediately versus pausing for City Attorney alternatives due to North Carolina statutory preemption risks.
disagreements.side_a_position: Advance strong tenant rent-withholding protections immediately or keep pressure on slumlords despite litigation risk.
side_a_arguments: Charlotte has maintained a similar ordinance on the books, and Durham tenants facing unaddressed habitability failures need immediate relief.
Delaying for another work session stalls momentum built by Riverside High students, Legal Aid, and tenant unions.
disagreements.side_b_position: Hold for two weeks so the City Attorney can draft legally enforceable local alternatives under North Carolina law.
side_b_arguments: State Landlord-Tenant statutes likely preempt municipal ordinances altering private lease rent obligations, risking invalidation in court.
Enacting unenforceable remedies could mislead vulnerable tenants into nonpayment evictions rather than delivering real code enforcement.
disagreements.resolution: Council directed the City Attorney's Office to return at the next work session with two legally vetted code-enforcement and tenant-relief alternatives.

disagreements.meeting_title: Durham City Council Work Session September 18, 2025
disagreements.issue: City Manager Contract Approval Authority Thresholds
disagreements.summary: Council split during the work-session preview on whether raising the Manager's services contract signing limit to $500,000 overly curtails Council transparency.
disagreements.side_a_position: Raise delegated authority across goods, construction, utilities, and services to reduce agenda friction.
side_a_arguments: Outdated $50,000 limits force routine operational renewals and minor change orders onto Council agendas.
Peer North Carolina cities grant higher administrative procurement authority to city managers.
disagreements.side_b_position: Keep professional services contracts capped lower (around $100,000-$250,000) to preserve public visibility.
side_b_arguments: High-dollar consulting and services contracts raise policy questions that residents expect elected officials to review in public.
Goods and construction bids are more standardized than discretionary service contracts.
disagreements.resolution: Placed on the October 6 General Business Agenda for formal vote (ultimately settled at a $250,000 services cap).

meetings.title: Durham City Council Work Session - Strategic Plan Visioning Workshop September 18, 2025
meetings.executive_summary: Mayor Leonardo Williams, City Manager Bo Ferguson, staff, and Fountain Works consultants facilitated a three-hour Strategic Plan Visioning Workshop for FY27-29 with all seven Council members ultimately participating. No formal votes were taken as members debated whether to elevate Affordable Housing and Climate/Environment to standalone strategic goals and whether to merge or keep separate the outward community engagement goal and the internal high-performing organization goal, concluding with direction for staff to synthesize alternative goal frameworks.

agenda_items.title: FY27-29 Strategic Plan Refresh Architecture and Gallery Walk Review

agenda_items.title: Shared Economic Prosperity and Wealth-Building Goal Alignment

agenda_items.title: Community Engagement vs. Internal Organizational Excellence Goal Structure

disagreements.meeting_title: Durham City Council Work Session - Strategic Plan Visioning Workshop September 18, 2025
disagreements.issue: Standalone Affordable Housing and Climate Goals vs. Existing Five-Goal Structure
disagreements.summary: Council members diverged on whether affordable housing and climate change should become standalone top-level strategic plan goals or remain distinct priorities within a concise five-goal framework.
disagreements.side_a_position: Elevate Affordable Housing (and environmental/climate goals) to standalone top-level strategic goals.
side_a_arguments: Durham's housing affordability crisis is Council's foremost public priority and deserves explicit top-line visibility rather than sitting inside a broad built-environment goal.
Elevating housing makes performance metrics and budget alignment clearer to residents.
disagreements.side_b_position: Keep the concise five-goal structure while establishing Affordable Housing as a prominent priority under 'Vibrant Built and Natural Environment.'
side_b_arguments: Expanding beyond five top-level goals dilutes strategic focus and fragments cross-cutting linkages between land use, transit, and housing.
Maintaining housing alongside climate and infrastructure inside a single built-environment goal mirrors comprehensive planning.
disagreements.resolution: No formal vote taken; consultants and staff were directed to draft synthesized options for a follow-up session.

disagreements.meeting_title: Durham City Council Work Session - Strategic Plan Visioning Workshop September 18, 2025
disagreements.issue: Separating vs. Merging Community Engagement and High-Performing Organization Goals
disagreements.summary: Council disagreed over whether internal municipal workforce and operational excellence should remain a standalone strategic goal separate from outward-facing community engagement and equity.
disagreements.side_a_position: Keep 'Innovative and High-Performing Organization' separate from 'Connected, Engaged, and Inclusive Communities.'
side_a_arguments: Internal operations, employee support for Durham's 2,600 staff, and fiscal stewardship require dedicated focus separate from community engagement programs like participatory budgeting.

disagreements.side_b_position: Streamline and merge overlapping civic engagement and high-performing service delivery themes.
side_b_arguments: Every goal should center resident outcomes rather than treating city government operations as an isolated inward bucket.
Reducing redundant goal categories sharpens strategic measurement across departments.
disagreements.resolution: Deferred without consensus; staff tasked with returning revised options before launching public engagement.

meetings.title: Durham City Council September 15, 2025
meetings.executive_summary: With all seven Council members present, Mayor Leonardo Williams opened the regular meeting with proclamations for Welcoming Week, Constitution/Resident Involvement Week, and World Alzheimer's Day, followed by extended remarks addressing community gun violence and clarifying free-speech boundaries around Police Chief Patrice Andrews's personal social media post. agenda_items.title: Proclamations and Extended Council Remarks on Safety and Chief Andrews Social Media Post

During Council announcements, members extended condolences over recent gun violence and a fatal youth hit-and-run, highlighted Vanguard and Liberty Street groundbreakings, and Mayor Williams addressed public reaction to Police Chief Patrice Andrews's social media post regarding Charlie Kirk while clarifying the Police Chief reports to the City Manager rather than Council.

meetings.title: Durham City Council Work Session September 4, 2025
meetings.executive_summary: Mayor Pro Tem Mark-Anthony Middleton presided over the work session (joined midway by Mayor Leonardo Williams), settling the September 15 regular agenda unanimously while hearing major briefings on FY24-25 Q4 finances and the Western Intake Partnership water plant, where partner pullouts leave Durham leading Phase 1 ($700M+ total program) toward a 2031 launch. Public speaker Dale McKiel exposed flawed CIP Stoplight reporting showing stalled Third Fork Creek, R. Kelly Bryant Bridge, and Rail Trail projects as 'Green,' prompting staff pledges to overhaul Q1 FY26 tracking, while Chelsea Cook clashed with colleagues over accelerating an affordable-housing update on 505 W. Chapel Hill St. and initiated a wildlife feeding ordinance.

agenda_items.title: Clerk Report on Board Appointments and Moving Item 1 (DHA) to General Business Agenda
agenda_items.discussion_summary: The City Clerk flagged non-residency allegations raised against two Durham Housing Authority nominees including Angela R. Holmes, prompting Council to move Item 1 to the September 15 General Business Agenda for verification. Chelsea Cook and DeDreana Freeman cautioned against airing unvetted residency allegations about residents on the public record.
agenda_items.vote_summary: Moved Item 1 to General Business Agenda

agenda_items.title: Pulled Consent Review: Museum of Durham History, Eno-Haw Hazard Mitigation, East End/Long Meadow Parks CMAR, and Eckerd Connects
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Council reviewed pulled consent items including Museum of Durham History support, the Eno-Haw Regional Hazard Mitigation Plan presented by Nate Sanders, the Balfour Beatty/Holt Brothers CMAR contract for East End and Long Meadow Parks (where Wade Walcott explained Long Meadow will start first pending NCDEQ East End lead testing by end of 2025), and Carl Rist's request for measurable performance metrics in Eckerd Connects's NCWorks Career Center statement of work.

agenda_items.title: FY24-25 Q4 Financial Report and CIP Stoplight Report Accuracy Critique
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Budget Director Christina Reirden and Finance Director Tim Flora reported projected FY24-25 General Fund expenditures of $304.9M ($14.8M under budget) against $295M in revenue (drawing roughly $9.4M-$9.5M from fund balance while keeping ~$60M in reserve above the 16.7% policy floor). Resident Dale McKiel exposed major inaccuracies in the CIP Stoplight Report showing multi-year delayed projects (Third Fork Creek Phase II, R. Kelly Bryant Bridge, Durham Rail Trail) marked Green, leading staff JJ Scott and Henry Prosper to commit to an overhauled Q1 FY26 tracker and Council to demand tougher NCDOT escalation.

agenda_items.title: Western Intake Partnership Regional Water Supply Project Update
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Water Management Director Don Greeley, Sid Miller, and HDR consultant Jeff Atkins briefed Council that OWASA opted out of Phase 1 and Chatham/Pittsboro merged with Sanford's TriRiver Water (considering only 1 MGD), leaving Durham largely carrying Phase 1 of the 20 MGD Jordan Lake plant (scalable to 77 MGD) targeting a 2031 online date. Estimated costs include roughly $500M for the treatment plant, $136M for the intake, $73M for internal pipelines, $4M+ for land, and $4.7M to mitigate a three-year closure at Vista Point Park.

agenda_items.title: Other Matters: 505 W. Chapel Hill St. Redevelopment Timeline and Wildlife Feeding Ordinance
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Council debated Chelsea Cook's request for an October 9 interim update to partition 505 W. Chapel Hill St. for affordable housing versus keeping the scheduled November 20 comprehensive briefing, while Mayor Williams asked to preserve historic-site coordination with Preservation NC. agenda_items.vote_summary: Kept Nov. 20 target for 505 W. Chapel Hill; directed wildlife feeding report

meetings.title: Durham Joint City County Planning Committee (JCCPC) - September 3, 2025

agenda_items.title: Opening Roll Call and Approval of August 6, 2025 Minutes
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Chair Wendy Jacobs opened the session and invited approval of the August 6, 2025 JCCPC minutes, which passed unanimously on a motion by Nate Baker and second by Commissioner Valentine. agenda_items.title: New UDO Affordable Housing Density Bonus and Case-Study Program Review

votes.item_title: Approve August 6, 2025 JCCPC Meeting Minutes

votes.discussion_detail: Chair Wendy Jacobs opened the September 3 JCCPC session and called for approval of the August 6, 2025 meeting minutes. City Council member Nate Baker moved approval and County Commissioner Valentine seconded the motion. disagreements.meeting_title: Durham Joint City County Planning Committee (JCCPC) - September 3, 2025
disagreements.issue: New UDO Affordable Housing Density Bonus Design (Deep 30% AMI Subsidies vs. Broader 70%-80% AMI By-Right Bonuses)
disagreements.summary: JCCPC members debated how the New UDO's affordable housing density bonus should balance modest by-right incentives at 70%-80% AMI against deeper affordability targets at 30% AMI that typically require direct public subsidy.
disagreements.side_a_position: Focus zoning bonuses on feasible market-driven thresholds (e.g., 60%-80% AMI or Austin-style 100% affordable by-right deregulation) paired with fee-in-lieu flexibility.
side_a_arguments: By-right zoning bonuses cannot mathematically cross-subsidize 30% AMI units without LIHTC or local bond dollars, so overly steep rules go unused.
Austin's 'Affordability Unlocked' model proves stripping height, parking, and setback barriers unlocks significantly more subsidized supply.
disagreements.side_b_position: Guard against eroding resident leverage and ensure density bonuses deliver meaningful deeply affordable units and neighborhood benefits.
side_b_arguments: Durham's greatest unmet shortage is for households at 30%-50% AMI, which developers routinely skip when bonuses stop at 80% AMI.
Giving away extra height and density by-right without calibrated requirements risks upzoning land values without proportionate community benefit.
disagreements.resolution: Informational workshop only; consultants and planning staff recorded committee feedback to calibrate draft UDO housing incentives.

Directing the City Manager to enforce constitutional warrant standards on City premises and assess staff training needs, the resolution passed unanimously 6-0.

agenda_items.title: Public Hearing: Courtyards at Oak Grove Annexation and Rezoning (1502 Doc Nichols Rd & Kinard Rd)
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Council reviewed Epcon Communities's 22.54-acre proposal for 67 single-family homes and townhomes, including an $80,000 Dedicated Housing Fund contribution and $10,500 for Durham Public Schools. Responding to watershed concerns, the applicant lowered its maximum impervious surface proffer from 70% to 50%, and Council approved annexation, PDR 2.988 zoning, and consistency 6-0.

agenda_items.title: Public Hearing: Durham Gateway at Brier Creek Annexation and Rezoning (308.38 Acres, US 70 / Leesville Rd)
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Council held a two-hour public hearing on Beacon Partners and HM Partners's 308.38-acre industrial and residential project spanning Durham and Wake counties, featuring 1.28M sq. ft. of industrial space, up to 1,750 homes, $39.5M in private infrastructure, a 7-acre donation for 175 units at 80% AMI plus $1M Housing Fund, and $350,000 for Fire/EMS. After rejecting a Planning Commission denial recommendation and Nate Baker and Chelsea Cook's call to remand for design revisions, Council passed annexation 4-2 before approving the IL(D)/PDR 10.649 zoning and consistency statement 6-0.

votes.item_title: Excuse Council Member DeDreana Freeman from September 2, 2025 Meeting
votes.notes: DeDreana Freeman was absent and excused.
votes.discussion_detail: Mayor Leonardo Williams opened the September 2 regular Council meeting and introduced a priority procedural motion to excuse Council Member DeDreana Freeman's absence. No objections were voiced by the six seated Council members. The excusal motion passed unanimously 6-0.

votes.item_title: Item 20A: East Durham Water, Sewer, and Stormwater Phase 1A Contract with Moffett Pipe Inc. (NTE $10,648,571.40)
votes.notes: Pulled by Nate Baker solely to read a community thank-you letter regarding 'The Branch' stream improvements.
votes.discussion_detail: Council Member Nate Baker pulled Item 20 from consent to share a message of appreciation from Grant Street neighborhood residents recognizing the City's $400,000 stormwater and stream restoration investment known as 'The Branch.' No concerns were raised regarding the contractor, Moffett Pipe Inc., or the scope of East Durham water and sewer infrastructure upgrades. Council voted unanimously 6-0 to authorize the $10,648,571.40 construction contract.

votes.item_title: Item 20B: Establish East Durham Water/Sewer/Stormwater Phase 1A Contingency Fund ($1,018,978)
votes.notes: Companion contingency for Moffett Pipe Inc. contract.
votes.discussion_detail: Immediately following the base utility construction contract approval, Council voted on establishing the $1,018,978 project contingency fund for East Durham Phase 1A infrastructure work. No further remarks were requested on the dais. The motion passed unanimously 6-0.

votes.item_title: Item 20C: Authorize Modifications for East Durham Phase 1A Contract (Total NTE $11,757,549.40)
votes.notes: Sets total not-to-exceed modification cap including contingency.
votes.discussion_detail: Concluding Item 20, Council considered the companion authorization permitting the City Manager to execute change orders and contract modifications up to $11,757,549.40 for East Durham Phase 1A utility improvements. All six members present voted Aye, passing the motion 6-0.

votes.item_title: Item 4 (GBA): Appoint Juan P. Montes to Durham Planning Commission
votes.notes: Term expiring June 30, 2027; followed majority paper-ballot selection.
votes.discussion_detail: Because Council had deadlocked on Planning Commission nominees at the August 21 work session, Item 4 was resolved via General Business Agenda paper-ballot selection. The City Clerk tallied the written ballots and announced Juan P. Montes had secured a majority. Council then cast a formal electronic confirmation vote appointing Montes unanimously 6-0 for a term through June 30, 2027.

votes.item_title: Item 26: Adopt Fourth Amendment Workplace Resolution
votes.notes: Presented in English and Spanish with community coalition partners Siembra NC, Durham Workers Rights Commission, Durham CAN, and UE Local 150.
votes.discussion_detail: Moved forward from the bottom of the agenda to accommodate waiting residents, Javiera Caballero presented the Fourth Amendment Workplace Resolution affirming that City workplaces uphold constitutional protections requiring judicial warrants for non-public federal immigration enforcement searches. Representatives from Siembra NC, Durham Workers Rights Commission, Durham CAN, and UE Local 150 spoke in strong support, and the resolution text was read in both English and Spanish. Council members praised the collaborative worker-protection effort and adopted the resolution unanimously 6-0.

votes.item_title: Item 24A: Courtyards at Oak Grove Annexation Ordinance and UEA (1502 Doc Nichols Rd & 6102/6124/6202 Kinard Rd)
votes.notes: 22.54 acres for 67 Epcon Communities homes/townhomes, $80,000 Housing Fund proffer, and $10,500 DPS contribution.
votes.discussion_detail: Council held a public hearing on Epcon Communities's 22.54-acre project for 67 residential units at Doc Nichols and Kinard roads, backed by an $80,000 Dedicated Housing Fund contribution and $10,500 for Durham Public Schools. Responding to council and environmental questions about Falls/Jordan watershed runoff, the applicant's representative voluntarily lowered the maximum impervious surface proffer on the record from 70% to 50%. Satisfied with that concession and the modest density, all six members voted 6-0 to approve annexation and the utility extension agreement.

votes.item_title: Item 24B: Courtyards at Oak Grove Zoning Map Change (RR / Falls Jordan B to PDR 2.988)
votes.notes: Rezones 22.54 acres to Planned Development Residential 2.988 Falls/Jordan District B.
votes.discussion_detail: Following the annexation vote for Courtyards at Oak Grove, Council voted on the companion zoning map change from county Rural Residential to City Planned Development Residential 2.988 inside the Falls/Jordan B watershed overlay. With the newly committed 50% impervious limit incorporated into the text commitments, no opposition remained on the dais. Council passed the rezoning unanimously 6-0.

votes.item_title: Item 24C: Courtyards at Oak Grove Consistency Statement (NCGS 160D-605)
votes.notes: Statutory consistency finding for Item 24.
votes.discussion_detail: After approving the Courtyards at Oak Grove rezoning, Council adopted the required NCGS 160D-605 statement confirming the map change's alignment with the Comprehensive Plan. No additional discussion was needed. The statement passed unanimously 6-0.

votes.item_title: Item 25A: Durham Gateway at Brier Creek Annexation Ordinance and UEA (308.38 Acres, US 70 / Leesville Rd)
votes.notes: Planning Commission had recommended denial; Nate Baker and Chelsea Cook sought remand to Planning Commission, while Carl Rist called the question.
votes.discussion_detail: Beacon Partners and HM Partners, represented by attorney Jamie Schwedler, sought annexation and mixed-use/industrial zoning for 308.38 acres at US 70 and Leesville Road proposing 1.28M sq. ft. of light industrial space, up to 1,750 homes, 150,000 sq. ft. of retail, $39.5M in private road and utility infrastructure, a 7-acre donation valued at $2.5M for 175 affordable units at 80% AMI, $1M for the Dedicated Housing Fund, and $350,000 for Fire/EMS. Although neighboring HOAs testified in support due to buffer and stormwater concessions, Nate Baker and Chelsea Cook urged remanding the case to the Planning Commission to ban big-box retail, strengthen walkability and parks, and ensure 4% LIHTC certainty. Majority members Williams, Middleton, Caballero, and Rist argued the infrastructure, flood mitigation, and $3.5M housing value merited approval now, passing the annexation 4-2 after Rist called the question.

votes.item_title: Item 25B: Durham Gateway at Brier Creek Zoning Map Change (to IL(D) and PDR 10.649)
votes.notes: After voting Nay on the 4-2 annexation, Nate Baker and Chelsea Cook both voted Aye on the zoning ordinance itself.
votes.discussion_detail: Immediately after the 4-2 annexation passage, Council voted on the companion zoning ordinance establishing Industrial Light with Development Plan (IL(D)) and Planned Development Residential 10.649 across the 308.38-acre Durham Gateway site, incorporating 100-year residential storm detention, submerged gravel wetlands, and a 75-foot Stuart buffer. Once annexation had already carried by a four-vote majority, Nate Baker and Chelsea Cook joined the four annexation supporters on the zoning vote. The zoning ordinance passed 6-0.

votes.item_title: Item 25C: Durham Gateway at Brier Creek Consistency Statement (NCGS 160D-605)
votes.notes: Statutory consistency finding for Item 25.
votes.discussion_detail: Council concluded Item 25 by voting on the statutory NCGS 160D-605 consistency statement evaluating the Durham Gateway at Brier Creek rezoning against the Comprehensive Plan. All six present Council members voted in favor, adopting the statement 6-0.

disagreements.meeting_title: Durham City Council September 2, 2025
disagreements.issue: Durham Gateway at Brier Creek Annexation and Planning Commission Remand
disagreements.summary: Council split 4-2 on annexing the 308-acre Durham Gateway at Brier Creek development and clashed over whether to send the application back to the Planning Commission following its denial recommendation.
disagreements.side_a_position: Approve annexation and zoning without further delay to secure $39.5M in infrastructure, enhanced stormwater controls, and $3.5M in affordable housing value.
side_a_arguments: The developer secured unprecedented support from surrounding neighborhood associations by committing to 100-year storm detention, a 75-foot buffer, and $39.5M in self-funded roads and utilities.
Donating 7 free acres valued at $2.5M plus $1M in cash and $350,000 for Fire/EMS delivers substantial public benefit that could unravel if delayed.
disagreements.side_b_position: Remand the proposal to the Planning Commission and oppose annexation unless stricter urban design, anti-big-box, park, and LIHTC commitments are locked in.
side_b_arguments: The Planning Commission recommended denial, and major site plan deficiencies around walkability, public parkland, and unconditioned commercial formats remain unresolved.
Relying on 4% LIHTC timing for the 175 donated-land units creates execution risk if tax credits are delayed.
disagreements.resolution: Annexation passed 4-2; Baker and Cook subsequently joined the majority in passing the zoning ordinance and consistency statement 6-0.

meetings.title: Durham City Council Work Session August 21, 2025
meetings.executive_summary: With six members present (Mark-Anthony Middleton excused), Mayor Leonardo Williams led Council in approving a closed session on EEOC litigation, receiving City Manager priority updates, and finalizing the September 2 regular agenda. Highlights included Chief Patrice Andrews's Q2 Crime Report showing violent crime down ~20% and staffing rising to 75.2%, Durham Next's Reimagine Durham Freeway Study (favoring Boulevard or Cap concepts over status-quo modernization), and policy debates over recurring non-competitive nonprofit funding (El Centro Hispano), unfit housing rent withholding, and December 2025 swearing-in timing.

agenda_items.title: Closed Session Motion (EEOC Charge Delphia Cruz v. City of Durham) and City Manager Priority Items
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Senior Deputy City Attorney Fred Lamar requested a closed session under NCGS 143-318.11(a)(3) regarding EEOC Charge #433-2025-01026 (Delphia Cruz v. City of Durham) to be held at the end of the session, and DCM Bertha Winbush asked to present the Q2 Crime Report today and discuss the December 2025 organizational meeting under Other Matters. Both procedural motions passed 6-0.

agenda_items.title: Board Nominations and Public Comment (UDO Hearings and Youth Safety)
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Council reached consensus on nominees for Racial Equity, Workforce Development, Citizens Advisory, Historic Preservation, and Environmental Affairs boards (after Chelsea Cook shifted to establish a four-vote consensus for David Baron on EAB), while a three-way split sent the Planning Commission appointment to the General Business Agenda. Public commenters Katie Ross (citing Barefoot v. County of Durham on UDO hearings) and DeWarren Langley (urging investments in boys and men of color) addressed Council.

agenda_items.title: Pulled Consent Review: El Centro Hispano, Crisis Comms ILA, Brinks, InfoSend, HUD Action Plan, Eckerd Connects, and ParkDurham
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Members reviewed pulled consent contracts and debated equity in recurring non-competitive nonprofit grants under Item 7 (El Centro Hispano), requesting Budget Director Christina Reirden compile a full list of city-funded nonprofits. Transportation staff also detailed ParkDurham's upcoming Apple Pay fix, DPAC gate-lifting, and a tripled $35/month 80% AMI employee parking program (~75 permits).

agenda_items.title: FY27-29 Strategic Plan Refresh Briefing
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Strategic Initiatives staff Sherri Metcalf, Andrew Holland, Cecily Hamilton, and ICMA fellow Jesse Wren previewed the structure and engagement timeline for the September 18 Strategic Plan Visioning Workshop.

agenda_items.title: Q2 2025 Crime Report and Police Staffing Update
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Police Chief Patrice Andrews reported violent crime fell roughly 20% in Q2 2025 (with aggravated assaults at a 10-year low, persons shot down 33.6%, and property crime down 4%), alongside 44 federal case adoptions and sworn staffing climbing to 75.2% (401 of 533 positions plus 38 incoming recruits). Council discussed stolen guns from unlocked vehicles, youth prevention, avoiding neighborhood stigmatization, and protecting local policing autonomy.
agenda_items.vote_summary: Informational / Kept on September 2 Consent Agenda

agenda_items.title: Reimagine Durham Freeway Study Presentation
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Evian Patterson, Aaron Convery, and Durham Next's Tara Kenchin presented three concepts for NC 147: Modernization ($350M, reclaiming 14 acres), Boulevard Conversion ($450M, reclaiming 20-22 acres with the highest equity score), and Freeway Caps ($450M-$800M+, reclaiming 3-25 acres). Council members broadly favored advancing transformative Boulevard or Cap concepts backed by economic-impact modeling and community land trust exploration.

agenda_items.title: Other Matters: Rent Withholding, Fourth Amendment Resolution, Dec. 2025 Swearing-In, and Sept. 2 Agenda
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Council directed legal and neighborhood staff to research Charlotte's rent-withholding ordinance for September 18, added Javiera Caballero's Fourth Amendment Workplace Resolution to the September 2 agenda, and debated timing for the December 2025 post-election organizational meeting (deferred pending County election certification timelines) before adopting the September 2 regular agenda.

votes.item_title: Closed Session Motion: Attorney-Client Consultation on EEOC Charge #433-2025-01026 (Delphia Cruz v. City of Durham)
votes.notes: Mark-Anthony Middleton was excused absent; closed session scheduled to convene at the end of the work session under NCGS 143-318.11(a)(3).
votes.discussion_detail: Senior Deputy City Attorney Fred Lamar requested a closed session pursuant to North Carolina General Statutes 143-318.11(a)(3) so Council could consult with legal counsel regarding EEOC Charge #433-2025-01026, Delphia Cruz v. City of Durham. Mayor Leonardo Williams noted the closed session would convene following the public business items at the end of the meeting. With Mark-Anthony Middleton excused absent, all six present members approved the closed session unanimously by voice vote.

votes.item_title: Receive City Manager Priority Items (Item 18 Crime Report and Dec. 2025 Organizational Meeting)
votes.notes: Placed Q2 Crime Report presentation on the Aug. 21 agenda and added Dec. 2025 swearing-in schedule discussion to Other Matters.
votes.discussion_detail: Deputy City Manager Bertha Winbush presented two administrative agenda requests from the City Manager's Office: advancing Item 18 (Q2 2025 Crime Report) for presentation during the work session and placing a scheduling discussion for the December 2025 post-election organizational meeting under Other Matters. Council raised no objections to accommodating both items. The six members present approved the priority additions unanimously by voice vote.

votes.item_title: Settle September 2, 2025 Regular City Council Meeting Agenda
votes.notes: Consent: Items 1-3, 5-21; General Business Agenda: Item 4; Public Hearings: Items 24 and 25.
votes.discussion_detail: Before entering closed session, Council voted to finalize the September 2, 2025 regular meeting docket. Items 1-3 and 5-21 were assigned to the Consent Agenda, the three-way-split Planning Commission appointment (Item 4) was placed on the General Business Agenda, Items 24 and 25 remained scheduled Public Hearings, and Javiera Caballero's Fourth Amendment Workplace Resolution was added as Item 26. All six present members approved the settled agenda unanimously by voice vote.

disagreements.meeting_title: Durham City Council Work Session August 21, 2025
disagreements.issue: Recurring Non-Competitive Nonprofit Contracts vs. Competitive Grant Equity (El Centro Hispano)
disagreements.summary: Council members debated whether continuing recurring annual contracts for organizations added via prior budget amendments (such as El Centro Hispano) undermines fairness for nonprofits competing in open RFP cycles.
disagreements.side_a_position: Scrutinize recurring direct-award nonprofit contracts and transition toward transparent competitive funding criteria.
side_a_arguments: Rolling over past council-earmarked awards year after year creates an uneven playing field against peer community organizations.
Council needs a comprehensive inventory of all recurring nonprofit contracts to ensure equitable evaluation.
disagreements.side_b_position: Maintain continuity for established core service partners that deliver critical bilingual and community navigation services.
side_b_arguments: El Centro Hispano's contract funds essential front-line municipal partnership staffing originally requested by Council in 2022.
Sudden funding cuts disrupt vital services for vulnerable residents before alternative grant mechanisms exist.
disagreements.resolution: Kept Item 7 on the September 2 Consent Agenda while directing Budget Director Christina Reirden to compile a complete inventory of city-funded nonprofits.

disagreements.meeting_title: Durham City Council Work Session August 21, 2025
disagreements.issue: Timing of the December 2025 Post-Election Organizational Meeting
disagreements.summary: Facilitated by Mary Grace Stone King, Council weighed holding the December 2025 swearing-in on December 1 versus December 4 or 15 amid post-canvass election certification timelines.
disagreements.side_a_position: Swear in newly elected or re-elected members as early as legally certified on December 1 or December 4.
side_a_arguments: Prompt seating respects voters' mandate and avoids lame-duck votes after the municipal election.
Standard early-December organizational meetings align with longstanding Council calendar traditions.
disagreements.side_b_position: Delay until December 15 or verify statutory canvass/recount windows before setting a binding date.
side_b_arguments: Close municipal races, provisional ballots, or recount windows can delay official Board of Elections certification past December 1.
Locking a date without City Attorney verification risks scheduling conflicts with statutory certification rules.
disagreements.resolution: No consensus reached; deferred to the next work session pending City Attorney verification of election certification deadlines.

meetings.title: Durham City Council August 18, 2025
meetings.executive_summary: Presided over by Mayor Pro Tem Mark-Anthony Middleton with six members present (Mayor Leonardo Williams traveling), Council excused absences, referred Item 3 back to the City Clerk, and adopted the Consent Agenda unanimously. In four consecutive public hearings, Council unanimously adopted Durham's first neighborhood-scale Small Area Plan for Walltown (after Nate Baker withdrew a late floor amendment locking in existing Northgate Mall zoning rules), approved the 100% income-restricted 220-unit Fayetteville Flats rezoning, approved the 200-unit 40%-affordable 4218 South Alston Ave. rezoning with a sidewalk construction proffer, and passed a 10.25-acre US 70 Light Industrial cleanup rezoning.

agenda_items.title: Excuse Absences of Mayor Leonardo Williams (Aug. 18) and Mayor Pro Tem Mark-Anthony Middleton (Aug. 21)
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Council voted 6-0 to excuse Mayor Leonardo Williams's business travel absence from the August 18 meeting. DeDreana Freeman then conducted a 6-0 vote excusing Mark-Anthony Middleton from the August 21 work session so he could attend the funeral of Joe Harris's mother.

agenda_items.title: Consent Agenda (Items 1-2, 4-21, 26-29; Item 3 Referred Back to City Clerk)
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Following a Clerk priority request referring Item 3 (annual attendance reports) back to the City Clerk's office, Council unanimously adopted the remaining Consent Agenda items with no items pulled by members or residents.

agenda_items.title: Public Hearing: Walltown Small Area Plan and Place Type Map Amendment (Case A25001)
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Senior Planner Carl Kolosna presented Durham's first neighborhood Small Area Plan covering Walltown and the nearly 60-acre Northgate Mall site, alongside place-type conversions at 1406 Broad St., 1400/1402 Clarendon, and 1303/1305 W. Club Blvd. Walltown and Hayti advocates urged locking in current Northgate height/use limits against the New UDO, prompting Nate Baker to propose and later withdraw a floor amendment after Javiera Caballero and Planning Director Sarah Young warned against putting regulatory locks in an advisory document; both adoption resolutions passed 6-0.
agenda_items.vote_summary: Small Area Plan and Map Amendment Approved 6-0 (two votes)

agenda_items.title: Public Hearing: Zoning Map Change — Fayetteville Flats (3707 Fayetteville Street)
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Attorney Nil Ghosh representing Elmington Capital Group presented a 9.77-acre rezoning adjacent to Hillside High School from RU-5 to PDR 22.449 for up to 220 100%-income-restricted LIHTC apartments without city or county subsidy, plus a bus shelter and $9,000 DPS contribution. Despite resident Anita Scott Neville raising traffic and Hillside capacity questions, Council praised the model infill project and approved the rezoning and consistency statement 6-0.

agenda_items.title: Public Hearing: Zoning Map Change — 4218 South Alston Avenue
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Dan Jewell of Thomas & Hutton presented a 4.83-acre rezoning from RU-5(2) and OI to PDR 41.408 for up to 200 apartments, proffering 40% of units at 60% AMI for 20 years, $15,000 for DPS, 80% native trees, and construction funding for a missing sidewalk gap up to Carpenter Fletcher Road. Historic Lowes Grove neighbors Sarah Moyer, Fadi Aler, and Dr. Jim Akre opposed the 80-foot height and lack of sidewalks or parks, while Council welcomed the 40% affordability and passed the rezoning and consistency statement 6-0.

agenda_items.title: Public Hearing: Zoning Map Change — 303 US 70 Warehouse
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Katie Hamilton of Gander Development sought a general cleanup rezoning of under one acre on a 10.25-acre US 70 Service Road parcel from RS-8 to match the rest of the Industrial Light site for a ~90-employee manufacturing/assembly facility. Neighbor Stanley Ballard questioned traffic and rail backups along NC 98, while Hamilton confirmed primary vehicle access will use US 70 Service Road toward I-885 and Council approved the rezoning and consistency statement 6-0.

votes.item_title: Excuse Mayor Leonardo Williams from August 18, 2025 Regular Meeting
votes.notes: Mayor Leonardo Williams was traveling on business.
votes.discussion_detail: Opening the August 18 regular meeting as presiding chair, Mayor Pro Tem Mark-Anthony Middleton called for a procedural motion to excuse Mayor Leonardo Williams's absence due to out-of-town business travel. No member raised any objection to the request. All six Council members present voted Aye, passing the excusal 6-0.

votes.item_title: Excuse Mayor Pro Tem Mark-Anthony Middleton from August 21, 2025 Work Session
votes.notes: Vote conducted by DeDreana Freeman for Middleton to attend the funeral of Joe Harris's mother.
votes.discussion_detail: Council Member DeDreana Freeman took the gavel briefly to entertain a procedural motion excusing Mayor Pro Tem Mark-Anthony Middleton from the upcoming August 21 work session so he could attend the funeral of Joe Harris's mother. Colleagues offered condolences and raised no objection. The excusal passed unanimously 6-0.

votes.item_title: Item 22A: Resolution Amending Comprehensive Plan to Include the Walltown Small Area Plan
votes.notes: Nate Baker proposed and then withdrew a floor amendment intended to advise retaining current Northgate height/use caps until a rezoning application; Chelsea Cook confirmed her Aye vote after electronic screen ambiguity.
votes.discussion_detail: Senior Planner Carl Kolosna presented Durham's first Comprehensive Plan Small Area Plan covering Walltown and the nearly 60-acre Northgate Mall site, following years of grassroots organizing by the Walltown Community Association. Public speakers including Brandon Williams, Ezra Norberg, Cynthia Williams (CAT), Angel Iset Dozier (Hayti), Mimi Kessler, and Audrey Mitchell urged adoption while warning that draft New UDO CX-5 zoning could erode negotiation leverage at Northgate. Nate Baker moved a late community-requested amendment advising that existing Northgate height and R&D limits stay in place until a rezoning, backed by DeDreana Freeman, before withdrawing it after Javiera Caballero, Carl Rist, and Planning Director Sarah Young noted advisory plans lack regulatory force and bypass JCCPC/County review. After Middleton reminded speakers that small area plans are non-binding without public funding commitments, Council adopted the plan unanimously 6-0.

votes.item_title: Item 22B: Resolution Amending Place Type Map (Case A25001, Walltown Small Area Plan Attachment C)
votes.notes: Reclassifies city-owned stream-affected parcels at 1406 Broad St. and 1400/1402 Clarendon to Recreation/Open Space and Walltown Graded School parcels at 1303/1305 W. Club Blvd. to Community Institution.
votes.discussion_detail: As the second formal action under Item 22, Council voted on Attachment C (Case A25001) implementing targeted Place Type Map adjustments from the Walltown Small Area Plan. The amendment shifts city-owned stream-encumbered parcels at 1406 Broad Street and 1400 and 1402 Clarendon Street into Recreation and Open Space (preserving a neighborhood pedestrian cut-through near Paper Street A) and reclassifies the historic Walltown Graded School site at 1303 and 1305 West Club Boulevard to Community Institution. With Riverside senior Ezra Norberg and Council members praising preservation of the cut-through and school use, Council adopted the map amendment 6-0.

votes.item_title: Item 23A: Zoning Map Change — Fayetteville Flats (3707 Fayetteville Street, RU-5 to PDR 22.449)
votes.notes: 9.77 acres for up to 220 100%-income-restricted LIHTC apartments adjacent to Hillside High School, with bus stop shelter and $9,000 DPS proffer.
votes.discussion_detail: Attorney Nil Ghosh representing Elmington Capital Group requested rezoning 9.77 acres at 3707 Fayetteville Street from RU-5 to Planned Development Residential 22.449 to build up to 220 100%-income-restricted 4% LIHTC apartments without city or county subsidy. The developer also proffered native landscaping, reduced impervious surface limits, a new transit bus shelter near existing routes, and $9,000 to Durham Public Schools ($500 per projected student). Resident Anita Scott Neville questioned neighborhood notification, traffic, and Hillside High capacity, while Council members praised the 100% affordable walkable infill project and passed the rezoning 6-0.

votes.item_title: Item 23B: Fayetteville Flats Consistency Statement (NCGS 160D-605)
votes.notes: Consistent with Apartment and Townhouse Neighborhood place type designation.
votes.discussion_detail: Following approval of the Fayetteville Flats rezoning, Council voted on the NCGS 160D-605 consistency statement confirming the project aligns with the Comprehensive Plan's Apartment and Townhouse Neighborhood place type. No further debate occurred on the dais. The consistency statement passed unanimously 6-0.

votes.item_title: Item 24A: Zoning Map Change — 4218 South Alston Avenue (RU-5(2) & OI to PDR 41.408)
votes.notes: 4.83 acres at 4212-4302 S. Alston Ave. for up to 200 apartments (40% at 60% AMI for 20 years, $15,000 DPS proffer, 80% native trees); shifts Place Type from General Industrial to Apartment & Townhouse Neighborhood.
votes.discussion_detail: Dan Jewell of Thomas & Hutton presented Dermite Holdings's proposal to rezone 4.83 acres at 4212-4302 South Alston Avenue to PDR 41.408 for up to 200 apartments (40% income-restricted at 60% AMI for 20 years without local public subsidy), $15,000 for Durham Public Schools, and 80% native tree plantings. Historic Lowes Grove residents Sarah Moyer, Fadi Aler, and neighbor/dentist Dr. Jim Akre opposed the 80-foot height near an 1849 home and 1928 residence, citing missing sidewalks across active rail tracks to NC 55 buses, gridlock at Carpenter Fletcher Road, and lack of public parks. In response, Jewell formally proffered full construction-cost funding for the missing sidewalk link when right-of-way is secured, and Council approved the rezoning 6-0, emphasizing the exceptional 40% affordability commitment and industrial-study transition.

votes.item_title: Item 24B: 4218 South Alston Avenue Consistency Statement (NCGS 160D-605)
votes.notes: Accompanies Place Type Map shift from General Industrial to Apartment and Townhouse Neighborhood.
votes.discussion_detail: Because 4218 South Alston Avenue converted land designated General Industrial on the Place Type Map to residential apartments, Council voted on the NCGS 160D-605 consistency and plan-amendment finding. Staff had noted the site was not prioritized for industrial retention in the Industrial Land Use Study. All six present Council members voted Aye, passing the statement 6-0.

votes.item_title: Item 25A: Zoning Map Change — 303 US 70 Warehouse (RS-8 & IL to Industrial Light, Falls/Jordan B)
votes.notes: 10.25-acre parcel cleanup rezoning less than 1 acre of split RS-8 zoning to match Industrial Light for a ~90-employee manufacturing/assembly facility.
votes.discussion_detail: Katie Hamilton of Gander Development sought a general cleanup rezoning of under one acre on a 10.25-acre US 70 Service Road property formerly used as an I-885 construction laydown yard so the entire site falls under Industrial Light for a ~90-employee manufacturing and assembly facility. Resident Stanley Ballard questioned warehouse impacts on congested NC 98 train crossings and neighborhood traffic, while Hamilton confirmed vehicle access would run exclusively onto US 70 Service Road toward I-885 and noted wetlands and a 50-foot buffer protect adjoining residential lots. Council accepted the cleanup rationale and unanimously approved the rezoning 6-0.

votes.item_title: Item 25B: 303 US 70 Warehouse Consistency Statement (NCGS 160D-605)
votes.notes: Consistent with General Industrial place type designation.

No further debate took place. The statement passed 6-0 prior to adjournment at 9:35 p.m.

disagreements.meeting_title: Durham City Council August 18, 2025
disagreements.issue: Walltown Small Area Plan Floor Amendment Locking Current Northgate Mall Zoning Limits
disagreements.summary: Council debated a floor amendment introduced by Nate Baker (from Walltown Community Association testimony) advising that Northgate Mall's existing height and research-and-development limits stay locked until a rezoning application, despite the pending New UDO rewrite.
disagreements.side_a_position: Insert explicit plan language protecting current Northgate Mall height and use restrictions so the New UDO does not grant by-right upzoning without community negotiation.
side_a_arguments: Upzoning Northgate to CX-5 by right in the New UDO strips Walltown residents of leverage to negotiate affordable housing and community benefits.
Neighborhood-specific small area guidance is the proper place to protect historical community organizing.
disagreements.side_b_position: Reject inserting late regulatory zoning locks into an advisory Comprehensive Plan document without JCCPC/County review.
side_b_arguments: Comprehensive and small area plans are advisory rather than regulatory, and New UDO district conversions do not map one-for-one to old districts.
Major late edits to a joint City-County planning document should go through the New UDO rewrite and JCCPC review process.
disagreements.resolution: Nate Baker withdrew the floor amendment before final voting, and Council adopted the Walltown Small Area Plan and Place Type Map Amendment unanimously 6-0.

disagreements.meeting_title: Durham City Council August 18, 2025
disagreements.issue: 4218 South Alston Avenue Density, Height, and Connectivity Near Historic Lowes Grove
disagreements.summary: Council members weighed neighbor objections over an 80-foot apartment building lacking direct parks or finished sidewalks against a rare 40% affordable housing proffer at 60% AMI.
disagreements.side_a_position: Approve the 200-unit apartment rezoning with a sidewalk construction proffer to secure 80 unsubsidized affordable homes.
side_a_arguments: Committing 40% of units at 60% AMI without city or county subsidy helps address urgent workforce housing needs along a transitioning corridor.
The applicant committed to fully fund the missing sidewalk segment to Carpenter Fletcher Road once right-of-way is secured.
disagreements.side_b_position: Challenge the lack of 30-year affordability, public green space, and immediate pedestrian/transit safety for future residents.
side_b_arguments: A 20-year affordability term falls short of Durham's standard 30-year benchmark, and nearby parks and bus-stop pedestrian access remain incomplete.
Doubling by-right height to 80 feet impacts adjacent 19th- and early-20th-century Lowes Grove historic residences.
disagreements.resolution: Despite voicing affordability-term, historic-context, and open-space concerns, both Chelsea Cook and DeDreana Freeman joined colleagues in passing the rezoning 6-0.
