meetings.title: Durham City Council Work Session August 7, 2025
meetings.executive_summary: The Durham City Council convened on August 7, 2025, to review and settle the consent and general business agendas for the August 18, 2025 City Council meeting. Council Members pulled five items for substantive questioning, including boards and commissions attendance audit discrepancies, the 2026 meeting schedule, an ARPA digital equity hotspot contract with Verizon, a $2 million project management consulting amendment with Turner & Townsend Heery LLC, and water plant turbidimeter replacements. The Council also added four supplemental affordable housing financing items, deferred the Walltown Small Area Plan presentation to August 18, and unanimously settled the agenda 7-0.

agenda_items.title: Council Announcements, Manager Priority Items & Clerk Nominations
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Council Member Chelsea Cook proposed bringing a resolution requiring regular FOIA requests to DHS regarding ICE operations in Durham, while Council Members DeDreana Freeman and Carl Rist highlighted community anniversaries, declining downtown rental pressures (12% vacancy), and DHA's new 72-unit Vanguard property. Mayor Leonardo Williams and Mayor Pro Tempore Mark-Anthony Middleton discussed youth violence interruption initiatives ahead of October's Joint City-County meeting, prompting Cook and Middleton to urge using formal agenda items rather than announcements for policy proposals. City Manager Bo Ferguson moved Item 22 (Walltown Small Area Plan presentation) to August 18 and added four supplemental housing financing items (Items 26-29), and the Clerk reported board nominations.

agenda_items.title: Boards, Committees, Commissions and Taskforces Fiscal Year 2024-25 Annual Attendance Reports
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Council Member Carl Rist pulled Item 3 after identifying mathematical errors in the attendance report, such as members showing 111% attendance or 31% attendance caused by blacked-out cells after former member Dan Hudgins exited the DHA board in October 2024. Deputy City Clerk Lola Roland acknowledged the calculation discrepancies across individual board spreadsheets. Council asked the Clerk's Office to coordinate with staff liaisons to scrub and standardize attendance tracking going forward.

agenda_items.title: 2026 Durham City Council Meeting Schedule
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Council Member Javiera Caballero pulled the 2026 calendar to resolve holiday and recess conflicts, proposing to shift the December 18, 2025 work session to December 16 and the December 23, 2026 work session to December 21. Members also discussed bumping the July 23, 2026 work session to August and coordinating the November 19 work session with the December 7 organizational meeting. Council Member Chelsea Cook noted a standing Tuesday 4:00 PM teaching commitment that staff agreed to factor into the finalized calendar.

agenda_items.title: ARPA Interlocal Agreement & Digital Equity Hotspot Contract with Cellco Partnership d/b/a Verizon Wireless
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Council Member Chelsea Cook questioned the timeline, eligibility criteria, and funding source for the Verizon digital equity hotspot distribution contract. Community Engagement staffer Patrice Carroll clarified that Durham County ARPA funds—which must be fully expended by December 31, 2026—cover both hardware devices and free internet service through November 2026 for income-qualified residents. Staff confirmed outreach targets digitally underserved households before the federal ARPA deadline.

agenda_items.title: Second Amendment to Service Agreement for Project Management Consulting Services with Turner & Townsend Heery, LLC
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Council Members Chelsea Cook and Carl Rist pulled the $2 million contract amendment (bringing the fee to a flat 3.7% across roughly 100 active capital projects including the Rail Trail, 505 West Chapel Hill Street, and South Ellerbe Creek). Deputy City Manager Gina Propst and City Manager Bo Ferguson explained that the cooperative purchasing contract provides flexible project delivery capacity without adding permanent city headcount. Council Members Javiera Caballero and Nate Baker asked for a deeper cost-benefit comparison of consultants versus in-house staff during the upcoming budget cycle.

agenda_items.title: Purchase Order with Swan Analytical USA, Inc. for Water Treatment Plant Turbidimeters and Controllers
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Council Member Chelsea Cook pulled the Swan Analytical purchase order to clarify the operational role and urgency of replacing turbidimeters at the Brown and Williams Water Treatment Plants. Water Management Acting Assistant Director Dirk Carter and Brown Plant Superintendent Thomas Lucas explained that regulatory compliance requires turbidity below 0.3 NTU measured every 15 minutes and that existing analyzers are obsolete. Council expressed satisfaction with the sole-source equipment justification.

agenda_items.title: Motion to Settle Agenda for August 18, 2025 City Council Meeting
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Mayor Leonardo Williams resumed the gavel from Mayor Pro Tempore Mark-Anthony Middleton and entertained a motion to settle the agenda after all pulled items were reviewed. Consent items were set as Items 1 through 21 and supplemental affordable housing Items 26 through 29, while Items 22 through 25 were placed on the General Business Agenda for Public Hearings. The Council approved the settled agenda unanimously by voice vote before adjourning at 2:00 PM.

meetings.title: Durham Joint City County Planning Committee (JCCPC) - August 6, 2025
meetings.presiding_chair: Wendy Jacobs (JCCPC Chair; Vice Chair Nate Baker present)
meetings.executive_summary: The Joint City-County Planning Committee met on August 6, 2025, approving two excused absences and the June 4, 2025 meeting minutes before receiving four planning briefings. Staff presented on the Comprehensive Plan Evaluation and Assessment Report (EAR), updates to the Historic Preservation Commission Interlocal Agreement, proposed Dark Sky and bird-friendly UDO standards, and new UDO zoning capacity and map refinements. A major policy debate emerged between Council Member Nate Baker and Council Members Javiera Caballero and Mark-Anthony Middleton over whether broad by-right upzoning undermines affordable housing density bonuses.

agenda_items.title: Roll Call, Excused Absences & Approval of June 4, 2025 Minutes
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Chair Wendy Jacobs convened the JCCPC with Vice Chair Nate Baker, Javiera Caballero, Mark-Anthony Middleton, County Commissioner Mike Lee, and Planning Commissioner Burton present. Members voted unanimously to excuse Planning Commissioners Steven Valentine and Kim Cameron and approved the June 4, 2025 meeting minutes.

agenda_items.title: Comprehensive Plan Evaluation and Assessment Report (EAR) & Community Goals and Objectives Report Card
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Planning staff Aaron Cain and Kayla Seibel outlined the two-phase biennial EAR and CGO review, Durham's first comprehensive check since 2018. Phase 1 (October-November 2025) will deliver an equity report card across eight indicators alongside technical policy edits and non-private PTM/UGB adjustments, followed by Phase 2 in winter/spring 2026.

agenda_items.title: Historic Preservation Commission (HPC) Interlocal Cooperative Agreement Update
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Planner Carla Rosenberg presented updates to the City-County HPC Interlocal Agreement updating statutory citations to NCGS Chapter 160D, adding two at-large alternate members to the existing nine seats, and enabling City-appointed commissioners to receive city stipends. The updated agreement will advance to City Council and the Board of County Commissioners for formal adoption.

agenda_items.title: New UDO Dark Sky Certification and Bird-Friendly Design Standards
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Planner Robin Schultz detailed proposed UDO environmental provisions including tightened light trespass caps (0.5 and 5 foot-candles), native plant mandates, a 2026 landscape manual update toward a 55% tree canopy goal by 2040, and voluntary bird-friendly glazing opt-ins given NCGS 160D design restrictions. Staff also outlined barriers to full Dark Sky Community certification, including Duke Energy LED contracts and municipal lighting retrofits.

agenda_items.title: New UDO Potential Zoning Capacity & Draft Zoning Map Concerns
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Planning staff Scott Whiteman and Bo Dobrzynski reported that Durham's Comprehensive Plan projects 60,000-65,000 additional housing units by 2050-2055 alongside an existing 17,000+ unit gap, and that proposed new UDO districts increase by-right urban growth boundary capacity by 46% from 136,445 to 200,072 units. Staff also reviewed mapping adjustments such as shifting county-jurisdiction RR/RS-20 parcels inside the UGB to RB, refining CX height tiers along transit corridors, and addressing neighborhood concerns on RX3 infill parcels at 4500 Auburn Street and Garrett Road.

votes.item_title: Excuse Absence of Planning Commissioner Steven Valentine
votes.notes: Joint City-County committee vote; City Council members Nate Baker, Javiera Caballero, and Mark-Anthony Middleton voted Aye alongside County/Planning representatives.
votes.discussion_detail: At the start of the August 6, 2025 JCCPC meeting, Chair Wendy Jacobs noted a request from Planning Commissioner Steven Valentine for an excused absence. Council Member Javiera Caballero moved to grant the excused absence, and Planning Commissioner Burton seconded the motion. The committee approved the absence unanimously by voice vote without debate.

votes.item_title: Excuse Absence of Planning Commissioner Kim Cameron
votes.notes: Joint City-County committee vote.
votes.discussion_detail: Following the roll call, Chair Wendy Jacobs brought forward a request for an excused absence from Planning Commissioner Kim Cameron. Council Member Javiera Caballero moved to excuse Cameron's absence, seconded by Council Member Mark-Anthony Middleton. The committee voted unanimously by voice vote to approve the motion.

votes.item_title: Approval of June 4, 2025 JCCPC Meeting Minutes
votes.notes: Approval of minutes from the prior June 4, 2025 JCCPC session.
votes.discussion_detail: Chair Wendy Jacobs called for a motion to approve the minutes of the June 4, 2025 JCCPC meeting. Vice Chair Nate Baker moved approval, and Council Member Mark-Anthony Middleton seconded. Without corrections or discussion, the committee adopted the minutes unanimously by voice vote.

disagreements.meeting_title: Durham Joint City County Planning Committee (JCCPC) - August 6, 2025
disagreements.issue: New UDO Broad By-Right Upzoning vs. Preserving Base Zoning Leverage for Affordable Housing Density Bonuses
disagreements.summary: Committee members clashed over staff's draft UDO zoning capacity analysis, which increases by-right residential capacity inside the Urban Growth Boundary by 46% from 136,445 to 200,072 units.
disagreements.side_a_position: Hold base by-right zoning closer to current capacity and tie significant additional height/density to calibrated affordable housing and green-building density bonuses.
side_a_arguments: Expanding by-right zoning to 200,072+ units gives away valuable development rights for free, especially under North Carolina's recent ban on local downzoning.
Without holding base zoning low enough to require developers to opt in, Durham loses leverage to extract affordable units and green building features via density bonuses.
Extra height (such as increasing 3-story corridors to 10-30 stories) should be unlocked through market-calibrated bonus tiers rather than unconditioned by-right entitlements.
disagreements.side_b_position: Maintain broad by-right residential upzoning inside the UGB to expand total housing supply, support walkable 15-minute neighborhoods, and rely on direct public subsidies for deep affordability.
side_b_arguments: Durham's existing 15% affordable housing density bonus has historically produced very few units because 0-30% AMI housing requires direct capital subsidies and revolving loan funds rather than zoning trades alone.
Restricting base supply risks Chapel Hill-style exclusionary outcomes—declining school enrollment, soaring home prices, and loss of Black residents.
Recent local market data (12% multifamily vacancy) indicates increased by-right supply helps moderate market rents while containing sprawl within the Urban Growth Boundary.
disagreements.resolution: No formal vote taken; committee directed Planning staff to return with data on historical density bonus uptake, Minneapolis inclusionary zoning comparisons, and visual scenario illustrations.

meetings.title: Durham City Council August 4, 2025
meetings.executive_summary: The Durham City Council met on August 4, 2025, unveiling new electronic voting and audiovisual upgrades in Council Chambers, issuing proclamations for Black Business Month and National Emergency Management Awareness Month, and approving the consent agenda 7-0. Council adopted Stormwater Facility Replacement Fund code updates, approved the 2025-2029 HUD Consolidated Plan and Annual Action Plan, and unanimously appointed four members to the Recreation Advisory Commission. In major contentious land-use votes, Council voted 5-2 to accept Sterling Bay and Akan Group's last-minute withdrawal of the Heritage Square rezoning (401 E. Lakewood Ave) over objections from waiting speakers, and voted 1-6 to deny the Durham Rescue Mission's East Main Street rezoning due to inconsistency with Transit Opportunity Area goals.

agenda_items.title: Proclamations, Storm Chantal Recovery, Decorum Warnings & Hearing Reordering
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Mayor Leonardo Williams presented proclamations for Black Business Month and National Emergency Management Awareness Month alongside Durham County OES Director Mark Lockhart, and members discussed flood recovery after Post-Tropical Storm Chantal and federal/state funding cuts. Council Members Nate Baker and Mark-Anthony Middleton condemned audience attacks questioning Council Member Javiera Caballero's citizenship, while Mayor Williams issued chamber decorum warnings. Mayor Williams reordered public hearings so Items 25, 28, and 29 would be heard before Items 26 and 27.

agenda_items.title: Consent Agenda Including Pulled Items 1 & 5 (Excluding Item 3 & Referred Item 20)
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Residents Victoria Peterson and Mr. Zedi pulled Items 1 and 5 to raise questions regarding autism recreation programming at W.D. Hill Recreation Center and soil lead remediation at city parks. Item 20 was referred back to Technology Solutions and Item 3 was placed on the General Business Agenda. Council approved the consent agenda including pulled Items 1 and 5 unanimously.

agenda_items.title: Cliff Street Partial Street Closing (SC25001)
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Applicant Eric Hamilton requested closing 42 linear feet (0.46 acres) of unimproved Cliff Street right-of-way to recombine with 1700 Cliff Street, which the Bicycle and Pedestrian Advisory Commission opposed because it would block access to the planned Rockwood Trail. Council Members DeDreana Freeman, Chelsea Cook, and Nate Baker expressed reluctance to surrender public right-of-way connectivity, whereas Mayor Pro Tempore Mark-Anthony Middleton cautioned against speculative future trail planning burdening property owners. With the applicant's agreement, Council referred the item back to staff and continued the public hearing to October 20, 2025.

agenda_items.title: Revisions to Durham City Code Chapter 70 Articles 10 & 11 (Stormwater Facility Replacement Fund)
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Staff presented two code amendment ordinances bringing Durham's Stormwater Facility Replacement Fund into compliance with NCGS 160D-925 (Session Law 2023-108) by terminating the fund and authorizing refunds under new Section 70-753. Council passed both ordinances unanimously in consecutive 7-0 votes.

agenda_items.title: Draft 5-Year 2025-2029 Consolidated Plan, 2025 Annual Action Plan & Citizen Participation Plan
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Maggie Carnegie presented Durham's federal HUD entitlement allocation plan totaling $1,936,725 in CDBG, $977,820 in HOME, $176,108 in ESG, and $1,106,643 in HOPWA funds. During the public hearing, Dr. Haley Cunningham of the Coalition to End the HIV Epidemic criticized untouched prior-year HOPWA funds and zero HIV/AIDS cases listed in the draft plan. Council adopted the plans 7-0.

agenda_items.title: Zoning Map Change: 401 East Lakewood Avenue & 600 Fayetteville Street (Heritage Square)
agenda_items.discussion_summary: After the June 16 continuance, applicant attorney Jamie Schwedler presented a $2.3M+ community benefits package on behalf of Sterling Bay and Akan Group (including a 250-ft height cap, discounted retail, scholarships, and St. Mark's parking/escrow), then stated that the 'writing is on the wall' and moved to withdraw the rezoning under UDO 3.5.7B4. Council debated whether to accept withdrawal immediately without hearing ~40 waiting speakers or to hold the hearing and trigger a 12-month refiling bar. Council voted 5-2 to accept the withdrawal without a public hearing.

agenda_items.title: Zoning Map Change: Durham Rescue Mission, East Main Street (15 Parcels / 3.52 Acres)
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Durham Rescue Mission sought to rezone 3.52 acres on East Main Street to Industrial Light (IL) with a textual development plan for a 75,000-sq-ft Career Development Center, bus pullout pad, and home relocations, which Planning staff reversed to 'generally inconsistent' because it downzones a Transit Opportunity Area without housing or mixed-use density. Pastor Rob Tart and alumni testified in support of DRM's services, while neighbors warned a suburban industrial-style building would deaden the East Durham transit gateway. Council rejected the rezoning 1-6 (Middleton Aye) and unanimously adopted the consistency statement 7-0.

agenda_items.title: Durham Recreation Advisory Commission Appointments
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Following ballot adjustments clarified at the morning work session, Council voted on three at-large appointments (Laura J. Debar, Gabrielle Rivero, and Gregory Williams) and one seat for a person with a disability (Larry Dale McKiel) for terms expiring August 8, 2028. The appointments passed 7-0.

votes.item_title: Adopt Consent Agenda Including Pulled Items 1 & 5 (Excluding Item 3 & Referred Item 20)
votes.notes: Electronic board vote; Item 20 referred back to Technology Solutions Department; Item 3 moved to General Business Agenda.
votes.discussion_detail: The August 4, 2025 consent agenda included routine contracts, settlements, and board appointments, with Item 20 referred back to Technology Solutions and Item 3 moved to the General Business Agenda. Residents Victoria Peterson and Mr. Zedi pulled Items 1 and 5 to address autism recreation programming at W.D. Hill Recreation Center and lead soil remediation across Durham parks. After hearing the speakers' comments, Council Members voted unanimously 7-0 using the newly installed electronic voting system in chambers to approve the consent agenda including Items 1 and 5.

votes.item_title: Item 28a: Ordinance Amending City Code Chapter 70, Article 10 (§70-742 to §70-743) & Article 11 (§70-750 to §70-752) Regarding Stormwater Facility Replacement Fund
votes.notes: Aligns municipal code with NCGS 160D-925 / Session Law 2023-108.
votes.discussion_detail: City staff presented revisions to Chapter 70 of the Durham City Code to comply with North Carolina Session Law 2023-108 (NCGS 160D-925), which restricts municipal stormwater facility replacement reserve funds. The first ordinance updated Articles 10 and 11 (§70-742 through §70-743 and §70-750 through §70-752) to sunset collection into the replacement fund. No members of the public spoke in opposition during the public hearing, and Council unanimously approved the ordinance 7-0 on the electronic voting board.

votes.item_title: Item 28b: Ordinance Amending City Code Chapter 70, Article 11 Creating §70-753 (Stormwater Facility Replacement Fund Refunds)
votes.notes: Companion ordinance establishing refund procedures under §70-753.
votes.discussion_detail: Immediately following passage of the first Stormwater Facility Replacement Fund code revision, Council took up the companion ordinance creating Section 70-753 to authorize refund disbursements from the discontinued fund in compliance with state law. With public hearing comments closed and no objections raised by Council Members, the ordinance passed unanimously 7-0 via electronic roll call vote.

votes.item_title: Item 29: Adopt Draft 5-Year 2025-2029 Consolidated Plan, 2025 Annual Action Plan & Citizen Participation Plan
votes.notes: Clerk noted Council Member DeDreana Freeman missed tapping her touchscreen initially before confirming her Aye vote for a 7-0 tally.
votes.discussion_detail: Community Development staff member Maggie Carnegie presented Durham's 2025-2029 Consolidated Plan and 2025 Annual Action Plan covering federal HUD grants: $1,936,725 in CDBG, $977,820 in HOME, $176,108 in ESG, and $1,106,643 in HOPWA funding. During the public hearing, Dr. Haley Cunningham of the Coalition to End the HIV Epidemic urged greater urgency in spending prior-year HOPWA balances and corrected the draft plan's omission of local HIV/AIDS prevalence statistics. Council closed the hearing and voted unanimously 7-0 to adopt the Consolidated Plan, Annual Action Plan, and updated Citizen Participation Plan.

votes.item_title: Item 26: Accept Applicant's Request to Withdraw Zoning Map Change for 401 E. Lakewood Ave & 600 Fayetteville St (Heritage Square)
votes.notes: Accepted withdrawal under UDO 3.5.7B4 prior to public hearing; roughly 40 speakers were signed up.
votes.discussion_detail: Continued from June 16 with approximately 40 community speakers waiting to testify, applicant attorney Jamie Schwedler outlined a $2.3 million community benefits package for Heritage Square before abruptly announcing that 'the writing is on the wall' and requesting to withdraw the rezoning application under UDO 3.5.7B4. Council Members DeDreana Freeman and Chelsea Cook sharply criticized allowing a withdrawal without hearing residents who had waited through two separate meetings, noting the difference between a 6-month withdrawal waiting period (UDO 3.5.7D) and a 12-month denial waiting period (UDO 3.5.15A). Mayor Pro Tempore Mark-Anthony Middleton, Council Member Carl Rist, and Council Member Javiera Caballero argued that Council precedent permits withdrawal and that holding a hearing on a withdrawn case is legally futile. Council voted 5-2 to accept the withdrawal, with Nate Baker and DeDreana Freeman voting No and Cook ultimately voting Yes despite her procedural frustration.

votes.item_title: Item 27a: Zoning Map Change Ordinance — Durham Rescue Mission, East Main Street (Z2300025 / IL with Textual Plan)
votes.notes: Staff recommended denial/inconsistency with Transit Opportunity Area place type; Mayor Leonardo Williams offered to partner with DRM on an alternative site or design.
votes.discussion_detail: Durham Rescue Mission applied to rezone 15 parcels (3.52 acres) on East Main Street to Industrial Light (IL) with a textual development plan for a 75,000-square-foot Career Development Center capped at 35 feet in height, adding a bus pullout pad and relocating two houses. Planning staff member Andy Lester reported that staff reversed its earlier assessment and now found the project generally inconsistent with the Transit Opportunity Area (TOA) place type because it omitted residential uses and introduced low-density industrial zoning near transit. Pastor Rob Tart and program alumni testified to DRM's vital workforce and recovery services, while nearby residents opposed a suburban 'big-box' warehouse form on the East Durham gateway. While Mayor Pro Tempore Mark-Anthony Middleton praised DRM's responsiveness and essential homeless services as the sole Aye vote, the remaining six Council Members rejected the rezoning 1-6 to protect TOA mixed-use housing potential.

votes.item_title: Item 27b: NCGS 160D-605 Consistency Statement for Denial of Durham Rescue Mission Rezoning (East Main Street)
votes.notes: Required statutory consistency statement affirming inconsistency with the Comprehensive Plan following the 1-6 denial.
votes.discussion_detail: Following the 1-6 failure of the Durham Rescue Mission East Main Street rezoning ordinance, Council was required under North Carolina General Statute 160D-605 to adopt a formal consistency statement documenting the grounds for denial. The statement affirmed that the requested Industrial Light designation was inconsistent with the Comprehensive Plan's Transit Opportunity Area place type. Despite having dissented on the underlying rezoning vote, Mayor Pro Tempore Mark-Anthony Middleton joined the rest of Council to approve the statutory consistency statement 7-0.

votes.item_title: Item 3: Durham Recreation Advisory Commission Appointments (Laura J. Debar, Gabrielle Rivero, Gregory Williams, Larry Dale McKiel)
votes.notes: Three at-large vacancies (Debar, Rivero, Williams) and one disability-representation seat (McKiel) for terms expiring August 8, 2028.
votes.discussion_detail: Moved from the consent agenda to the General Business Agenda to clarify ballot categories—placing Gregory Williams in an at-large slot alongside Laura J. Debar and Gabrielle Rivero and confirming Larry Dale McKiel in the seat designated for a person with a disability—Item 3 was taken up at the conclusion of the public hearings. Council Member Chelsea Cook moved approval of the four appointments for terms expiring August 8, 2028, and Council Member Nate Baker seconded. Council unanimously confirmed the appointments 7-0.

disagreements.meeting_title: Durham City Council August 4, 2025
disagreements.issue: Cliff Street Unimproved Right-of-Way Closure vs. Future Rockwood Trail Connectivity
disagreements.summary: Council Members split over whether to vacate 42 linear feet of unimproved Cliff Street right-of-way requested by an adjoining homeowner or preserve public access for a future Rockwood Trail connection.
disagreements.side_a_position: Protect public right-of-way and greenway connectivity aligned with Transportation Policy 57 and Bike/Ped Advisory Commission concerns.
side_a_arguments: Once vacated, public right-of-way for pedestrian and trail access is permanently lost.
Staff and BPAC identified the corridor as important to future Rockwood Trail connectivity under the Comprehensive Plan.
disagreements.side_b_position: Avoid letting speculative long-range trail plans indefinitely restrict an adjacent resident's reasonable property and driveway use.
side_b_arguments: Speculative trail concepts without active funding or timeline should not override existing resident access requests.
Residents deserve certainty when maintaining driveway and yard boundaries.
disagreements.resolution: With the applicant's consent, Council referred the matter back to staff to explore an easement compromise and continued the public hearing to October 20, 2025.

disagreements.meeting_title: Durham City Council August 4, 2025
disagreements.issue: Accepting Heritage Square Developer's Withdrawal Prior to Public Comment (Item 26)
disagreements.summary: Council divided 5-2 over whether to accept Sterling Bay and Akan Group's last-minute request to withdraw their 401 E. Lakewood Ave rezoning before ~40 signed-up residents could speak.
disagreements.side_a_position: Accept the applicant's withdrawal immediately under UDO 3.5.7B4 without conducting a public hearing on a moot application.
side_a_arguments: Once an applicant withdraws an application, there is no pending rezoning case for the public to comment on.
Council precedent consistently honors developer withdrawal requests prior to hearing testimony.
disagreements.side_b_position: Refuse immediate withdrawal and hear waiting community members or enforce the 12-month denial refiling bar.
side_b_arguments: Roughly 40 community members waited through two long Council meetings (June 16 and August 4) and deserved to place their views on the public record.
Allowing last-minute withdrawal shortens the refiling waiting period from 12 months (denial under UDO 3.5.15A) to 6 months (withdrawal under UDO 3.5.7D).
disagreements.resolution: Council voted 5-2 to accept the withdrawal without holding the public hearing (Cook voiced concern over waiting speakers and the refiling bar but voted Aye).

disagreements.meeting_title: Durham City Council August 4, 2025
disagreements.issue: Durham Rescue Mission East Main Street Industrial Rezoning in a Transit Opportunity Area (Item 27)
disagreements.summary: Council voted 1-6 to reject Durham Rescue Mission's rezoning to Industrial Light for a 75,000-sq-ft Career Development Center inside an East Durham Transit Opportunity Area.
disagreements.side_a_position: Deny the rezoning as inconsistent with Transit Opportunity Area land-use goals calling for dense, walkable mixed-use and housing near transit.
side_a_arguments: Planning staff reversed its prior stance and found low-density Industrial Light uses with zero housing generally inconsistent with the Comprehensive Plan TOA place type.
Converting a prime East Main Street transit corridor into a suburban 'big-box' industrial-style facility undermines long-term walkable neighborhood revitalization.
disagreements.side_b_position: Approve the rezoning to support Durham Rescue Mission's workforce training and homelessness services.
side_b_arguments: Durham Rescue Mission provides critical, life-saving addiction recovery and job training services for unhoused residents.
The applicant worked in good faith with neighbors to cap building height at 35 feet, add a concrete bus pullout pad, and relocate two homes.
disagreements.resolution: Rezoning ordinance failed 1-6; Council adopted the statutory inconsistency statement 7-0, and Mayor Williams offered to help DRM find an alternative site or design.

meetings.title: Durham City Council Work Session August 4, 2025
meetings.executive_summary: The Durham City Council held a morning work session on August 4, 2025 (with Council Member Chelsea Cook on an excused absence), introducing newly appointed City leadership and upgraded chamber voting and broadcast systems. Members reviewed five pulled consent items—covering Fair Housing audit delays, the DA/AOC Domestic Violence & Gang Reduction ADA agreement, Stantec creek pollutant tracking, Durham Small Business Opportunity Fund Phase 2 loan guarantees, and the GoDurham Access paratransit contract—plus an Upper Neuse River Basin Association (UNRBA) FY26 budget briefing. Council Members debated performance targets for small business pandemic relief loans and unanimously settled the evening agenda 6-0.

agenda_items.title: Staff Introductions, Fourth Amendment Resolution Notice, Nominations & Public Comment
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Council congratulated Nate Baker on the July 10 birth of his daughter, and Javiera Caballero announced a supplemental Fourth Amendment Workplace Resolution for August 7. City Manager Bo Ferguson introduced OEWD Director Joshua Gunn, Deputy City Manager Gina Propst, interim Communications Director Amy Blalock, and upgraded chamber audiovisual/DTN systems, while residents Jacqueline Wagstaff and Julie Messina spoke on protective housing remarks and Durham NC Parkrun's 12th anniversary.

agenda_items.title: Neighborhood Improvement Services Fair Housing Investigation Audit Delays
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Council Member Javiera Caballero pulled Item 6 regarding Fair Housing case investigation audit delays within the Neighborhood Improvement Services Human Relations division. Staff briefed Council on workflow bottlenecks and remediation steps to clear investigative backlogs.

agenda_items.title: FY26 District Attorney / Administrative Office of the Courts Domestic Violence & Gang Reduction Agreement
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Council Members Nate Baker, Javiera Caballero, and Mayor Leonardo Williams questioned the renewed FY26 contract funding state Assistant District Attorneys—part of 19 state ADA positions funded locally since 1999—focusing on domestic violence and gang reduction prosecution. District Attorney Satana Deberry explained state court data tracking limitations and how the positions operate within her office.

agenda_items.title: Stantec Pollutant Source Tracking in Rock Creek & Stirrup Iron Creek
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Council Members Carl Rist, DeDreana Freeman, and Nate Baker pulled the Stantec stormwater consulting contract covering pollutant source tracking in Rock Creek and Stirrup Iron Creek. Baker inquired whether the city can recover public remediation costs from Brenntag Midsouth related to chemical pollution near Burton Park.

agenda_items.title: Durham Small Business Opportunity Fund Phase 2 with Carolina Small Business Development Fund
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Council Members Carl Rist, DeDreana Freeman, Mark-Anthony Middleton, and Javiera Caballero questioned Kevin Dick of Carolina Small Business Development Fund regarding Phase 2 support for 50 early-stage businesses and 18-40 loan guarantees ($25,000-$75,000). Rist urged establishing explicit target outcome metrics, while Freeman and Middleton cautioned against imposing rigid underwriting targets on pandemic small-business relief.

agenda_items.title: GoDurham Access Paratransit Contract with WeDriveU
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Council Member Carl Rist pulled Item 21 to examine service performance, rider capacity, and operational oversight under the GoDurham Access paratransit contract with WeDriveU. Transportation Director Sean Egan responded with operational details and contractor performance benchmarks.

agenda_items.title: Upper Neuse River Basin Association (UNRBA) FY26 Budget Presentation
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Staff and UNRBA representatives presented the FY26 UNRBA budget requiring an assessment of over $162,000 from Durham alongside Falls Lake nutrient rules updates. The briefing compared Stage 1 versus Stage 2 compliance milestones and an alternative investment-based compliance strategy.

agenda_items.title: Violence Interruption Exploration, Recreation Commission Ballot Fix & Agenda Settlement
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Mayor Pro Tempore Mark-Anthony Middleton requested placing an item on the October Joint City-County agenda to explore reviving a city-county community violence interruption program following the termination of Bull City United. Council Member Nate Baker explained a ballot correction on Item 3 (Recreation Advisory Commission) assigning Gregory Williams to an at-large seat and reappointing Dale McKiel to the disability-representation seat. Council unanimously settled the August 4 evening agenda 6-0 before adjourning for chamber voting training.

disagreements.meeting_title: Durham City Council Work Session August 4, 2025
disagreements.issue: Strict Target Metrics vs. Flexible Underwriting for Small Business Opportunity Fund Phase 2 (Item 17)
disagreements.summary: Council Members differed on whether Phase 2 of the Durham Small Business Opportunity Fund ($25k-$75k loan guarantees administered by Carolina Small Business Development Fund) should enforce strict quantitative loan-delivery targets.
disagreements.side_a_position: Require explicit numerical performance targets for guaranteed loans and early-stage businesses served.
side_a_arguments: Clear quantitative metrics help Council evaluate return on public economic development dollars.
Targets establish accountability for reaching 50 early-stage businesses and 18-40 loan guarantees.
disagreements.side_b_position: Maintain underwriting flexibility rather than rigid numeric quotas for pandemic-era small business relief.
side_b_arguments: Early-stage small businesses recovering from pandemic disruption face uneven credit profiles that rigid targets could distort.
Partnering with experienced CDFIs like Carolina Small Business Development Fund requires trust in adaptive technical assistance.
disagreements.resolution: Item remained on the Consent Agenda for evening approval without imposing rigid new contract quotas.

meetings.title: 6. FY2025-26 Budget & FY2026-31 CIP & other related ordinances fr. 6.16.25 mtg
meetings.executive_summary: This excerpt from the June 16, 2025 City Council meeting captures Item 6, the public comment and Council adoption of City Manager Bo Ferguson's first municipal budget exceeding $700 million and the FY2026-31 Capital Improvement Plan. Residents Sharita Burrus and Karen Abram Jones pulled the item, with Burrus criticizing Durham Housing Authority maintenance failures and requesting strict oversight over city aid. All seven Council Members praised investments in the Durham Minimum Livable Wage, fare-free buses, HEART expansion, park lead remediation ($12M total), one-way street conversions, eviction diversion, and low-income homeowner property tax relief before passing the budget unanimously 7-0.

agenda_items.title: FY2025-26 Budget and FY2026-31 Capital Improvement Plan (CIP) Ordinance and Related Ordinances
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Residents Sharita Burrus and Karen Abram Jones pulled Item 6; Burrus questioned DHA's $5M Duke Energy debt, unaddressed mold and air conditioning repairs, and ERAP spending, urging strict oversight of city funds. All seven Council Members commended Manager Bo Ferguson's balanced $700M+ budget at a 43.71-cent tax rate post-revaluation, highlighting Durham Minimum Livable Wage raises, part-time step boosts, fare-free GoDurham service, HEART expansion, $7M additional park lead remediation, Duke/Gregson and Roxboro/Mangum street conversions, $500k in homeowner tax relief, eviction diversion, immigrant legal defense, guaranteed income, and youth violence grants. Council unanimously adopted the budget 7-0.

votes.item_title: Adopt FY2025-26 Budget and FY2026-31 Capital Improvement Plan (CIP) Ordinance and Related Ordinances
votes.notes: Clip corresponds verbatim to Item 6 of the full June 16, 2025 City Council meeting (Dc4_5Ecg8kQ), where the clerk announced unanimous 7-0 adoption.
votes.discussion_detail: Item 6 was pulled from the consent agenda by residents Sharita Burrus and Karen Abram Jones; Burrus delivered pointed testimony demanding transparency and maintenance accountability from Durham Housing Authority before additional city funds flow to public housing. Following public comment, every Council Member praised City Manager Bo Ferguson's inaugural $700M+ budget and FY2026-31 CIP, noting that roughly half of the property tax rate increase (to 43.71 cents per $100 following a 71.6% average revaluation) stems from voters' November 2024 $200M bond package. Members highlighted signature investments in the Durham Minimum Livable Wage, fare-free buses, HEART team expansion, $7M more ($12M total) for park lead soil remediation, one-way street safety conversions, $500k in low-income homeowner relief, eviction diversion, immigrant defense, guaranteed income, and youth violence grants. Moved and seconded collectively by the entire Council as printed, the budget ordinance passed unanimously 7-0.

meetings.title: Durham City Council June 16, 2025
meetings.executive_summary: At its June 16, 2025 regular meeting, the Durham City Council issued proclamations for Cleft and Craniofacial Awareness Month and Juneteenth Week 2025, then approved the consent agenda 7-0 alongside separate recusal-adjusted 6-0 votes for Downtown Durham Inc. contracts and Legal Aid of NC's $725,000 Eviction Diversion Program. Council unanimously passed a $1.5M conditional loan commitment to the Durham Housing Authority and adopted the $700M+ FY2025-26 Budget and FY2026-31 CIP 7-0. In public hearings, Council approved the Methodist Street Townhouses rezoning 6-1 (Carl Rist Nay), unanimously approved the East Cornwallis Road townhome rezoning 7-0, continued the Heritage Square rezoning (401 E. Lakewood Ave) to August 4, and voted to cancel July meetings and excuse Chelsea Cook from the August 4 morning work session.

agenda_items.title: Proclamations, Community Announcements & Referral Back of Item 24
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Council issued proclamations for Cleft and Craniofacial Awareness Month (accepted by Isabella Roberts) and Juneteenth Week 2025 (accepted by Aya Shabu of the Durham Juneteenth Collective). Members reflected on the assassinations of Minnesota lawmakers, the No Kings march, ICE enforcement, Urban Ministries cuts, $300k in Bull City Future Fund grants, and Communications Director Beverly Thompson's retirement, while City Manager Bo Ferguson referred Item 24 (401 Morreene Rd condemnation) back to General Services.

agenda_items.title: Consent Agenda Adoption (Excluding Items 6, 7, 8, 29, 30, GBA Items & Referred Item 24)
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Council approved the bulk of the June 16 consent agenda—covering board appointments, Habitat for Humanity minor repairs, homelessness services contracts, the SLBE ordinance, fire/city hall facility designs, and water/sewer infrastructure awards—while pulling Items 6, 7, 8, 29, and 30 and keeping Items 13, 39, 40, and 41 on the General Business Agenda.

agenda_items.title: Downtown Durham, Inc. Municipal Service District Amendment ($2,278,030) & Economic Development Agreement ($170,048)
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Council Member Carl Rist recused himself from both Downtown Durham, Inc. (DDI) items as DDI's representative. Council approved the Fifth Amendment to the FY22-26 Municipal Service District contract ($2,278,030 FY26, $8,370,230 cap) and the $170,048 FY26 economic development agreement in consecutive 6-0 votes.

agenda_items.title: Legal Aid of North Carolina Eviction Diversion Program Contract ($725,000)
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Previously pulled at work session and placed on the General Business Agenda for recusal, Item 13 authorized Legal Aid of North Carolina to continue administering Durham's Eviction Diversion Program for $725,000. Council Member Chelsea Cook recused herself, and the remaining six members passed three motions—approving the recommendation, executing the contract, and authorizing sundry non-cost-increasing modifications—by 6-0 tallies.

agenda_items.title: Amendment to Interlocal Agreement for City-County Strategic Youth Initiatives
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Resident Alexandria Valderez pulled Item 8 to highlight Phase I and II of the Youth Mentoring Alliance led by the Youth Mentoring Collaborative and the Office on Youth, including a community resource map presented nationally in Minneapolis. Council thanked the advocates and approved the amended Interlocal Agreement 7-0.

agenda_items.title: Durham Housing Authority (DHA) $1,500,000 Conditional Binding Commitment of Loan Assistance
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Mayor Leonardo Williams pulled Item 7 to clarify earlier work-session remarks, stressing that chronic federal HUD underinvestment—not local blame-shifting—drove DHA's crisis while insisting that DHA and residents uphold mutual accountability alongside city aid. Council adopted three motions issuing the $1.5M conditional loan commitment, authorizing execution of loan documents, and permitting favorable modifications in unanimous 7-0 votes.

agenda_items.title: FY2025-26 Budget and FY2026-31 Capital Improvement Plan (CIP) Ordinance & Related Ordinances
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Following Sharita Burrus's testimony demanding DHA accountability and Karen Abram Jones's signup, all seven Council Members highlighted key investments in the $700M+ budget (43.71 cents tax rate post-revaluation, DMLW raises, fare-free buses, HEART expansion, park lead remediation, one-way street conversion design, and homeowner property tax relief). Council unanimously adopted the budget 7-0.

agenda_items.title: Zoning Map Change: Methodist Street Townhouses (2403 & 2405 S. Miami Blvd)
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Silver Developers (Vince DeFreitas and owner Mr. Singh) requested rezoning 1.19 acres from Commercial Neighborhood to PDR 15.126 for 18 townhomes priced around $400k-$600k, proffering $5,000 to Durham Public Schools during the hearing after initially declining proffers. Carl Rist opposed the rezoning as inconsistent with the Neighborhood Services place type and lacking affordable housing or transit proffers, while Mark-Anthony Middleton, Nate Baker, and Leonardo Williams supported giving grace to a first-time local infill builder. The rezoning passed 6-1, and the consistency statement passed 7-0.

agenda_items.title: Zoning Map Change: 1606 & 1608 East Cornwallis Road
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Applicant representative Pam Porter (TMTLA) presented a residential rezoning from RS-20 to PDR 10.205 on 0.98 acres for up to 10 townhomes—replacing a 2022 commercial application that was denied—with commitments for a bus shelter/pullout if needed, $1,000 to DPS, $5,000 to the Dedicated Housing Fund, and native plantings. Council unanimously approved the rezoning and consistency statement 7-0.

agenda_items.title: Zoning Map Change: 401 East Lakewood Avenue & 600 Fayetteville Street (Heritage Square Continuance)
agenda_items.discussion_summary: With 25 speakers signed up, applicant attorney Jamie Schwedler requested continuing the Heritage Square (DDS1/DDS2 to DDC) hearing to August 4 to continue negotiating a Declaration of Restrictive Covenants with Hayti leaders and institutions including St. Mark's AME Zion Church. Mayor Leonardo Williams and Mayor Pro Tempore Mark-Anthony Middleton emphasized that only Council-adopted development conditions—not private side agreements—are enforceable by the city, and Council granted the continuance by consensus.

agenda_items.title: July Recess Rescheduling & Excused Absence for Council Member Chelsea Cook
agenda_items.discussion_summary: After rescinding an initial 9:00 AM proposal, Council voted 7-0 to cancel July meetings and reschedule the July 24 work session to August 4, 2025 at 10:00 AM. Council also opened an electronic vote granting Chelsea Cook an excused absence for the August 4 morning session because she was starting a new job that day, before adjourning at 10:14 PM.

votes.item_title: Adopt Consent Agenda (Excluding Pulled Items 6, 7, 8, 29, 30, GBA Items 13, 39-41, and Referred Item 24)
votes.notes: Item 24 referred back to General Services; Items 29-30 pulled for Rist recusal; Item 13 on GBA for Cook recusal; Items 6, 7, 8 pulled for discussion.
votes.discussion_detail: After Mayor Leonardo Williams noted Item 24's referral back to General Services and Council and residents pulled Items 6, 7, 8, 29, and 30 from consent, Council took up the remainder of the consent agenda (including Items 1-5, 9-12, 14-23, 25-28, 31-38, 43, and 45). Council Member Chelsea Cook moved adoption with the noted exceptions, and Council Member Nate Baker seconded. The consent agenda passed unanimously 7-0.

votes.item_title: Item 29: Fifth Amendment to FY2022-26 Contract with Downtown Durham, Inc. for Municipal Service District Operations ($2,278,030 FY26 / $8,370,230 Cap)
votes.notes: Council Member Carl Rist recused himself as DDI board/organizational representative.
votes.discussion_detail: Council Member Carl Rist pulled Item 29 from the consent agenda in order to recuse himself due to his affiliation with Downtown Durham, Inc. (DDI). The fifth amendment authorized $2,278,030 for FY2025-26 Municipal Service District operations, raising the total multi-year contract cap to $8,370,230 subject to budget adoption. After initially misreading the tally as 7-0, the Clerk corrected the record to 6-0 with Rist recused.

votes.item_title: Item 30: FY2025-26 Economic Development Programs and Services Agreement with Downtown Durham, Inc. ($170,048)
votes.notes: Council Member Carl Rist recused himself as DDI representative.
votes.discussion_detail: Pulled alongside Item 29 for conflict-of-interest recusal by Council Member Carl Rist, Item 30 authorized the City Manager to execute an economic development agreement with Downtown Durham, Inc. not to exceed $170,048 for FY2025-26 using City funds. The motion was moved, seconded, and approved 6-0 with Rist recused.

votes.item_title: Item 13a: Approve Recommendation to Contract with Legal Aid of North Carolina for Eviction Diversion Program
votes.notes: Council Member Chelsea Cook recused herself due to employment/affiliation with Legal Aid of NC.
votes.discussion_detail: Moved to the General Business Agenda at the June 5 work session to accommodate Council Member Chelsea Cook's recusal, Item 13 required three separate formal actions for the Eviction Diversion Program contract with Legal Aid of North Carolina (LANC). On the first motion approving the staff recommendation to enter into the contract, Council voted 6-0 with Cook recused.

votes.item_title: Item 13b: Authorize Execution of $725,000 Eviction Diversion Program Contract with Legal Aid of North Carolina
votes.notes: Funds mediation, legal assistance, and tenant/landlord education for low-to-moderate income renters.
votes.discussion_detail: As the second motion under Item 13, Council considered authorizing the City Manager to approve and execute a $725,000 contract with Legal Aid of North Carolina providing mediation, legal representation, and tenant/landlord education for low- to moderate-income renters facing eviction for nonpayment of rent. With Council Member Chelsea Cook recused, the remaining six Council Members approved the contract 6-0.

votes.item_title: Item 13c: Authorize City Manager to Make Sundry Scope Changes to Legal Aid of NC Contract (Within Total Amount)
votes.notes: Council Member Chelsea Cook recused.
votes.discussion_detail: In the final motion under Item 13, Council authorized the City Manager to execute sundry modifications to the Eviction Diversion Program scope of services with Legal Aid of North Carolina so long as the $725,000 total contract cap remains unchanged. With Council Member Chelsea Cook recused, the motion carried 6-0.

votes.item_title: Item 8: Execute Amended Interlocal Agreement with Durham County for City-County Strategic Youth Initiatives
votes.notes: Pulled by resident Alexandria Valderez to showcase Youth Mentoring Alliance mapping and Phase I-II achievements.
votes.discussion_detail: Item 8 was pulled by resident speaker Alexandria Valderez, who spoke in support of the Youth Mentoring Alliance's partnership with Durham's Office on Youth, noting its zip-code mentoring resource map and national presentation in Minneapolis. Council Members commended the youth-led mentoring coalition and moved to authorize execution of the amended City-County Strategic Youth Initiatives Interlocal Agreement. The motion passed unanimously 7-0.

votes.item_title: Item 7a: Issue Conditional Binding Commitment of Loan Assistance up to $1,500,000 to Durham Housing Authority (DHA)
votes.notes: Mayor Leonardo Williams pulled Item 7 to clarify federal HUD underfunding context alongside expectations for DHA operational sustainability.
votes.discussion_detail: Mayor Leonardo Williams pulled Item 7 to address online backlash to his June 5 work-session comments on Durham Housing Authority rent collections, emphasizing that decades of federal HUD underinvestment created DHA's structural crisis while reiterating that DHA must maintain operational accountability alongside city aid. After Mayor Williams initially misread the wrong motion text, he entertained the correct motion authorizing a conditional binding loan commitment of up to $1,500,000 to DHA. Council passed the commitment unanimously 7-0.

votes.item_title: Item 7b: Authorize City Manager to Execute All Necessary Documents for $1,500,000 DHA Loan Commitment
votes.notes: Second of three implementing motions for DHA operational assistance commitment.
votes.discussion_detail: Immediately after approving the $1.5 million conditional binding commitment to the Durham Housing Authority, Council voted on the second required motion authorizing the City Manager to execute all legal documents and instruments needed to carry out the commitment. The motion was seconded and approved unanimously 7-0.

votes.item_title: Item 7c: Authorize City Manager to Make Non-Cost-Increasing Changes to DHA Commitment Favorable to City Interests
votes.notes: Third of three motions under Item 7.
votes.discussion_detail: In the third and final motion under Item 7, Council authorized the City Manager to make necessary and appropriate adjustments to the Durham Housing Authority loan commitment provided such changes do not increase the City's financial obligations and remain favorable to Durham's interests. The motion passed unanimously 7-0.

votes.item_title: Item 6: Adopt FY2025-26 Budget and FY2026-31 Capital Improvement Plan (CIP) Ordinance and Related Ordinances
votes.notes: Budget surpasses $700M with a 43.71-cent property tax rate post-revaluation; moved and seconded by entire Council.
votes.discussion_detail: Pulled by Sharita Burrus and Karen Abram Jones, Item 6 featured public testimony from Burrus urging accountability for DHA maintenance and $5M Duke Energy arrears before any new aid. All seven Council Members then offered detailed remarks praising City Manager Bo Ferguson's first budget, highlighting the $200M bond debt service, Durham Minimum Livable Wage raises, fare-free buses, HEART expansion, $12M total for park lead remediation, one-way street safety conversions, eviction diversion, immigrant defense, guaranteed income, and $500k in low-income homeowner relief. Moved and seconded as printed by the entire Council, the FY2025-26 Budget and FY2026-31 CIP passed unanimously 7-0.

votes.item_title: Item 39a: Zoning Map Change Ordinance — Methodist Street Townhouses (2403 & 2405 S. Miami Blvd, CN to PDR 15.126)
votes.notes: Up to 18 townhomes on 1.19 acres; property owner Mr. Singh added a $5,000 proffer to Durham Public Schools during the hearing.
votes.discussion_detail: Applicant Vince DeFreitas and owner Mr. Singh of Silver Developers sought to rezone 1.19 acres at 2403 and 2405 South Miami Boulevard from Commercial Neighborhood to PDR 15.126 for 18 townhomes priced between $400,000 and $600,000. Planning staff found the request generally inconsistent with the Neighborhood Services place type, and Council Member Carl Rist questioned the lack of affordable housing or transit proffers before voting No. After owner Singh offered a $5,000 proffer to Durham Public Schools from the podium, Mayor Pro Tempore Mark-Anthony Middleton, Nate Baker, and Mayor Leonardo Williams argued for extending grace to a small first-time local infill developer, carrying the rezoning 6-1.

votes.item_title: Item 39b: NCGS 160D-605 Consistency Statement for Methodist Street Townhouses Rezoning (2403 & 2405 S. Miami Blvd)
votes.notes: Updates Place Type Map designation from Neighborhood Services to Apartment and Townhouse Neighborhood.
votes.discussion_detail: Following the 6-1 approval of the Methodist Street Townhouses rezoning on South Miami Boulevard, Council took up the companion statutory consistency statement under NCGS 160D-605 amending the Place Type Map from Neighborhood Services to Apartment and Townhouse Neighborhood. Despite his dissent on the rezoning itself, Council Member Carl Rist joined the rest of Council to approve the consistency statement unanimously 7-0.

votes.item_title: Item 40a: Zoning Map Change Ordinance — 1606 & 1608 East Cornwallis Road (RS-20 to PDR 10.205)
votes.notes: Up to 10 townhomes on 0.98 acres with $5,000 Dedicated Housing Fund proffer, $1,000 DPS proffer, and transit bus shelter/pullout commitment.
votes.discussion_detail: Representative Pam Porter of TMTLA presented a rezoning request for 0.98 acres at 1606 and 1608 East Cornwallis Road from RS-20 to PDR 10.205 to permit up to 10 townhomes, replacing a commercial rezoning application previously denied in 2022. The revised residential proposal committed to native plantings, a bus shelter or pullout pad if requested by transit staff, $1,000 for Durham Public Schools, and $5,000 for the Dedicated Housing Fund. With no objections from speakers or Council, the rezoning passed unanimously 7-0.

votes.item_title: Item 40b: NCGS 160D-605 Consistency Statement for 1606 & 1608 East Cornwallis Road Rezoning
votes.notes: Required statutory consistency finding following unanimous rezoning approval.
votes.discussion_detail: Immediately after approving the 1606 and 1608 East Cornwallis Road townhome rezoning 7-0, Council voted on the companion NCGS 160D-605 consistency statement. Without further debate, Council adopted the consistency statement unanimously 7-0.

votes.item_title: Reschedule July 24, 2025 Work Session to August 4, 2025 at 10:00 AM (Canceling July Council Meetings)
votes.notes: Initial 9:00 AM proposal was rescinded in favor of 10:00 AM prior to the formal vote.

After rescinding an initial 9:00 AM start time suggestion, Council settled on 10:00 AM so both meetings could occur on August 4 with a midday break. meetings.title: Joint City County Committee Meeting June 10, 2025
meetings.executive_summary: The Joint City-County Committee met with Mayor Pro Tempore Mark-Anthony Middleton representing City leadership while Mayor Leonardo Williams was traveling. Staff from Durham County Justice Services, the City Community Safety Department (HEART), Housing for New Homes, and Duke University presented cross-system data and pilot results from the Familiar Faces / Familiar Neighbors initiative, alongside plans to launch a homelessness strategic plan with Community Solutions in July 2025. The Coalition to End the HIV Epidemic in Durham proposed a $2.5 million three-year coordinated care and housing system and criticized DSS/Entry Point bottlenecks, prompting pushback from elected officials over existing Continuum of Care workflows, dashboard integration, and competitive RFP requirements. Committee members also reviewed a $500,000 joint funding request from the Durham Museum of History—debating whether local governments should fund nonprofit operating costs—and discussed coordinating fragmented before- and after-school childcare with Durham Public Schools; no formal votes were taken.

agenda_items.title: Call to Order, Welcome, and Opening Remarks
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Committee leaders opened the Joint City-County Committee meeting at City Hall and noted that Mayor Leonardo Williams was traveling on behalf of the City while Mayor Pro Tempore Mark-Anthony Middleton was present. Elected officials from the City Council and Board of County Commissioners welcomed students, families, and Durham Public Schools staff before beginning the presentations.

agenda_items.title: Familiar Faces / Familiar Neighbors Initiative and Homelessness Strategic Plan
agenda_items.discussion_summary: County Justice Services Director, City Community Safety Director Ryan Smith, Housing for New Homes Executive Director Russell Pierce, Duke researcher Nicole, and Community Safety strategist Sheila presented merged detention, Duke Health ED, Alliance Health, and HEART crisis-response data showing that 76 residents accounted for roughly 15% of all 2024 arrests (12 to 36 arrests each) and that co-occurring serious mental illness, substance use disorder, and chronic homelessness drive repeated system cycling. Staff detailed intensive field outreach under the joint pilot—including cases taking over 400 days to secure IDs, SSI income, and permanent supportive housing—and highlighted gaps in non-congregate shelter, street psychiatry, and real-time data sharing. Officials also received an update on a City Manager-directed homelessness system strategic plan launching in July 2025 with Community Solutions (Built for Zero) to produce a governance framework by December 2025.

agenda_items.title: Coalition to End the HIV Epidemic in Durham — Housing and Care System Proposal
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Dr. Haley Cunningham and Yolanda Foster (Southeast Community Resources) presented on behalf of the Coalition to End the HIV Epidemic in Durham, emphasizing that Black and Latino residents comprise 74% of local HIV cases and that unstable housing sharply elevates AIDS mortality and blocks viral suppression. Presenters criticized fragmented City/County systems and centralized DSS/Entry Point bottlenecks, requesting $2.5 million over three years for a community-led 'no wrong door' care system, an integrated data dashboard, and inclusion in Five-Year Consolidated and Annual Action Plan planning. Committee members pushed back, stating Durham already operates a Continuum of Care 'no wrong door' coordinated entry system, insisting dashboards be integrated into the broader homeless strategy rather than siloed, and noting nonprofit funding requires a competitive RFP process.

agenda_items.title: Durham Museum of History Belt Line Facility and Funding Request
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Museum of History representatives outlined plans for a signature cultural destination along the Durham Belt Line / Rail Trail and requested $500,000 jointly from the City and County for feasibility planning and operating/living-wage staffing support (including an education coordinator). While some members expressed enthusiasm for the Belt Line trail-side museum vision and capital feasibility study, other committee members raised concerns that budget work sessions had already concluded and argued that local governments should limit funding to capital projects rather than underwriting recurring nonprofit operating expenses without a sustainability plan.

agenda_items.title: Before- and After-School Care Coordination and Joint City-County-DPS Work Planning
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Committee members discussed fragmented before- and after-school childcare across Durham Parks and Recreation, DPS Community Education waitlists, and nonprofit providers such as the Boys & Girls Club and Early Years/Durham PreK, recommending a focused presentation at the August joint meeting with DPS. Members also revisited a September 2024 DPS request for a three-entity (City, County, DPS) working group and urged staff to develop a more strategic, proactive multi-body work plan covering childcare, transit, school walk zones, land-use infrastructure, and economic development to avoid program duplication and reduce recurring tax increases.

disagreements.meeting_title: Joint City County Committee Meeting June 10, 2025
disagreements.issue: City-County Funding Scope for Durham Museum of History ($500,000 Capital vs. Operating Support)
disagreements.summary: Committee members split over whether the City and County should fulfill the Durham Museum of History's late-stage $500,000 request covering both feasibility planning and operating/staffing expenses.
disagreements.side_a_position: Support fulfilling the $500,000 joint request ahead of final budget adoption, including feasibility planning and living-wage staff support.
side_a_arguments: The amount is minimal relative to City and County budgets and builds directly on prior feasibility investments.
Supporting living-wage increases aligns with local government priorities and advances a signature Belt Line cultural and tourism destination.
disagreements.side_b_position: Restrict local government support to capital/feasibility planning and avoid last-minute budget additions for nonprofit operating expenses.
side_b_arguments: Final budget work sessions had already taken place, making late operating and new staff-position requests procedurally problematic.
Local governments cannot serve as an open checkbook for nonprofit operating costs across Durham's large nonprofit sector without a clear sustainability and fundraising plan.
disagreements.resolution: No formal vote was taken; committee members directed discussion toward capital/feasibility alignment and sustainability planning outside the committee session (individual speakers were not identified by name in the audio transcript).

disagreements.meeting_title: Joint City County Committee Meeting June 10, 2025
disagreements.issue: Coalition to End the HIV Epidemic Intake System Critique and Standalone Dashboard Request
disagreements.summary: Coalition presenters and committee officials disagreed on whether Durham's centralized DSS/Entry Point homelessness intake fails HIV-positive residents and whether the Coalition should receive $2.5 million for a separate system and dashboard.
disagreements.side_a_position: Replace reliance on centralized DSS/Entry Point intake with a decentralized, Coalition-led 'no wrong door' care system, standalone data dashboard, and $2.5 million in funding.
side_a_arguments: HIV-positive patients referred to DSS frequently fail to receive housing placements, and centralized intake creates privacy and access barriers.
Existing HIV providers lack funding, capacity, and a formal seat at Consolidated Plan and Action Plan tables despite HOPWA funds sitting unspent.
disagreements.side_b_position: Maintain Continuum of Care coordinated entry standards, integrate any HIV data into the unified homeless strategic plan, and award nonprofit funds only via competitive RFP.
side_b_arguments: Durham already operates a Continuum of Care-required 'no wrong door' coordinated entry system rather than an exclusionary single-door process.
Building a separate dashboard outside the broader homeless strategic plan duplicates effort, and under tight budgets any nonprofit funding must go through an RFP process.
disagreements.resolution: No formal vote was taken; officials asked staff to ensure HIV housing needs are coordinated within the broader homelessness strategic plan and RFP framework (individual speakers were not identified by name in the audio transcript).
