meetings.title: Durham City Council Work Session March 20, 2025 (livestream)
meetings.executive_summary: With Mayor Pro Tempore Mark-Anthony Middleton presiding throughout (Mayor Leonardo Williams arrived later and asked Middleton to continue presiding), Council suspended its rules to approve a $353,900 contract with Contact Tech Systems Inc. to overhaul Council Chambers broadcast equipment (6-0) and voted to hold a closed session under N.C.G.S. 143-318.11(a)(6). Residents of the Veranda at Whitted School senior apartments testified extensively about severe building security, sanitation, and maintenance failures, while Council reviewed pulled items including the Revised Code of Ethics (referred back to Procedures Committee), Sandy Ridge revenue bonds, Western Intake water partnership amendments, and biosolids hauling costs. Council also received detailed presentations on the Vision Zero Action Plan—sparking a pointed exchange over comparing traffic-fatality data tools to gun violence detection—and the draft Parks and Recreation Comprehensive Plan before settling the April 7 agenda (7-0).

agenda_items.title: City Manager's Priority Items, Broadcast Equipment Contract ($353,900), and Closed Session
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Council voted 6-0 to receive the City Manager's Priority Items, suspend rules to act immediately on Item 6, and approve a $353,900 contract with Contact Tech Systems Inc. to upgrade Council Chambers broadcast and AV equipment, followed by a 6-0 vote to hold a closed session at the conclusion of business regarding an employee reporting to the City Manager.

agenda_items.title: Public Comment on Veranda at Whitted School Senior Living Conditions and Disaster Preparedness
agenda_items.discussion_summary: DeWarren Langley spoke regarding Charles Hamilton Houston Foundation civic work, James Chavis raised disaster-preparedness concerns, and Jacqueline Wagstaff alongside Veranda at Whitted School residents Helen Pereira, Rhoda Blunt, Regina Royer, Pastor Ann Jacob, and Regina Mays testified about broken exterior doors, unauthorized occupants, drug smoke, sewage/water leaks, and unresponsive property management at the City-supported senior housing complex.

agenda_items.title: Revised City Code of Ethics (Pulled Item)
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Council Member Chelsea Cook pulled Item 5 to question proposed language governing council interactions with staff and other provisions in the revised Code of Ethics. Following discussion, the item was referred back to the Procedures Committee for further refinement.

agenda_items.title: Pulled Consent Items: Sandy Ridge Housing Bonds, Western Intake HDR Amendment, and Biosolids Hauling
agenda_items.discussion_summary: On Item 7, Community Development Assistant Director Tenya Coleman and Durham Housing Authority staff detailed the $42 million capital stack, RAD transfers, and $23 million total multifamily housing revenue bonds for Sandy Ridge Station and Sandy Ridge Villas. On Item 18, Water Management staff explained Amendment #4 with HDR for the Western Intake Partnership (securing Durham's 16.5 MGD Jordan Lake allocation alongside Chatham, Pittsboro, and OWASA), and on Item 19 staff explained rising PFAS landfill testing costs and staffing pressures on the biosolids hauling contract.

agenda_items.title: Vision Zero Action Plan Presentation
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Transportation Director Sean Egan and staffer Lauren Grove presented the Vision Zero Action Plan, showing that 10% of Durham's street network accounts for 74% of fatalities and serious injuries and setting targets of a 50% reduction by 2035 and zero fatalities by 2045. During Q&A, Mayor Leonardo Williams and Mark-Anthony Middleton pressed for applying similar data urgency and tracking to gun violence, prompting DeDreana Freeman to warn against diverting funds toward ShotSpotter-style policing surveillance over root-cause investments.

agenda_items.title: Draft Durham Parks and Recreation Comprehensive Plan
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Parks and Recreation Director Wade Walcutt and McAdams consultant Austin Bowman presented the draft Comprehensive Plan organized around five guiding principles and top 15 two-year action items, including expanding the Half Penny for Parks, land banking, and facility maintenance. Council members questioned park equity, financing, and neighborhood HOA park turnovers such as Carolina Arbors.

agenda_items.title: Settle Agenda for April 7, 2025 Regular City Council Meeting
agenda_items.discussion_summary: City Manager Bo Ferguson summarized the agenda configuration with Consent Items 1–4 and 6–19, Item 5 referred back to Procedures Committee, and GBA Public Hearing Item 21 (Sheffield Farms). Council voted unanimously 7-0 to settle the agenda before entering closed session.

votes.item_title: Receive City Manager's Priority Items (Item 6 Broadcast Contract, Item 16 Vision Zero Presentation, Closed Session Request)
votes.notes: Mayor Leonardo Williams was en route and arrived at 00:52:04.
votes.discussion_detail: Opening the March 20, 2025 Work Session, Mayor Pro Tempore Mark-Anthony Middleton noted that Mayor Leonardo Williams was running late and asked to receive the City Manager's Priority Items so Council could act quickly on urgent contract and schedule items. The priority package included suspending rules to vote on Item 6 (Council Chambers broadcast equipment), scheduling the Item 16 Vision Zero presentation, and requesting a closed session at the close of business. Without objection, a motion and second were offered and passed 6-0 by voice vote among all members present.

votes.item_title: Suspend Council Rules to Take Action on Item 6 During Work Session
votes.notes: Rules suspension required to award Item 6 contract at a Work Session; Leonardo Williams en route.
votes.discussion_detail: Because Durham City Council Work Sessions normally only review items for future Regular Meeting consent placement rather than taking final contract votes, Council needed to suspend its procedural rules to act on Item 6 immediately. Mayor Pro Tempore Mark-Anthony Middleton called for a motion to suspend the rules to consider the broadcast equipment contract. No member objected or requested delay. The motion was seconded and carried 6-0 by voice vote.

votes.item_title: Item 6: Contract with Contact Tech Systems Inc. for Council Chambers Broadcast Equipment Overhaul ($353,900)
votes.notes: Authorizes purchase contract not to exceed $353,900; finalized by clerk confirmation at 00:06:57; Leonardo Williams absent at time of vote.
votes.discussion_detail: Immediately following rules suspension, Council considered Item 6 to authorize a purchase contract with Contact Tech Systems Inc. for a broadcast and audio-visual equipment overhaul in City Council Chambers in an amount not to exceed $353,900. Staff had flagged the item as a time-sensitive priority so equipment procurement and installation could stay on schedule without waiting for the next Regular Meeting cycle. No questions or dissent were raised by the six Council members present. Council approved the contract 6-0 by voice vote, with the City Clerk confirming final recording at 00:06:57.

votes.item_title: Convene Closed Session Pursuant to N.C.G.S. 143-318.11(a)(6) at Conclusion of Meeting
votes.notes: Closed session under N.C.G.S. 143-318.11(a)(6) to consider qualifications, performance, or complaints concerning an individual employee reporting directly to the City Manager.
votes.discussion_detail: Mayor Pro Tempore Mark-Anthony Middleton read the statutory motion to convene a closed session at the conclusion of the Work Session pursuant to N.C.G.S. 143-318.11(a)(6) to consider personnel matters—specifically qualifications, competence, performance, or complaints involving an individual employee reporting directly to the City Manager. The motion specified that the closed session would occur after all open-session agenda business concluded. No Council member raised objections. The motion passed 6-0 by voice vote.

disagreements.meeting_title: Durham City Council Work Session March 20, 2025 (livestream)
disagreements.issue: Applying Data-Driven Policing and Gunshot Detection Tools Versus Root-Cause Investments in Gun Violence Response
disagreements.summary: Following the Vision Zero traffic-safety presentation, Council members disagreed over whether Durham should pair Vision Zero-style data dashboards with gunshot detection/law-enforcement technology or avoid expanding policing surveillance technologies.
disagreements.side_a_position: Apply Vision Zero-level urgency, dashboards, and gunshot-detection/law-enforcement technology alongside community efforts to curb gun violence.
side_a_arguments: Gun violence kills young people in Durham at devastating rates, warranting the same measurable goal-setting and public dashboard transparency as traffic fatalities.
Mayor Pro Tempore Mark-Anthony Middleton advocated a 'both/and' approach incorporating technology (referencing ShotSpotter and law enforcement tools) alongside community interventions.
disagreements.side_b_position: Reject diverting public tax dollars toward acoustic gunshot surveillance or punitive policing expansions rather than survivor and root-cause investments.
side_b_arguments: Technology like ShotSpotter did not demonstrate effective outcomes in Durham and risks diverting taxpayer funds from community-centered prevention.
Durham should prioritize investments in underlying socioeconomic causes and support for survivors and affected neighborhoods.
disagreements.resolution: Exchange ended without formal action during the Vision Zero Q&A.

meetings.title: Durham City Council March 17, 2025 with closed captioning
meetings.executive_summary: At its March 17, 2025 Regular Meeting with all seven members present, the Durham City Council approved the Consent Agenda (Items 1–28) 7-0, adopted a joint resolution urging the lifting of the federal USAID foreign-assistance stop-work order 7-0, and unanimously approved the Chin Page Road Apartments rezoning (up to 360 units with doubled 6% affordability at 60% AMI) and the 1012 Valmet Drive annexation and translational zoning. Following nearly two and a half hours of heated public testimony and Council debate, Council split 4-3 to approve the Pickett Apartments rezoning (up to 140 multifamily units adjacent to Sandy Creek Park with a bird-safe glass proffer and $300,000 redirected to Durham Parks Foundation for park connectivity), with Baker, Cook, and Freeman dissenting over sidewalk connectivity and riparian/watershed impacts. Council concluded by holding the Item 29 FY 2025-26 Budget and CIP public hearing until 11:56 PM.

agenda_items.title: Consent Agenda Adoption
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Following ceremonial Women's History Month and National Disability Awareness Month recognitions and announcements, Council adopted Consent Agenda Items 1 through 28 without pulling any items.

agenda_items.title: Resolution Calling for Immediate Lifting of Stop Work Order on Foreign Assistance Programs and Re-Opening of USAID
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Breanna Clark-Schwelm of the NC Global Health Alliance testified on devastating local layoffs and disrupted global health programs across Durham's Triangle-based nonprofits and universities caused by federal USAID funding halts. Council unanimously adopted the resolution.

agenda_items.title: Public Hearing: Zoning Map Change — Chin Page Road Apartments (Z2400001)
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Applicant attorney Nil Ghosh presented the 14.9-acre Chin Page Road rezoning for up to 360 multifamily units (PDR 24.115), adding on-the-record proffers increasing affordability from 3% to 6% at 60% AMI for 30 years, elevators, 21% tree preservation, native plantings, and industrial/warehouse exclusions. Council unanimously approved both the rezoning and its consistency statement.

agenda_items.title: Public Hearing: Consolidated Annexation and Translational Zoning — 1012 Valmet Drive
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Planning staff presented the 6.2-acre voluntary annexation and utility extension agreement for 1012 Valmet Drive (Virk Holding LLC) for up to 12 single-family homes under RS-20 Falls/Jordan District B Overlay zoning. Council unanimously approved annexation, translational zoning, and consistency.
agenda_items.vote_summary: Annexation, Zoning, and Consistency Statement approved 7-0

agenda_items.title: Public Hearing: Zoning Map Change — Pickett Apartments (Z2400024)
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Over more than two hours of public comment and Council deliberation, residents and environmental advocates raised sharp concerns over narrow Pickett Road's lack of sidewalks/transit, stormwater runoff into Sandy Creek, and loss of mature tree canopy, while proponents cited the need for 140 apartments inside the Urban Growth Boundary and the applicant added a bird-safe glass proffer and redirected $300,000 to Durham Parks Foundation for Pickett Rd/Sandy Creek connectivity. Council approved the rezoning 4-3 (Baker, Cook, Freeman opposed) and the consistency statement 6-1 (Freeman opposed).

agenda_items.title: Public Hearing: FY 2025-26 Budget and FY 2026-31 Capital Improvement Plan (CIP)
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Budget Director Christina Riordan introduced the FY 2025-26 Budget and FY 2026-31 CIP hearing amid the 2025 property revaluation, followed by extensive public testimony on fare-free GoDurham transit, 24/7 HEART expansion, park lead abatement, festivals funding, living wages, and affordable housing before adjournment at 11:56 PM.
agenda_items.vote_summary: Public Hearing held and closed / No vote taken

votes.item_title: Item 33: Joint Resolution Calling for Immediate Lifting of Stop Work Order on Foreign Assistance Programs and Re-Opening of USAID
votes.notes: Joint Triangle-wide resolution highlighting local Triangle economic and public health impacts of federal USAID freeze.
votes.discussion_detail: Mayor Leonardo Williams introduced Item 33, a joint resolution developed across Triangle municipalities condemning the federal stop-work order on foreign assistance and dismantling of USAID, noting North Carolina is the fourth-largest recipient of USAID funding with over $1 billion infused into the state economy and more than 2,700 local Triangle jobs at risk at firms like RTI and FHI 360. Breanna Clark-Schwelm of the NC Global Health Alliance testified that Durham-based researchers and nonprofits had already experienced furloughs and terminated grants affecting global infectious disease and maternal health work. Following brief supportive remarks from Council members underscoring Durham's workforce and civic values, Council adopted the resolution unanimously 7-0.

votes.item_title: Item 30: Zoning Map Change — Chin Page Road Apartments (Z2400001)
votes.notes: Rezones 14.9 acres at 4808-5006 Chin Page Rd to Planned Development Residential (PDR 24.115) for up to 360 multifamily units.
votes.discussion_detail: Planning staff presented Z2400001 to rezone 14.9 acres along Chin Page Road to PDR 24.115 for up to 360 multifamily apartments near Research Triangle Park employment centers. Applicant attorney Nil Ghosh read enhanced text commitments into the record at the hearing, doubling affordable housing from 3% to 6% of total units at 60% AMI for 30 years, committing to elevator access, 21% tree canopy coverage, native species landscaping, and prohibiting intensive commercial/industrial uses. No speakers appeared in opposition during the public hearing. Satisfied with the expanded affordability proffer and environmental commitments, Council voted unanimously 7-0 to approve the rezoning.

votes.item_title: Item 30: Comprehensive Plan Consistency Statement — Chin Page Road Apartments (Z2400001)
votes.notes: Required statutory consistency and reasonableness statement under N.C.G.S. 160D-605.
votes.discussion_detail: Immediately after approving the Chin Page Road rezoning 7-0, City Council considered the statutorily required plan consistency and reasonableness statement pursuant to N.C.G.S. 160D-605. Staff and Council found the multifamily residential density and enhanced affordable housing proffers aligned with the Durham Comprehensive Plan's growth and housing goals. A motion and second were heard on the floor. The consistency statement passed unanimously 7-0.

votes.item_title: Item 32: Consolidated Annexation and Utility Extension Agreement — 1012 Valmet Drive
votes.notes: Contiguous voluntary annexation of 6.2 acres (Virk Holding LLC) for up to 12 single-family lots.
votes.discussion_detail: Planning staff presented Item 32, a voluntary contiguous annexation petition and utility extension agreement with Virk Holding LLC covering 6.2 acres at 1012 Valmet Drive for up to 12 single-family residential lots inside the Urban Growth Boundary. No opposition speakers addressed the public hearing, and Council members raised no objections to extending water and sewer service under the utility agreement. A motion and second to adopt the annexation ordinance and authorize the utility extension agreement were made. Council approved the annexation unanimously 7-0.

votes.item_title: Item 32: Translational Zoning Map Change — 1012 Valmet Drive (RS-20 Falls/Jordan District B Overlay)
votes.notes: Applies identical RS-20 and Falls/Jordan District B watershed overlay zoning under City jurisdiction.
votes.discussion_detail: Following adoption of the 1012 Valmet Drive annexation ordinance, Council voted on the companion translational zoning map change to bring the 6.2-acre parcel from Durham County jurisdiction into City zoning while preserving its RS-20 and Falls/Jordan District B watershed overlay designation. Staff confirmed no density increase was sought beyond existing residential zoning. Council moved, seconded, and approved the translational zoning unanimously 7-0.

votes.item_title: Item 32: Comprehensive Plan Consistency Statement — 1012 Valmet Drive
votes.notes: N.C.G.S. 160D-605 consistency statement for 1012 Valmet Drive translational zoning.
votes.discussion_detail: As the third companion action on Item 32, Council voted on the statutory N.C.G.S. 160D-605 consistency and reasonableness statement for the 1012 Valmet Drive translational zoning map change. No additional debate occurred. The consistency statement passed unanimously 7-0.

votes.item_title: Item 31: Zoning Map Change — Pickett Apartments (Z2400024)
votes.notes: Rezones 6.12 acres at 3117-3127 Pickett Rd from RS-20 to PDR 36.176 for up to 140 apartments adjacent to Sandy Creek Park.
votes.discussion_detail: Item 31 drew nearly two and a half hours of contentious testimony and Council deliberation over rezoning 6.12 acres at 3117–3127 Pickett Road from RS-20 to PDR 36.176 for up to 140 apartments abutting Sandy Creek Park. Neighboring residents, Friends of Sandy Creek Park supporters, and environmentalists opposed the project due to narrow Pickett Road's lack of sidewalks and transit service, stormwater runoff, floodplain/riparian impacts along Sandy Creek, and tree loss, while housing advocates and the applicant cited acute housing scarcity and added modified proffers for bird-safe glass (ABC threat factor <=30) and $300,000 directed to the Durham Parks Foundation earmarked for Pickett Road/Sandy Creek connectivity. Council Members Nate Baker, Chelsea Cook, and DeDreana Freeman opposed the rezoning, arguing the site lacked safe pedestrian/transit access and stronger environmental protections (such as dark-sky lighting and pervious surfaces). Mayor Leonardo Williams, Mayor Pro Tempore Mark-Anthony Middleton, Javiera Caballero, and Carl Rist voted in favor, emphasizing the value of 140 infill apartments inside the Urban Growth Boundary near a park compared with 12 by-right single-family homes, passing the rezoning 4-3.

votes.item_title: Item 31: Comprehensive Plan Consistency Statement — Pickett Apartments (Z2400024)
votes.notes: Required N.C.G.S. 160D-605 statement following 4-3 rezoning passage; Baker and Cook joined majority on consistency/reasonableness while Freeman voted Nay.
votes.discussion_detail: Immediately after the 4-3 approval of the Pickett Apartments rezoning, Council voted on the required N.C.G.S. 160D-605 plan consistency and reasonableness statement. Council Members Nate Baker and Chelsea Cook joined Mayor Leonardo Williams, Mark-Anthony Middleton, Javiera Caballero, and Carl Rist in affirming the procedural consistency finding, whereas Council Member DeDreana Freeman maintained her opposition. The consistency statement passed 6-1.

disagreements.meeting_title: Durham City Council March 17, 2025 with closed captioning
disagreements.issue: Pickett Apartments Rezoning (Z2400024): Infill Housing Density Near Sandy Creek Park Versus Pedestrian Safety and Environmental Buffers
disagreements.summary: Council split 4-3 on whether a 140-unit multifamily development on narrow Pickett Road next to Sandy Creek Park appropriately advances infill housing goals or poses unmitigated pedestrian, transit, and watershed risks.
disagreements.side_a_position: Approve the 140-unit infill rezoning with enhanced bird-safe glass and a $300,000 Durham Parks Foundation connectivity proffer.
side_a_arguments: The parcel sits inside the Urban Growth Boundary adjacent to a major public park and can deliver 140 apartments—including affordable commitments—compared to roughly 12 by-right single-family homes.
The developer added meaningful proffers including ABC bird-friendly glass standards and $300,000 earmarked to Durham Parks Foundation for Pickett Road and Sandy Creek Park pedestrian connectivity.
disagreements.side_b_position: Deny the rezoning due to inadequate pedestrian/transit access on Pickett Road and insufficient stormwater, dark-sky, and riparian protections near Sandy Creek.
side_b_arguments: Pickett Road is narrow, lacks continuous sidewalks and high-frequency transit, and creates safety hazards for added multifamily traffic and pedestrians.

Intensifying impervious cover directly adjacent to Sandy Creek and mature upland/riparian canopy risks stormwater runoff and habitat degradation without stronger dark-sky and pervious-surface proffers.
disagreements.resolution: Rezoning approved 4-3 (consistency statement approved 6-1 with Freeman opposed).

meetings.title: Durham City Council Work Session March 6, 2025 (livestream)
meetings.executive_summary: With Council Member DeDreana Freeman excused absent, City Council approved receiving the City Manager's Priority Item (EBOP Annual Report presentation) 6-0 and convening a closed session at the end of business 6-0. Council reviewed pulled consent items—including opioid settlement RFP allocations, HR vendor pre-qualification agreements, pavement preservation contracts, early 2024 GO Bond contracting, the Duke/Gregson Street safety feasibility study, large water meter testing, and resident comments from Betsy Ross on Pickett Road—and received the 2024 Equal Business Opportunity Program (EBOP) report showing certified M/WBE vendor growth from 201 to 470. After Mayor Leonardo Williams introduced the joint Triangle USAID resolution for the General Business Agenda and Council settled the March 17 agenda, members debated whether residents should be allowed to opt out of City gravel street paving, ultimately advising staff against an opt-out mechanism.

agenda_items.title: Priority Item (EBOP Presentation) and Closed Session Motion
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Council voted 6-0 to receive the City Manager's Priority Item adding the 2024 EBOP Annual Report presentation (Item 10) and 6-0 to convene a closed session under N.C.G.S. 143-318.11(a)(6) following open-session business.

agenda_items.title: Community Matters Presentations
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Community speakers presented on youth empowerment initiatives including the Power Academy featuring Soofor Farms founder Kamal Bell, Dr. Deon Gray, and Durham Public Schools Superintendent Dr. Anthony Lewis.

agenda_items.title: Review of Pulled Consent Agenda and Public Hearing Items
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Council reviewed pulled items: Item 8 (opioid settlement RFP scoring across 18 proposals, Cook); Item 17 (HR pre-qualified vendor agreements, Middleton); Item 21 (pavement preservation/microsurfacing cost-effectiveness vs full repaving, Baker & Cook); Item 23 (starting 2024 Street & Sidewalk Bond projects using reserves ahead of the first $100M bond tranche, Cook); Item 24 (Duke/Gregson corridor safety feasibility study options including two-way conversion or BRT lanes, Baker & Caballero); Item 27 (outsourcing 3–6 inch large water meter testing, Cook); and Item 31 (Pickett Road public comments by Betsy Ross ahead of the March 17 hearing).

agenda_items.title: 2024 Equal Business Opportunity Program (EBOP) Annual Report Presentation
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Deputy CFO Sheila Facet and UBC Manager Timothy Jackson presented the 2024 EBOP Annual Report, noting adoption of the EBOP implementation policy effective July 1, 2024, RFP scoring incentives (up to 5 points), data scrubbing that raised certified M/WBE vendors from 201 to 470, over $1M increases in subcontractor payments across categories except Hispanic firms, and an ongoing one-year disparity study slated for contract award by June.

agenda_items.title: Draft Joint Resolution on USAID Stop-Work Order and Agenda Settling
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Mayor Leonardo Williams introduced and read the draft joint Triangle resolution calling for lifting the federal USAID stop-work order and correcting the cited executive order to EO 14169. Council unanimously voted to settle the March 17 agenda with Consent items 1–28, GBA public hearings 29–32, and Item 33 on GBA.

agenda_items.title: Paving Gravel Streets and Potential Resident Opt-Out Discussion

Nate Baker and Carl Rist favored exploring an opt-out option for neighborhood character and traffic calming, while Mark-Anthony Middleton, Javiera Caballero, and ultimately Cook argued against opt-outs due to historic racial inequities, emergency vehicle access, and maintenance burdens, giving staff clear direction not to create an opt-out.

disagreements.meeting_title: Durham City Council Work Session March 6, 2025 (livestream)
disagreements.issue: Allowing Resident Petition Opt-Outs from City Gravel Street Paving
disagreements.summary: Council debated whether residents living on unpaved gravel streets should be permitted to petition to opt out of City street paving, weighing neighborhood traffic-calming preferences against equity and public infrastructure standards.
disagreements.side_a_position: Explore an opt-out petition option where street residents prefer keeping unpaved streets.
side_a_arguments: Unpaved streets can serve as natural traffic calming and reflect some residents' desire to avoid paving assessments or faster cut-through traffic.
A transparent petition mechanism could respect strong neighborhood consensus on specific low-volume streets.
disagreements.side_b_position: Maintain City paving of gravel streets without an opt-out option.
side_b_arguments: Unpaved streets in Durham carry a painful racial and economic legacy ('other side of the tracks' disinvestment) and should be brought to uniform city standards.
Gravel streets impair emergency vehicle access, generate dust and stormwater runoff, and shift ongoing maintenance burdens back onto the City.
Chelsea Cook, who initially raised the inquiry, concluded she opposed an opt-out after hearing colleagues' equity and infrastructure arguments.
disagreements.resolution: Staff received consensus guidance not to pursue a resident opt-out mechanism and to proceed with planned paving.

meetings.title: Durham Joint City County Planning Committee (JCCPC) - March 3, 2025
meetings.executive_summary: Chaired by County Commissioner Chair Jacobs with City Vice Chair Nate Baker, Council Member Javiera Caballero, and Mayor Pro Tempore Mark-Anthony Middleton attending, the March 3, 2025 Joint City County Planning Committee approved February 5 minutes and excused absences for Kim Cameron, Vice Chair Lee, and Commissioner Valentine. Staff presented the draft Walltown Small Area Plan—highlighting paper-street pocket parks, flood/stormwater mitigation, preserving George Wall's home at 1015 Onslow Street, and Northgate Mall policies—prompting candid remarks from Middleton on avoiding 'theater' regarding past displacement while Baker and Caballero urged pairing honest history with actionable short- and long-term improvements. Staff also previewed UDO Module 2 transitions and screening rules, including upper-story stepbacks, wall/landscaping reductions, natural buffer preservation, and Low Impact Development stormwater alignment.

agenda_items.title: Roll Call and Approval of February 5, 2025 Minutes
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Chair Jacobs called roll with Nate Baker, Javiera Caballero, Mark-Anthony Middleton, Planning Commissioner Chagaris, Vice Chair Lee, and Commissioner Valentine present. On motion of Baker seconded by Valentine, the committee unanimously approved the February 5 minutes.

agenda_items.title: Draft Walltown Small Area Plan Presentation and Public Engagement Timeline
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Planning staff presented the draft Walltown Small Area Plan covering public land/paper streets (partnering with OPI Love Your Block grants), flooding and stormwater, transportation/Guest Road safety, and preserving George Wall's home at 1015 Onslow Street, with Northwood comfortable with Northgate Mall policies ahead of May 13 Planning Commission review. Mayor Pro Tempore Middleton cautioned against framing the plan as stopping past gentrification in a largely transformed neighborhood, while Baker and Caballero backed documenting that history and balancing short-term wins with long-term vision.

agenda_items.title: New UDO Draft Module 2: Transitions, Screening, and Tree/Soil Preservation
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Assistant Planning Director Bo Dobrzenski presented proposed Module 2 transitions and frontage screening rules consolidating scattered UDO buffers, introducing upper-story stepbacks, allowing buffer width reductions with walls, and using the Urban Growth Boundary for berm allowances. Members asked for real-world architectural photos rather than abstract diagrams, landscaping in front of retaining walls, Low Impact Development stormwater options, and Arborist Robin Schultz's tree-protection safeguards.

agenda_items.title: Excused Absences for Kim Cameron, Vice Chair Lee, and Commissioner Valentine

meetings.title: Durham City Council Budget Retreat - Feb 28, 2025 (livestream)
meetings.executive_summary: At Day 2 of the FY 2025-26 Budget Retreat with all seven members present, Council examined structural financial pressures in Transit (facing post-ARPA fare-free operating deficits and bus-electrification cost hurdles), Parking ($2.5M annual deficit), General Services Sustainability goals, Solid Waste ($5M deficit and zero-waste contracting), and Council budget request priorities. Budget Director Christina Riordan then presented property revaluation math showing the current 59.62-cent rate translating to a 38.87-cent revenue-neutral rate (42.87 cents to balance base operations, where one penny equals ~$6.8M), before polling Council via seven non-binding budget-guideline votes. Majorities signaled willingness to consider rates above revenue-neutral/balancing caps across General Fund, Half Penny for Parks, Debt Service, Solid Waste (with one abstention), Dedicated Housing, and Transit (unanimous 7-0), while adding an Option B on the Downtown BID to consider keeping its 7-cent rate.

agenda_items.title: Transit Fund & Parking Fund Long-Term Financial Outlook
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Transportation Director Sean Egan presented record GoDurham ridership (650,000+ trips in Oct 2024) alongside a looming fiscal cliff after federal relief exhaustion, estimating a 50% transit tax revenue growth need unless fares ($2 base fare option) or taxes change, plus $600k/bus added costs for electric vs diesel buses. Council expressed strong multi-year consensus to stay fare-free via property tax support, split over buying diesel buses temporarily without federal grants vs maintaining electric-only fleet targets, and debated Parking's $2.5M deficit and potential lot redevelopment.
agenda_items.vote_summary: Policy guidance provided / No formal vote

agenda_items.title: General Services: Sustainability & Carbon Neutrality Action Plan Progress
agenda_items.discussion_summary: General Services staff reported downward emissions trending ahead of 2030 targets thanks to HVAC/LED retrofits and upcoming Green Source Advantage solar (late 2027/early 2028, shifting to variable pricing), $11.1M in IRA/Duke incentives, and a $297k resilience hub battery grant at W.D. Hill. Council affirmed climate commitments while Chelsea Cook cautioned against solely using local tax dollars to backfill lost federal grants.
agenda_items.vote_summary: Policy guidance provided / No formal vote

agenda_items.title: Solid Waste Management Operations and Financial Deficit
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Solid Waste staff presented operations and an approximately $5 million structural deficit in the Solid Waste fund requiring a 0.74-cent tax increment above the 3.64-cent revenue-neutral rate just to balance base operations, alongside council questions on service delivery efficiencies and zero-waste initiatives.
agenda_items.vote_summary: Policy guidance provided / Formal guideline poll held later

agenda_items.title: Council Budget Requests Ranking & Prioritization Results
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Council reviewed its ranked budget requests—led by keeping GoDurham fare-free (ranked #1), 24/7 HEART expansion, homelessness/eviction prevention, and affordable housing—noting roughly $34.6M in requests overlapping partially with $120M+ in departmental CIP/operating requests.

agenda_items.title: Property Revaluation Analysis & FY 2025-26 Budget Guidelines Polling
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Budget Director Christina Riordan walked through post-revaluation rates (38.87-cent total revenue-neutral vs 42.87-cent base-balancing rate, with 1 cent generating ~$6.8M) and conducted seven show-of-hands guideline polls across General Fund, Half Penny for Parks, Debt Service, Solid Waste, Dedicated Housing, Transit, and Downtown BID ahead of formal guidelines adoption in April.
agenda_items.vote_summary: Seven directional straw-poll guideline votes taken

votes.item_title: Budget Guidelines Poll 1: General Fund Tax Rate Ceiling (Option A +1c Cap at 24.08c vs Option B Above 24.08c vs Option C Revenue Neutral 23.08c)
ayes: All remaining council members (Option B majority)
votes.notes: Show-of-hands directional budget guideline poll. Option B carried, giving the City Manager flexibility to consider rates above 24.08 cents for prioritized Council requests.
votes.discussion_detail: Budget Director Christina Riordan presented three General Fund tax-rate options following the 2025 revaluation: Option A (raising the rate up to 1 cent above the 23.08-cent revenue-neutral rate to 24.08 cents to balance existing services), Option B (considering a rate above 24.08 cents to fund prioritized Council requests), and Option C (holding at 23.08 cents revenue-neutral with deep cuts). City Manager Bo Ferguson framed Option B not as a guaranteed tax increase, but as direction allowing staff to model top Council priorities while scrutinizing costs. DeDreana Freeman stated later at 06:34:45 that she favored keeping FY26 at the overall 38.87-cent revenue-neutral baseline except for Debt Service, Solid Waste, and Transit. In the 06:14:56 show-of-hands poll across Options A, B, and C, Option B carried as staff direction for the proposed budget.

votes.item_title: Budget Guidelines Poll 2: Half Penny for Parks (Option A Revenue Neutral 0.33c vs Option B Maintain 0.50c)
votes.notes: Show-of-hands directional poll. Option B carried (retaining 0.50-cent earmark, +0.17c above revenue-neutral); Carl Rist and Chelsea Cook voiced reservations or preference for Option A/general fund absorption during discussion.
votes.discussion_detail: Council debated whether to drop the 'Half Penny for Parks' earmark to its post-revaluation revenue-neutral level of 0.33 cents (Option A) or maintain the full 0.50-cent rate (Option B), which captures revaluation growth as an effective 0.17-cent increase for Parks and Recreation maintenance and small capital projects. Mark-Anthony Middleton, Javiera Caballero, and Mayor Leonardo Williams supported Option B, emphasizing parks and trails as Durham's most egalitarian public spaces and economic drivers. Carl Rist argued in favor of Option A because Parks already received steady baseline funding and other priorities compete for tax capacity, while Chelsea Cook questioned expanding the earmark before seeing the finished Parks Master Plan. On the show-of-hands poll at 06:28:23, Option B carried.

votes.item_title: Budget Guidelines Poll 3: Debt Service Fund (Option A up to 9.76c for 2024 Bond vs Option B Consider Above 9.76c)
votes.notes: Show-of-hands directional poll. Option B carried to allow modeling additional general CIP requests above 9.76 cents.
votes.discussion_detail: On the Debt Service Fund, staff noted that 2.26 cents above the 7.50-cent revenue-neutral rate (9.76 cents total) is required to service voter-approved 2024 Connecting Durham GO Bonds under Option A, while Option B allows considering additional debt capacity above 9.76 cents for new CIP requests. Chelsea Cook requested a dedicated pre-publication work session to review trade-offs once draft numbers are modeled, and Javiera Caballero reiterated she would prioritize housing over parks if forced to choose later. Mayor Pro Tempore Mark-Anthony Middleton argued setting an arbitrary ceiling before seeing full bond math made no sense, and in the show-of-hands poll Option B carried unanimously without recorded hands for Option A.

votes.item_title: Budget Guidelines Poll 4: Solid Waste Fund (Option A up to 4.38c Balancing Rate vs Option B Above 4.38c)
votes.notes: Show-of-hands poll recorded as 'Option B and one abstention'; Carl Rist spoke for Option A and Mark-Anthony Middleton voiced a 'soft A' during debate.
votes.discussion_detail: Staff presented Solid Waste options: Option A adds 0.74 cents above the 3.64-cent revenue-neutral rate (reaching 4.38 cents) to close the fund's ~$5 million structural deficit without new initiatives, while Option B allows rates above 4.38 cents for new waste-reduction and operational proposals. Chelsea Cook leaned toward Option B to support waste-reduction innovation while awaiting answers to earlier staffing/overtime questions, and Nate Baker supported Option B as giving the manager flexibility. Mark-Anthony Middleton voiced a 'soft A' and Carl Rist argued explicitly for Option A to force operational prioritization within the balancing cap; when hands were called at 06:45:35, Option B carried with one abstention noted.

votes.item_title: Budget Guidelines Poll 5: Dedicated Housing Fund (Option A Revenue Neutral 2.20c vs Option B Above 2.20c)
votes.notes: Show-of-hands directional poll. Option B carried; Mark-Anthony Middleton spoke in favor of Option A during debate while Javiera Caballero strongly backed Option B.
votes.discussion_detail: Staff outlined Dedicated Housing Fund options combining the historical two-penny operating earmark (1.30 cents revenue-neutral) and housing bond debt service (0.90 cents revenue-neutral) into a 2.20-cent revenue-neutral Option A versus Option B allowing increases above 2.20 cents to preserve the full two cents' purchasing power or fund new initiatives. Mark-Anthony Middleton argued he felt comfortable with Option A given ongoing Forever Home bond funds and developer donations while awaiting a sunset review, whereas Javiera Caballero strongly advocated Option B to fund the Durham Affordable Housing Loan Fund, City-County-Schools housing recommendations, and backfill lost ARPA construction-overrun dollars. Carl Rist asked staff to report remaining Forever Home capacity at upcoming budget workshops. On the show-of-hands poll at 06:54:55, Option B carried.

votes.item_title: Budget Guidelines Poll 6: Transit Fund (Option A Revenue Neutral 2.45c vs Option B Above 2.45c)
votes.notes: Called unanimous for Option B by staff/Chair at 06:57:22 to preserve fare-free GoDurham transit and address the structural deficit.
votes.discussion_detail: Following the morning's deep dive into GoDurham's post-ARPA fiscal cliff, Budget Director Christina Riordan presented Transit Fund Option A (2.45 cents revenue-neutral, which draws down remaining fund balance for FY26 while leaving a multi-year deficit) versus Option B (considering a rate above 2.45 cents up toward restoring the 3.75-cent commitment). DeDreana Freeman stated Transit and Debt/Solid Waste were the key funds needing flexibility above revenue neutral, and Nate Baker stressed that along with General Fund needs, Transit was essential to move beyond revenue neutral so fare-free service remains intact. Carl Rist likewise emphasized prioritizing Transit rate capacity. On the show-of-hands poll, all seven Council members backed Option B unanimously.

votes.item_title: Budget Guidelines Poll 7: Downtown Business Improvement District (Option A Revenue Neutral 5c vs Option B Maintain 7c)
votes.tally: Polled (Option A vs added Option B)
votes.notes: Added Option B at Council request after DDI representative Carl Rist and Mark-Anthony Middleton backed maintaining 7 cents pending BID taxpayer feedback at public hearing.
votes.discussion_detail: Staff initially presented only Option A for the Downtown Business Improvement District (BID)—dropping the special district rate to the 5-cent revenue-neutral level (~$1.7M)—since BID assessments historically focused on flat revenue rather than penny earmarks. Downtown Durham Inc. representative Carl Rist and Mayor Pro Tempore Mark-Anthony Middleton opposed cutting the rate and asked to add Option B to maintain the 7-cent BID tax rate (generating roughly $2.4M, an extra $700,000 for Downtown Ambassadors and services). Javiera Caballero supported allowing DDI and BID property owners to weigh in at the public hearing before finalizing the rate. Staff added Option B on the spot and polled Council hands on Options A and B before moving to fund-balance and pay-plan guidelines.

disagreements.meeting_title: Durham City Council Budget Retreat - Feb 28, 2025 (livestream)
disagreements.issue: Maintaining 100% Battery-Electric Bus Procurement Versus Temporary Diesel Bus Purchases Amid Loss of Federal Grants
disagreements.summary: Council members split over whether GoDurham should purchase diesel buses when federal zero-emission grants are unavailable (~$600k cheaper per bus) or maintain its 2035 100% electric-fleet commitment using local tax dollars.
disagreements.side_a_position: Temporarily revert to diesel buses unless federal grants cover the electric price premium, prioritizing fare-free service and avoiding local tax spikes.
side_a_arguments: Battery-electric buses cost roughly $600,000 more per vehicle than diesel buses and federal FTA zero-emission grants are being reduced or eliminated.
Transit ridership itself cuts greenhouse gases far more than private cars, so preserving fare-free frequency with diesel buses advances community sustainability more affordably.
City taxpayers alone cannot absorb federal climate-policy reversals in a southern auto-oriented state.
disagreements.side_b_position: Maintain full commitment to electric buses and Carbon Neutrality Plan targets, funding clean transit through long-term local property taxes.
side_b_arguments: Diesel combustion is one of the dirtiest vehicle emissions sources and shifting back to diesel feels like going backward on Durham's 2035 climate commitment.
Local residents strongly value climate goals alongside fair wages and fare-free transit, and Council should build a sustainable city for the future rather than only tomorrow.
disagreements.resolution: City Manager Bo Ferguson summarized a majority willingness to consider diesel bus purchases when federal grant funding is absent to control Transit Fund costs while preserving fare-free service.

disagreements.meeting_title: Durham City Council Budget Retreat - Feb 28, 2025 (livestream)
disagreements.issue: Downtown Parking Philosophy: Subsidized First-Two-Hours Free and Asset Redevelopment Versus Higher Parking Fees to Deter Driving
disagreements.summary: Council divided over how to fix the Parking Fund's $2.5 million deficit—with some advocating discounted/free initial hours to aid downtown patrons and businesses, and others favoring higher fees and extended hours to cover costs and push mode shift to buses.
disagreements.side_a_position: Raise parking fees, extend paid enforcement hours past 7 PM, expand paid zones to other hubs, and oppose free initial hours to force cost recovery and bus usage.
side_a_arguments: Free first two hours reduces parking turnover and contradicts the City's 15-minute city and fare-free transit messaging.
Extending paid hours to 8–10 PM and charging in hubs like University Hill or Ninth Street helps the Parking Fund recover its own costs.
disagreements.side_b_position: Avoid across-the-board rate hikes, explore targeted first-two-hours-free validation/discounts (e.g., for Carolina Theater moviegoers), and repurpose underutilized lots or aging garages.
side_b_arguments: Durham's parking rates are already at or near the top of the NC market, and raising them further risks hurting downtown small businesses and cultural venues.
The deficit stems largely from Debt Service on overbuilt garages like Morgan-Rigsbee, so redeveloping surface lots or aging garages is a better structural fix than higher user fees.
disagreements.resolution: Council requested utilization/stay-duration/enforcement data (including Javiera Caballero and Chelsea Cook's data requests) and staff options on surface-lot redevelopment ahead of May budget proposals.

disagreements.meeting_title: Durham City Council Budget Retreat - Feb 28, 2025 (livestream)
disagreements.issue: Retaining Earmarked Tax Rates (Half Penny for Parks & Two Cents for Housing) Versus Revenue-Neutral Caps Post-Revaluation
disagreements.summary: During Budget Guidelines polling, Council members split on whether keeping fixed penny earmarks after a 74% property revaluation windfall represents an unjustified tax hike without vetted spending plans.
disagreements.side_a_position: Keep the full Half Penny for Parks (0.50c) and consider rates above revenue-neutral on Dedicated Housing and Solid Waste to capture growth for core amenities and housing.
side_a_arguments: Parks and trails are Durham's most egalitarian public spaces and need investment to correct disparities across neighborhoods.
Housing loses ARPA construction-overrun backfill funds and needs capacity for the Affordable Housing Loan Fund and City-County-Schools recommendations.
disagreements.side_b_position: Hold revenue-neutral or balancing caps (Option A) on Parks, Solid Waste, or Housing unless specific vetted expenditure plans justify higher rates.
side_b_arguments: Holding a 0.50-cent parks earmark after revaluation acts as a 0.17-cent tax increase without a finalized Parks Master Plan project list.
With dozens of competing priorities and major tax bill impacts on homeowners, agencies like Solid Waste and Parks should show operational efficiencies before exceeding balancing rates.
disagreements.resolution: Show-of-hands polls gave staff Option B flexibility on Parks, Housing, and Solid Waste, with Council scheduling follow-up budget workshops to scrutinize exact proposed expenditures.

meetings.title: Durham City Council Work Session February 20, 2025 (live stream)
meetings.executive_summary: Held virtually under Governor Stein's winter-storm State of Emergency with Mayor Pro Tempore Mark-Anthony Middleton presiding (Mayor Leonardo Williams excused absent), Council approved receiving the City Manager's Priority Items (6-0) and confirming Human Relations Commission and Planning Commission consensus appointments (6-0). Council reviewed pulled consent items (including downtown ambassador contracts, Durham Housing Authority/Fayette Place updates, and water system projects), heard the 4th Quarter Crime Report showing lower homicides and violent crime alongside rising vehicle-break-in gun thefts, and reviewed the ETC Police Satisfaction Survey and Q2 Financial Report showing slowing sales-tax growth. In the final hour, Council engaged in a substantive debate over whether a new competitive Eviction Diversion RFP should preserve legal representation and raise city funding toward $1 million before settling the March 3 agenda (5-0 after Cook's early departure).

agenda_items.title: Emergency Virtual Meeting Roll Call, Manager's Priority Items, and Clerk Consensus Appointments
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Mayor Pro Tempore Mark-Anthony Middleton opened the remote winter-storm meeting with Baker, Caballero, Cook, Freeman, and Rist present and Mayor Williams excused absent. Council voted 6-0 to receive the Manager's Priority Items (Crime Report, delayed Million Milers recognition, Budget Requests) and 6-0 to approve City Clerk consensus appointments of Kaylee A. Greene (Human Relations Commission) and Evan Bradley (Planning Commission).

agenda_items.title: Review of Pulled Consent Agenda Items
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Council reviewed four pulled items: Item 6 (downtown ambassador and clean-team service scope/performance metrics), Item 12 (Durham Housing Authority / Fayette Place housing redevelopment update), and Items 14 and 15 (Water Management infrastructure and utility agreements).
agenda_items.vote_summary: Informational / Placed on March 3 Consent Agenda

agenda_items.title: Durham Police Department 4th Quarter 2024 Crime Report and ETC Police Satisfaction Survey
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Chief Patrice Andrews presented 4th Quarter 2024 crime statistics highlighting modest drops in overall violent crime and homicides (with five homicides to date in 2025), improved officer retention and recruitment (23 recruits in Academy 61; 26% women toward 30x30), HEART call diversion, and upcoming Spring 2025 civilian traffic crash investigators, alongside a rise in firearms stolen from vehicles and delayed historical sexual assault reports. Council members asked about firearm NIBIN tracing, attainable 5-minute response-time benchmarks, free car gun safes rather than punitive mandates, and State/Federal victim-service grant risks, followed by the annual ETC Police Satisfaction Survey.

agenda_items.title: FY 2024-25 Q2 Financial Report
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Budget and Finance staff presented the FY25 Second Quarter Financial Report, flagging moderating sales-tax growth and departmental expenditure trends ahead of the February 28 Budget Retreat.

agenda_items.title: Council Budget Requests Discussion and Eviction Diversion RFP Debate
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Council discussed its 31 consolidated budget requests prior to online prioritization and February 28 retreat review, with Manager Bo Ferguson and Director Christina Riordan clarifying that Council should rank concepts regardless of overlapping staff asks. Nate Baker, Javiera Caballero, and DeDreana Freeman questioned why Eviction Diversion ($650k city base plus federal funds totaling $1M) was omitted during an RFP shift and insisted legal representation remain funded, while Middleton and DCM Chadwell argued a competitive RFP could also uncover upstream pre-court interventions alongside tracking 3-to-6-month outcomes.

agenda_items.title: Settle Agenda for March 3, 2025 Regular City Council Meeting
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Following Chelsea Cook's scheduled 3:00 PM departure, the five remaining Council members voted 5-0 by voice vote to settle the March 3 Regular Meeting agenda with Consent Items 1 through 20 and General Business Agenda public hearing Item 23 (Clegg Drive street closing).

votes.item_title: Receive City Manager's Priority Items (Item 9 Crime Report Presentation, Rescheduled Million Milers, Item 24 Budget Requests)
votes.notes: Mayor Leonardo Williams absent (excused); meeting held remotely under winter storm State of Emergency.
votes.discussion_detail: Opening the virtual February 20, 2025 Work Session convened under Governor Stein's winter storm State of Emergency, Mayor Pro Tempore Mark-Anthony Middleton noted Mayor Leonardo Williams' excused absence and presented the City Manager's Priority Items. The priority modifications postponed GoDurham Million Milers recognition to March 3, scheduled Chief Patrice Andrews' 4th Quarter Crime Report (Item 9), and added Council Budget Requests review (Item 24). A motion and second were heard on the floor without objection. All six Council members present voted Aye by voice vote.

votes.item_title: Approve City Clerk Board/Committee Report (Human Relations Commission & Planning Commission Consensus Appointments)
votes.notes: Confirms Kaylee A. Greene to Human Relations Commission and Evan Bradley to Planning Commission via four-vote consensus (Caballero, Middleton, Rist, plus Williams' prior ballot); Williams absent.
votes.discussion_detail: City Clerk staff presented the Board and Committee appointment report, noting consensus had been achieved for Kaylee A. Greene on the Human Relations Commission and that a four-vote consensus had been reached for Evan Bradley on the Planning Commission (combining votes from Javiera Caballero, Mark-Anthony Middleton, Carl Rist, and Mayor Leonardo Williams' pre-submitted ballot). Because of remote meeting rules, the Clerk read the tally and confirmed no further balloting was needed. Council moved and seconded acceptance of the Clerk's report. The motion passed 6-0 by voice vote.

disagreements.meeting_title: Durham City Council Work Session February 20, 2025 (live stream)
disagreements.issue: Eviction Diversion Competitive RFP Scope: Preserving Court Legal Representation Versus Pre-Court Root-Cause Interventions
disagreements.summary: Council members debated how Community Development should structure its upcoming competitive Eviction Diversion RFP and whether the City must commit additional funds above its $650,000 base toward $1 million to ensure legal defense for tenants in court.
disagreements.side_a_position: Ensure Legal Services / Legal Aid tenant representation remains a funded core component of Eviction Diversion and increase City funding toward $1M (+$350k above $650k base).
side_a_arguments: Tenants facing eviction have significantly better housing outcomes with an attorney, and losing federal funds leaves a $350,000 gap above the $650,000 City base.
DeDreana Freeman objected to using funds solely as landlord rental payouts without tenant legal advocacy and asked whether separate legal-services budget requests were needed.

Javiera Caballero noted County DSS rental assistance rules often force residents into court first, making Legal Aid mediation and representation vital while allowing nonprofit collaborations in the RFP.
disagreements.side_b_position: Keep the competitive RFP flexible to test upstream pre-court eviction-prevention models and track 3-to-6-month housing retention outcomes without locking out non-legal nonprofits.
side_b_arguments: Restricting the RFP strictly to law firms would exclude non-profit organizations that provide upstream 'on-ramp' eviction mediation before cases reach court.
Council should evaluate post-assistance outcomes 3 to 12 months later and remains free to reject RFP bids or fund legal services separately.
disagreements.resolution: Deputy City Manager Chadwell confirmed the RFP draft would allow collaborative bids and remain competitive, while City Manager Ferguson advised Council to add any funding increase above flat base into retreat prioritization.

meetings.title: Durham City Council Meeting February 17, 2025 with closed captioning
meetings.executive_summary: The Durham City Council approved its Consent Agenda (excluding pulled Items 11 and 12), accepted the Homeless Services Advisory Committee Annual Report, appointed Tasha D. Melvin to the Homeless Services Advisory Committee, and unanimously approved two major land-use cases: the Polanco Residence annexation and the 23.2-acre Hoover Road Assemblage rezoning for up to 402 residential units. Council referred Item 12 (an amendment to the UMCNC MWBE/Section 3 compliance contract) back to staff after a motion by Mayor Pro Tem Middleton to approve it immediately died for lack of a second. Members and the City Manager also addressed community anxiety following recent targeted federal ICE operations in Durham and welcomed local youth advocates from POOF and Haven 360 Project.

agenda_items.title: Roll Call, Proclamation for EPIC Day & Council Comments on ICE Operations
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Mayor Leonardo Williams called the roll with all seven Council members present and issued a proclamation declaring February 17, 2025 as Empowered Parents in Community (EPIC) Day. Mayor Williams and City Manager Bo Ferguson addressed recent federal ICE enforcement activity in Durham, affirming that the Durham Police Department does not act as an extension of federal immigration enforcement. Council members also discussed eviction court hardship, federal funding uncertainties, employee retention gains following budget pay increases, and heard from youth speakers affiliated with POOF and Haven 360 Project.

agenda_items.title: Consent Agenda (Items 1, 3-10, 13-32; excluding pulled Items 11 and 12)
agenda_items.discussion_summary: The City Manager noted supplemental information on Item 12 and the earlier HOPWA presentation under Item 35, and the City Clerk read the Consent Agenda. Items 11 and 12 were pulled for public comment and separate discussion, while Item 25 was briefly mentioned by Council Member Baker before being left on consent. Council adopted the remaining Consent Agenda items unanimously.

agenda_items.title: Homeless Services Advisory Committee (HSAC) Annual Report
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Item 11 was pulled for public speaker Sarah D'Amato of Legal Aid of North Carolina's Eviction Diversion Program, who urged Council to sustain investments in eviction prevention and homeless services amid rising demand. Council members thanked HSAC and community partners for their work across the Continuum of Care. Council voted unanimously to accept the annual report.

agenda_items.title: Amendment No. 1 to Contract #18421 with United Minority Contractors of North Carolina, Inc. (UMCNC)
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Council Member Carl Rist requested additional firm-level details and contract dollar data regarding MWBE, Workforce, Section 3, and Davis-Bacon compliance monitoring before voting on Amendment No. 1, and Community Development Director Reginald Johnson offered to supply the breakdown. Mayor Pro Tem Mark-Anthony Middleton argued there was no valid reason to delay the contract amendment and moved to approve it, but the motion received no second. Mayor Williams referred Item 12 back to staff to return with the requested firm-level information.
agenda_items.vote_summary: Referred back to staff (motion died for lack of second)

agenda_items.title: Appointment to the Durham Homeless Services Advisory Committee (Non-Profit Organization Category)
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Following a tie between Tasha D. Melvin and Drew Wooten at the February 6 work session when two Council members were absent, the City Clerk polled the full Council and reported a majority in favor of Tasha D. Melvin. Council voted unanimously to appoint Tasha D. Melvin to the Durham Homeless Services Advisory Committee.

agenda_items.title: Consolidated Annexation - Polanco Residence (4873 Stanley Road)
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Planning staff presented a voluntary non-contiguous annexation petition for 0.529 acres at 4873 Stanley Road owned by Rodrigo Polanco and Yenis Carolina Morales, with direct translational zoning to RS-20 in the Falls/Jordan Watershed District B. The applicants' surveyor Mary Elizabeth and contractor Bryan Sawyer explained the request was driven by septic system failure and the need for city sewer service. After the public hearing closed with no opposition, Council unanimously approved the annexation/utility extension agreement, zoning map change, and consistency statement.

agenda_items.title: Zoning Map Change - Hoover Road Assemblage
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Planning staff and attorney Patrick Byker presented a rezoning of 63 parcels totaling 23.204 acres west of Miami Boulevard and Hoover Road from RU-5, RU-5(2), and CN to PDR 17.325 for up to 402 residential units, including at least 25% townhomes and dedicated affordable housing with Durham Habitat for Humanity participation. Council members questioned native tree preservation, green infrastructure, the 20-year versus 30-year affordability commitment split between apartments and townhomes, and the removal of four Neighborhood Services Place Type parcels along Miami Boulevard. Following discussion, Council unanimously approved the utility extension agreement, rezoning ordinance, and plan consistency statement.

agenda_items.title: Bull City Futures Fund Clarification & Mayor Excused Absence Request
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Council Member DeDreana Freeman clarified funding distinctions between city resources and the privately raised Bull City Futures Fund for youth-serving nonprofits like POOF. Mayor Williams requested an excused absence for the February 20 work session due to scheduling and expected winter weather, passing the gavel briefly to Mayor Pro Tem Middleton for the vote. Council approved the excused absence by voice vote and adjourned at 8:41 p.m.
agenda_items.vote_summary: Excused absence approved by voice vote

votes.item_title: Adoption of Consent Agenda (Items 1, 3-10, 13-32; excluding Items 11 and 12)
votes.notes: Items 11 and 12 were pulled for separate consideration; Item 2 was previously placed on the General Business Agenda.
votes.discussion_detail: Following priority item updates from the City Manager and reading of the agenda by the City Clerk, Council members pulled Items 11 and 12 for public comment and additional scrutiny. Council Member Nate Baker initially inquired about Item 25 before retracting the pull so it remained on consent. With all seven seated Council members present, the motion to adopt the remaining Consent Agenda passed unanimously 7-0 via electronic voting.

votes.item_title: Item 11: Acceptance of the Homeless Services Advisory Committee Annual Report
votes.notes: Pulled from consent for public comment.
votes.discussion_detail: Item 11 was pulled from the Consent Agenda to hear registered speaker Sarah D'Amato from Legal Aid's Eviction Diversion Program. D'Amato highlighted eviction pressure facing Durham tenants and urged continued city support for eviction prevention and homeless services coordination. Council members thanked the committee and service providers for their annual reporting and unanimously voted 7-0 to accept the report.

votes.item_title: Item 2: Appointment of Tasha D. Melvin to the Durham Homeless Services Advisory Committee (Non-Profit Organization Category)
votes.notes: Resolved earlier February 6 work session tie after full Council polling by the City Clerk.
votes.discussion_detail: This General Business Agenda appointment had been placed on the voting agenda after the February 6 work session ended in a split decision between Tasha D. Melvin and Drew Wooten while two Council members were absent. The City Clerk reported that after polling Council Member Javiera Caballero and tallying full Council preferences, Tasha D. Melvin held the majority support. Council then formally voted 7-0 to appoint Melvin to the Non-Profit Organization seat on HSAC.

votes.item_title: Item 33 (Part 1): Consolidated Annexation Ordinance and Utility Extension Agreement - Polanco Residence (4873 Stanley Road)
votes.notes: 0.529-acre non-contiguous satellite annexation for single-family home experiencing septic failure.
votes.discussion_detail: Planning staff presented the voluntary annexation and utility extension agreement for a 0.529-acre single-family parcel at 4873 Stanley Road contiguous to existing satellite city limits. Representative Mary Elizabeth and contractor Bryan Sawyer testified that property owners Rodrigo Polanco and Yenis Carolina Morales needed municipal sewer access due to septic system issues. With no speakers in opposition during the public hearing, Council voted unanimously 7-0 to adopt the annexation ordinance and utility extension agreement.

votes.item_title: Item 33 (Part 2): UDO Zoning Map Change to RS-20 - Polanco Residence (4873 Stanley Road)
votes.notes: Direct translational zoning from County RS-20 to City RS-20 (Falls/Jordan Watershed District B); Mayor confirmed Council Member Cook's clicker registered.
votes.discussion_detail: Following approval of the annexation, Council considered the accompanying translational zoning map amendment to establish City RS-20 zoning in the Falls/Jordan District B watershed overlay. No modifications to density or permitted residential uses were sought beyond existing county zoning. After confirming all electronic voting clickers recorded properly, the clerk announced the motion passed unanimously 7-0.

votes.item_title: Item 33 (Part 3): Plan Consistency Statement - Polanco Residence (4873 Stanley Road)
votes.notes: Statutory consistency finding accompanying RS-20 zoning adoption.
votes.discussion_detail: Staff confirmed the translational RS-20 designation aligned with applicable comprehensive plan policies for existing single-family residential parcels near satellite municipal services. Council moved and seconded the required statutory plan consistency statement without further debate. The consistency statement passed unanimously 7-0.

votes.item_title: Item 34 (Part 1): Utility Extension Agreement with Hoover-Damn Investment, LLC - Hoover Road Assemblage
votes.notes: Utility extension agreement covering 23.204-acre assemblage for up to 402 units including Habitat for Humanity townhomes.
votes.discussion_detail: Attorney Patrick Byker presented the Hoover Road Assemblage on behalf of local owners including Durham Habitat for Humanity, detailing commitments for at least 25% townhomes, a $13,000 proffer to Durham Public Schools, and 20-year apartment and 30-year townhome affordability terms. PAC District 5 voiced support, while Council members questioned native tree preservation (Cook), 20-year vs. 30-year affordability duration (Baker), and the loss of Neighborhood Services commercial frontage along Miami Boulevard (Rist). Satisfied that the project provided substantial attainable housing within the urban growth boundary, Council approved the utility extension agreement 7-0.

votes.item_title: Item 34 (Part 2): UDO Zoning Map Change (RU-5/RU-5(2)/CN to PDR 17.325) - Hoover Road Assemblage
votes.notes: Covers 63 parcels totaling 23.204 acres west of Miami Boulevard and Hoover Road for up to 402 residential units.
votes.discussion_detail: Council voted on the zoning map amendment to rezone the 63-parcel assemblage to Planned Development Residential 17.325 with a development plan capping density at 402 units. While Council Member Rist noted regret over converting four parcels designated Neighborhood Services on the Place Type map into strictly residential zoning, he and the rest of Council weighed the affordable homeownership and multifamily supply positively. The rezoning passed unanimously 7-0.

votes.item_title: Item 34 (Part 3): Plan Consistency Statement - Hoover Road Assemblage
votes.notes: Adopted comprehensive plan consistency finding for PDR 17.325 rezoning.
votes.discussion_detail: Council considered the statutory plan consistency statement acknowledging the residential transition of four Neighborhood Services Place Type parcels along Miami Boulevard in favor of broader housing affordability and transit-adjacent infill goals. Members had completed policy questions on environmental commitments and retail frontage prior to closing the hearing. The consistency statement passed unanimously 7-0.

votes.item_title: Excused Absence Request for Mayor Leonardo Williams (February 20, 2025 Work Session)
votes.notes: Mayor Williams yielded the gavel to Mayor Pro Tem Middleton to facilitate the vote on his own excused absence request.
votes.discussion_detail: At the close of Other Matters, Mayor Leonardo Williams requested an excused absence for the upcoming Thursday, February 20, 2025 Council work session due to scheduling constraints and anticipated inclement weather. Mayor Williams yielded facilitation briefly to Mayor Pro Tem Mark-Anthony Middleton so the body could act cleanly on the request. A motion was moved, seconded, and approved unanimously by voice vote with no opposition.

disagreements.meeting_title: Durham City Council Meeting February 17, 2025 with closed captioning
disagreements.issue: Item 12 (UMCNC MWBE/Section 3 Consulting Contract Amendment #1) Readiness vs. Referral Back to Staff
disagreements.summary: Mayor Pro Tem Middleton moved to approve Amendment No. 1 to Contract #18421 immediately, whereas Council Member Rist sought firm-level subcontractor and dollar breakdowns first; Middleton's motion died for lack of a second and Mayor Williams referred the item back to staff.
disagreements.side_a_position: Hold the contract amendment and refer back to Community Development staff until firm-level MWBE, Workforce, Section 3, and Davis-Bacon contract data are provided in writing.
side_a_arguments: Following concerns raised at the February 6 work session, Council still lacked firm-specific names and dollar figures showing exact subcontractor participation and compliance deliverables.
Community Development Director Reginald Johnson indicated staff could compile and provide the firm-level amounts if referred back.
disagreements.side_b_position: Approve Amendment No. 1 immediately without further delay.
side_b_arguments: There was no substantive flaw demonstrated with UMCNC's compliance monitoring work or the contract amendment itself.
Delaying approval unnecessarily slows down active compliance oversight on federally and locally funded housing projects.
disagreements.resolution: Middleton's motion to approve received no second, and Mayor Williams referred Item 12 back to staff to bring back additional firm-level data.

disagreements.meeting_title: Durham City Council Meeting February 17, 2025 with closed captioning
disagreements.issue: Loss of Neighborhood Services Commercial Frontage on Miami Boulevard in Hoover Road Assemblage (Item 34)
disagreements.summary: Council Member Rist expressed concern over converting four Miami Boulevard frontage parcels designated Neighborhood Services on the Place Type map into purely residential PDR zoning, while the applicant and full Council ultimately prioritized the 402-unit housing and Habitat townhome package.
disagreements.side_a_position: Preserve Neighborhood Services commercial/walkable retail nodes along major corridors rather than allowing exclusively residential development to consume commercial Place Type frontage.
side_a_arguments: Four parcels along Miami Boulevard were designated Neighborhood Services to support neighborhood-scale commercial amenities and walkable services.
Replacing designated commercial frontage solely with apartments reduces future retail access for surrounding East Durham residents.
disagreements.side_b_position: Approve the residential PDR 17.325 rezoning to maximize housing units and support Durham Habitat for Humanity homeownership.
side_b_arguments: The 23.2-acre assemblage delivers up to 402 units including at least 25% townhomes and dedicated long-term affordable units in partnership with Habitat for Humanity.
Residential density and attainable housing within the urban growth boundary outweigh retaining commercial zoning on those four frontage parcels.
disagreements.resolution: Passed unanimously 7-0 after debate.
