meetings.title: Durham City Council Work Session October 10, 2024
meetings.executive_summary: During a wide-ranging nearly four-hour October 10, 2024 Work Session, Council discussed Durham County's 2025 property tax reappraisal (highlighting residential median prices rising from $239,500 in 2019 to $431,000 in 2024), low-income downtown worker parking discounts, 60 replacement bus shelters, and a rare Jordan Lake watershed boundary interpretation. Council deferred proposed deer bow hunting revisions for one cycle over safety concerns, sent the NACTO street-design guides resolution to General Business for legal review, and polled 6-1 in favor of an internal HR-led City Manager search over Mark-Anthony Middleton's preference for a closed-session direct-appointment discussion.

agenda_items.title: Hurricanes Helene/Milton Remarks, Oct 7 Meeting Apologies, and Freeman Excused Absences
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Javiera Caballero apologized for testy exchanges at the October 7 meeting and urged early voting and Western NC/Florida storm aid; Nate Baker requested adding City Manager search discussion to the agenda, which Mayor Williams routed to Other Matters. Council approved DeDreana Freeman's excused absences for Oct 21 and 24.

agenda_items.title: Public Comments on Senior Safety, Cultural Event Funding, and NACTO Street Standards
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Speakers raised 911 response delays and senior bus-stop seating on Hollowell Street (Susan Purvis), event-grant critiques from Slingshot/Moogfest (Kedra), and support for adopting NACTO street design guidelines for safer sidewalks and bike lanes (Chris Perin).

agenda_items.title: Updates to Low-Income Monthly Parking Discounted Voucher Program & Evening Parking Rate
agenda_items.discussion_summary: DDI CEO Nicole Thompson praised the General Fund-supported discounted monthly parking program for downtown hourly restaurant and service workers. Council commended staff for balancing worker access with transit goals.

agenda_items.title: Revisions to City Deer Bow Hunting Ordinance
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Chelsea Cook, Mark-Anthony Middleton, and DeDreana Freeman raised concerns over lowering bow hunting restrictions citywide in response to Treyburn HOA, prompting a one-cycle deferral for NC Wildlife input and legal review of time/notice restrictions.

agenda_items.title: Forest Hills Sprayground Design Contract & 60 GoDurham Bus Shelters
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Staff clarified MWBE/HUB utilization on the Forest Hills Sprayground design contract with With Architecture PA, and Transportation Director Sean Egan clarified at 01:16:18 that City Transit property-tax funds (not the ~$130M County Transit fund) provide the local match for replacing 60 older metal bus shelters.

agenda_items.title: Durham County 2025 Property Reappraisal Update and Tax Relief Programs
agenda_items.discussion_summary: County Tax Administrator Keyar Doyle, Deputy Assessor Starlin Beatty, James Roberts, and ACM Dwayne Brinson briefed Council on the 2025 reappraisal (residential median jumping from $239,500 to $431,000, commercial sales ratio at 0.53) and the four state/local relief programs, fielding sharp council questions on gentrification displacement, appeal equity, and LOHRP grant scaling.

agenda_items.title: Watershed Protection Overlay Interpretation Request at Patterson Place
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Planner Aaron Cain explained the rare request (first in 9 years) to forward sealed survey evidence on 14 parcels at Patterson Place—showing they lie over 5 miles from Jordan Lake normal pool—to the NC Environmental Management Commission, removing the 70% impervious limit. Cook moved the item to GBA for review.

agenda_items.title: Supplemental Resolution Adopting NACTO Urban Street & Bikeway Design Guides
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Council debated whether adopting NACTO guides by resolution creates binding legal mandates before the UDO rewrite. Following City Attorney clarification that the latest draft lacked final legal review, Item 31 moved to General Business.

agenda_items.title: City Manager Search Process Poll (HR-Led vs Search Firm vs Direct Appointment)
agenda_items.discussion_summary: HR Director Robin Wynn outlined three recruitment options; six members favored an HR-led search while Middleton preferred direct appointment and objected to polling without prior closed-session deliberation. Wynn was directed to draft an HR-led timeline.

agenda_items.title: Clerk B&C Report, Set the Agenda, and City Clerk Evaluation Closed Session
agenda_items.discussion_summary: The Clerk reported nominations (Discover Durham: Sean Umstead; REC: Elena Snavely; Planning: Khalila Karim; HRC: Christina Crosby; MHLC: Crystal Alvarez & Africa Dornera) plus a 3-3-1 DHAIC tie moved to GBA. Council then voted 7-0 to settle the agenda and enter closed session for Clerk Diana Schreiber's evaluation.

votes.item_title: Excuse Council Member DeDreana Freeman for October 21 and October 24, 2024 Meetings
votes.notes: Mark-Anthony Middleton joked about voting no before all members voted Aye.
votes.discussion_detail: During council announcements, DeDreana Freeman requested excused absences for the upcoming October 21 regular meeting and October 24 work session. Following brief remarks and good-natured banter from Mark-Anthony Middleton, Mayor Leonardo Williams entertained a motion to approve the absences. The motion was moved, seconded, and passed unanimously 7-0 by voice vote at 00:17:18.

votes.item_title: Set the Agenda for October 21, 2024 Regular City Council Meeting
votes.notes: Consent: Items 1-2, 4-8, 11-25; GBA: Items 3 (DHAIC tie), 10 (Patterson Place watershed), and 31 (NACTO guides); GBA Public Hearings: Items 27-30.
votes.discussion_detail: Following the Clerk's report showing a 3-3-1 tie on the Durham Affordable Housing Implementation Committee nomination (Item 3), City Manager Wanda Page set the October 21 regular meeting docket. Items 1-2, 4-8, and 11-25 were assigned to Consent; Items 3, 10 (Patterson Place watershed interpretation), and 31 (NACTO design guides) were placed on the General Business Agenda; and Items 27 and following (public hearings) were placed under General Business Public Hearings. Council moved, seconded, and unanimously adopted the agenda 7-0 at 03:57:22.

votes.item_title: Closed Session under NCGS 143-318.11(a)(6) (Annual Performance Evaluation of City Clerk Diana Schreiber)
votes.discussion_detail: After settling the October 21 meeting agenda, Mayor Leonardo Williams read a motion to convene in closed session pursuant to North Carolina General Statute 143-318.11(a)(6) to conduct the annual performance evaluation of City Clerk Diana Schreiber. No member objected to entering executive session, though staff needed a few minutes to halt the public livestream. The motion was seconded and passed unanimously 7-0 by voice vote at 03:57:48.

disagreements.meeting_title: Durham City Council Work Session October 10, 2024
disagreements.issue: Citywide Scope and Safety Protections in Proposed Deer Bow Hunting Ordinance Revisions (Item 9)
disagreements.summary: Council members questioned whether loosening bow hunting acreage and setback rules citywide for Treyburn HOA introduces safety and equity risks without sufficient data or time limits.
disagreements.side_a_position: Note existing 2013 ordinance safeguards (10-ft elevated stand requirement) and address Treyburn residents' documented deer overpopulation concerns promptly.
side_a_arguments: Treyburn cannot meet existing buffer limits even after consulting NC Wildlife and NC State.
Shooting downward from an elevated 10-foot stand is viewed by NC Wildlife officials as the primary safety protection, and no injuries have occurred under the 2013 ordinance.
disagreements.side_b_position: Defer the ordinance amendment by at least one cycle to investigate tighter calendar/daylight time limits, public notice, population thresholds, and citywide implications.
side_b_arguments: Ordinances apply the force of law citywide rather than solely to Treyburn, creating unforeseen risks for pets and pedestrians in denser areas.
Council must avoid rushing code changes for suburban deer complaints compared with gun-violence challenges elsewhere in Durham.
disagreements.resolution: Deferred one work-session cycle so DCM Bo Ferguson and the City Attorney's Office could consult NC Wildlife officials and research potential limits.

disagreements.meeting_title: Durham City Council Work Session October 10, 2024
disagreements.issue: 2025 Property Reappraisal Equity, Appeal Disparities, and LOHRP Grant Scaling (Item 26)
disagreements.summary: Council members pressed Durham County tax officials over whether rapid gentrification increases and unequal appeal access worsen racial tax burdens and whether local relief grants scale with post-reappraisal tax bills.
disagreements.side_a_position: Examine demographic appeal disparities, communicate relief programs more simply, and explore scaling LOHRP assistance when gentrifying home values jump above the countywide average.
side_a_arguments: Fixed-income homeowners in rapidly gentrifying neighborhoods face above-average assessment spikes, yet LOHRP grants remain tied to income rather than bill jumps.
National research documents racial disparities in effective sales ratios due to unequal access to appeals, and residents struggle to find clear guidance on County webpages.
disagreements.side_b_position: Emphasize that tax assessors follow market sales under strict state statute without demographic data and highlight Durham's 2021 UNC School of Government equity study and online evaluator.
side_b_arguments: Tax offices do not create property values and Durham's 2021 UNC SOG study found no consistent demographic bias in appeal outcomes, prompting expanded community outreach.
LOHRP is nearly unique in the South (funded $750K County / $500K City), while statutory fixes such as lifting the $36,700 state homestead cap require General Assembly action.
disagreements.resolution: Informational briefing; County staff agreed to share the UNC SOG audit and work with City Communications on clearer water-bill and web tax-relief messaging.

disagreements.meeting_title: Durham City Council Work Session October 10, 2024
disagreements.issue: Legal Effect of Adopting NACTO Urban Street and Bikeway Design Guides by Resolution (Item 31)
disagreements.summary: Council debated whether adopting NACTO design guides as 'official' guidelines via resolution prematurely locks staff into inflexible legal standards prior to the UDO rewrite.
disagreements.side_a_position: Adopt NACTO and ITE guides now as official reference guidelines to unlock federal Bipartisan Infrastructure Law flexibility and inform the UDO and Reference Guide updates.
side_a_arguments: Guidelines remain flexible reference documents rather than rigid cross-section construction standards.
Official adoption empowers Durham under the federal Bipartisan Infrastructure Law on federally funded city street projects.
disagreements.side_b_position: Avoid resolution language with mandatory legal force ahead of the UDO rewrite and require City Attorney review of the revised draft before any vote.
side_b_arguments: Using words like 'official' and 'adopt' in a resolution creates quasi-legal force that can cause disputes when field exceptions are warranted.
Staff had not finalized City Attorney review of the second draft and must ensure the UDO rewrite schedule is not delayed.
disagreements.resolution: Cook requested moving Item 31 to the General Business Agenda so the City Attorney's Office could complete review of the revised resolution before the October 21 vote.

disagreements.meeting_title: Durham City Council Work Session October 10, 2024
disagreements.issue: City Manager Search Process and Public Polling vs. Closed-Session Deliberation (Other Matters)
disagreements.summary: Mayor Williams polled members publicly on three City Manager selection paths, revealing a 6-1 preference for an internal HR-led search over Mark-Anthony Middleton's objection to the unannounced poll.
disagreements.side_a_position: Conduct an internal HR-led national posting process quickly and transparently rather than paying a 35% search-firm fee or waiting longer.
side_a_arguments: HR Director Robin Wynn confirmed internal capacity to post nationally on ICMA, NCLM, and diversity boards within a 30-day window without a ~35% search-firm fee.
Debating process transparently in public reassures residents the transition is moving promptly.
disagreements.side_b_position: Discuss leadership succession—including directly appointing from Durham's internal bench—in confidential closed session rather than an unannounced public poll.
side_b_arguments: Members had no prior notice that HR would queue up a live public poll during Other Matters.
Publicly stating preferences risks telegraphing personnel evaluations; Durham has an exceptional internal bench capable of direct appointment or interim service without rushing.
disagreements.resolution: Mayor Williams directed HR Director Robin Wynn to prepare an HR-led recruitment plan for Council review at the October 24 Work Session, noting no formal binding decision had yet been made.

meetings.title: Durham City Council Oct 7 2024
meetings.executive_summary: With all seven members present, Council proclaimed Minority Enterprise Development (MED) Week and Digital Inclusion Week before adopting the Consent Agenda and a River Forest Park temporary construction easement unanimously (7-0). Council approved companion right-of-way annexations for Bristolwood Drive (Wesley Downs culvert, 7-0 across three votes) and reconsidered Item 17 (Yates Road right-of-way annexation) after initially omitting the annexation/UEA vote, re-passing all three motions 7-0. Council unanimously approved Sunrock's Camden I concrete plant zoning (7-0 across two votes), while splitting 5-2 on two major land-use cases: Palmer Edge (183.17 acres, with Nate Baker and DeDreana Freeman opposing inclusion of 43 RR-zoned acres) and the 154.57-acre Duke Central Campus Addition rezoning to UC(G) across 60 parcels (with Nate Baker and Chelsea Cook dissenting over approving university-campus upzoning without a master site development plan first), though consistency statements for both passed 7-0.

agenda_items.title: Proclamations: Minority Enterprise Development (MED) Week and Digital Inclusion Week
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Mayor Leonardo Williams presented proclamations recognizing October 14–17 as MED Week (accepted by Deputy CFO Sheila Fossett and staff) and October 7–13 as Digital Inclusion Week (accepted by Assistant Technology Solutions Director Frederick Raven, Patrice Carroll, and Marcella Engman of Digital Durham).

agenda_items.title: Consent Agenda and Item 13 (River Forest Park Temporary Construction Easement)
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Council adopted the Consent Agenda unanimously (7-0) and then approved Item 13, granting a temporary construction easement at River Forest Park (7-0) after clarifying site compensation metrics.

agenda_items.title: Yates Road Right-of-Way Companion Annexation & Initial Zoning (RS-20) — Initial Vote and Reconsideration
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Council heard a companion right-of-way application for 0.239 acres of Yates Road adjacent to South Mineral Springs Road and initially voted 7-0 on the zoning map change and consistency statement while overlooking the annexation/UEA motion. Following Item 18, Council unanimously voted to reconsider Item 17 and re-adopted all three motions (Annexation/UEA, Zoning, Consistency) 7-0.

agenda_items.title: Bristolwood Drive Right-of-Way Annexation (0.089 Acres for Wesley Downs Culvert) and Initial Zoning
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Council held a public hearing on annexing 0.089 acres of Bristolwood Drive right-of-way so the City can maintain an infrastructure culvert associated with the approved Wesley Downs project that NCDOT declined to maintain. Speakers Mimi Kensor and Robert Brown testified before Council passed all three motions unanimously (7-0).

agenda_items.title: Palmer Edge (183.169 Acres) Annexation and Direct-Translation Zoning (IL & RR)
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Council considered annexing and directly translating county zoning for the 183.169-acre Palmer Edge site (IL and RR). Council Members Nate Baker and DeDreana Freeman opposed annexing 43 acres zoned Rural Residential without urban planning justification, resulting in 5-2 passage on annexation and zoning and a 7-0 consistency vote.

agenda_items.title: Sunrock Camden I Zoning Map Change (Concrete Plant)
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Council reviewed the zoning map change for Sunrock's Camden I concrete plant operation and approved both the zoning change and statutory consistency statement unanimously (7-0).

agenda_items.title: Duke University Central Campus Addition (60 Parcels / 154.57 Acres to University College District UC(G))
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Council debated rezoning 60 Duke-owned parcels totaling 154.57 acres along Central Campus to general University and College (UC(G)) zoning without a binding master development plan. Council Members Nate Baker and Chelsea Cook argued 'planning should precede zoning' and opposed blank-check campus entitlements, while the 5-member majority emphasized housing potential, institutional alignment, and prior outreach before approving UC(G) 5-2 and consistency 7-0.

disagreements.meeting_title: Durham City Council Oct 7 2024
disagreements.issue: Inclusion of 43 Rural Residential (RR) Acres in Palmer Edge Annexation (Item 19)
disagreements.summary: Council split 5-2 over whether to annex and directly translate 43 acres of Rural Residential land bundled inside the 183.169-acre Palmer Edge Light Industrial annexation.
disagreements.side_a_position: Approve annexation and direct IL/RR zoning translation for the full 183.169-acre site
side_a_arguments: Direct zoning translation preserves existing county density limits while bringing industrial/mixed land into City utilities and tax base
Consolidates parcel boundaries cleanly for unified master infrastructure
disagreements.side_b_position: Exclude or oppose annexing the 43 RR-zoned acres without urban development alignment
side_b_arguments: Extending municipal boundaries over 43 RR acres invites piecemeal future upzoning at the rural fringe
Questioned why non-industrial rural acreage needed immediate City annexation
disagreements.resolution: Annexation and zoning passed 5-2; consistency statement adopted 7-0.

disagreements.meeting_title: Durham City Council Oct 7 2024
disagreements.issue: Upzoning Duke Central Campus (154.57 Acres) to UC(G) Without a Development Plan (Item 21)
disagreements.summary: Council debated whether to rezone 60 Duke University parcels totaling 154.57 acres to general University and College (UC(G)) zoning prior to receiving a specific campus master plan or development commitments.
disagreements.side_a_position: Approve UC(G) general zoning to unify Central Campus parcels under university standards
side_a_arguments: Brings disparate single-family/legacy parcels onto the same campus zoning framework as surrounding Duke holdings
Enables future student housing, transit connectivity, and campus redevelopment on largely vacant/underused land
Duke conducted extensive pre-submittal neighborhood outreach
disagreements.side_b_position: Oppose general UC(G) zoning unless preceded by a specific campus plan and enforceable commitments
side_b_arguments: Planning should come before zoning rather than granting high-intensity general entitlements without site plans or affordability/transit conditions
General rezoning leaves neighboring residents without enforceable development guarantees
disagreements.resolution: UC(G) rezoning passed 5-2; consistency statement adopted 7-0.

meetings.title: Joint City-County Planning Committee October 2, 2024
meetings.executive_summary: Chaired by Council Member Javiera Caballero, the October 2, 2024 Joint City-County Planning Committee (JCCPC) approved June 5 and September 4 minutes and reviewed five major new rezoning cases—highlighting 4802 Cheek Road as the first proposal outside the Urban Growth Boundary. The committee also heard updates on the Heritage Communities Program and engaged in substantive policy debates over market feasibility in the Walltown/Northgate Mall small area plan and whether the new UDO should rely on pure by-right districts or opt-in affordability/design bonuses.

agenda_items.title: Call to Order, Excused Absence of Vice Chair Howerton, and Approval of Minutes
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Chair Javiera Caballero noted Durham County Vice Chair Brenda Howerton's excused absence and led the unanimous approval of minutes from the June 5 and September 4, 2024 JCCPC meetings.

agenda_items.title: New Rezoning Cases Summary (Durham Gateway, Page Corners, Oak Grove, 4802 Cheek Rd, Wake Forest Hwy)
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Planner Aaron Cain summarized five new cases plus two non-annexation rezonings, flagging that 4802 Cheek Road (201 units) is the first application submitted outside the Urban Growth Boundary, while Page Corners represents a 100% affordable LIHTC apartment proposal.

agenda_items.title: Walltown Small Area Plan and Former Northgate Mall Site Policies
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Planner Carl Plaza presented draft policies for the former Northgate Mall site calling for 20-30% affordable housing, affordable grocery/retail, public spaces, and tree canopy to cool an urban heat island. Northwood owner Sandy Spurgeon and attorney Nil Ghosh asked for phased feasibility flexibility, while Middleton and Commissioner Jacobs cautioned against misleading residents with unrealistic market promises vs. Baker urging public TIF/land-value capture.

agenda_items.title: Heritage Communities Program Update
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Planners Carla Rosenberg and Anna-Christina Hoffman outlined non-regulatory recognition for 50+-year historic communities featuring council resolutions, $2,500 interpretive signs funded by the department, GIS story maps, and County Library archives.

agenda_items.title: New Unified Development Ordinance (UDO) Draft Zoning Districts
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Planner Bo Dobrzenski presented Code Studio's consolidated draft districts—including Residential Preserve (3-acre outside UGB), Residential Diverse (5,000 sq ft minimum with compact and affordable opt-ins), RX3/RX5/RX8, CX3/CX5/CX8/CX20, Industrial Mixed Use, and Conservation—sparking debate on pure by-right density versus opt-in bonuses and greenfield conditional zoning.

agenda_items.title: 2025 Monthly JCCPC Schedule and Chair/Vice Chair Rotation
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Director Sara Young recommended returning to monthly meetings starting January 8, 2025 (skipping July 2025) for UDO workload, and Chair Caballero noted the January rotation naming Commissioner Wendy Jacobs as Chair and Council Member Nate Baker as Vice Chair.

votes.item_title: Approve Minutes of June 5, 2024 and September 4, 2024 JCCPC Meetings
votes.notes: Joint City-County Planning Committee meeting chaired by Javiera Caballero; County Commissioner Vice Chair Brenda Howerton had an excused absence; observed participants included Javiera Caballero, Mark-Anthony Middleton, Nate Baker, County Commissioner Wendy Jacobs, and County Commissioner Nimasheena Burns.
votes.discussion_detail: Chair Javiera Caballero opened the October 2, 2024 Joint City-County Planning Committee meeting by noting the excused absence of Vice Chair Brenda Howerton. With no adjustments requested to the agenda, Caballero called for a motion to approve the minutes from both the June 5 and September 4, 2024 committee meetings. A motion was moved and seconded and passed unanimously by voice vote at 00:01:05.

disagreements.meeting_title: Joint City-County Planning Committee October 2, 2024
disagreements.issue: Aspirational Equity Targets vs. Market Feasibility in the Walltown / Northgate Mall Small Area Plan
disagreements.summary: Committee members differed on whether draft policies calling for 30% affordable housing, affordable retail, and a grocery store risk overpromising to legacy Walltown residents without public subsidy.
disagreements.side_a_position: Keep bold 30% affordability, public open-space, and neighborhood-grid targets in the plan while exploring public tools like TIF or land-value capture to help finance them.
side_a_arguments: Small area plans legitimize years of Walltown organizing and set clear public expectations for phasing and street connectivity.
With public skin in the game—such as state-enabled TIF or LIHTC co-location near an anchored grocery store—the City can help move closer to the 30% goal.
disagreements.side_b_position: Avoid misleading legacy residents with an aspirational wish list (such as dictating private grocery stores or banning car washes while requiring EV chargers) that government cannot compel under market economics.
side_b_arguments: Durham County's own 500 E Main Street and Shops at Hope Valley experiences show government cannot force private grocers or low-rent retailers to open without 10,000-25,000 monthly foot traffic.
Much of legacy Walltown has already displaced, and putting unfeasible 30% encumbrances on private land risks leaving the mall vacant.
disagreements.resolution: Staff noted they would incorporate phasing and feasibility context while returning revised draft policies in November/December.

disagreements.meeting_title: Joint City-County Planning Committee October 2, 2024
disagreements.issue: Pure By-Right Simplicity vs. Opt-In Density Bonuses and Conditional Zoning in the New UDO Draft
disagreements.summary: Members debated whether the new UDO should allow higher missing-middle density unconditionally by right or rely on opt-in bonuses tied to affordability and design safeguards.
disagreements.side_a_position: Minimize extra 'opt-in boxes' and allow the urban density and 15-minute city forms desired by Council cleanly by right.
side_a_arguments: Requiring developers to jump through extra opt-in tiers slows housing supply; as Austin and Minneapolis showed, high supply stabilizes rents.
If Council truly wants walkable density, it should write it straight into base by-right standards.
disagreements.side_b_position: Retain opt-in standards, conditional Development Plans, and large-parcel sprawl safeguards so increased density delivers affordability, design quality, and anti-displacement protections.
side_b_arguments: Opt-in options remain by right (skipping 12-18 months of public hearings) while ensuring compact units, active street facades, or affordable percentages are legally secured.
Removing conditional zoning and letting 50-100 acre annexations build purely single-family sprawl undermines complete communities.
disagreements.resolution: Planning Director Sara Young supported keeping opt-in safeguards alongside existing Development Plan/Development Agreement tools and committed to bringing zoning maps and collapsing-district options back to JCCPC.

meetings.title: Durham City Council Work Session September 19, 2024 (Live Stream)
meetings.executive_summary: With all seven members present, Mayor Williams piloted moving ceremonial proclamations into the September 19, 2024 Work Session by proclaiming 'Week Without Driving,' while Council also condemned recent demonstrations at Temple Beth El. Council devoted nearly 75 minutes to a feasibility presentation on a new 500-key headquarters hotel and Convention Center ($540 million new build versus $93 million expansion), dividing over downtown tax-restricted economic-multiplier investments versus opportunity costs for housing, roads, and childcare as well as union/living-wage standards. Council then debated a NACTO Urban Street and Bikeway Design Guides endorsement resolution (Item 22) and referred it to the October 10 work session to soften directive language and evaluate city liability. Council concluded by unanimously settling the October 7 regular agenda and entering two closed sessions for PFAS litigation (NCGS 143-318.11(a)(3)) and personnel matters regarding an interim City Manager search and evaluations of City Manager Page and City Attorney Rehberg (NCGS 143-318.11(a)(6)).

agenda_items.title: Proclamation: Week Without Driving (Sept 30–Oct 6) and Council Announcements
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Council Member Carl Rist read the Week Without Driving proclamation to streamline regular Monday meetings, joined virtually by BPAC advocate Mary Rose. During announcements, Council highlighted GO bond senior town halls, Museum of Life and Science red wolves, White House Hispanic Heritage Month recognition, and condemned anti-Israel/antisemitic demonstration incidents outside Temple Beth El.

agenda_items.title: Pulled Consent Items: ETR Services Engagement, Carryover/Opioid Funds, DAP Study, River Forest Park Easement, and WIOA Eckerd Contracts
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Council reviewed pulled October 7 consent items including ETR Services' community-conversations contract (Item 8), FY24 carryover and opioid-settlement appropriations (Item 9), Durham Area Transit/Accessibility Plan (DAP) feasibility study (Item 12), River Forest Park temporary easement (Item 13), and WIOA workforce contracts with Eckerd Connects (Items 14–15).

agenda_items.title: Durham Convention Center & 500-Key Headquarters Hotel Feasibility Study ($540M New vs. $93M Expansion)
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Durham Next and consultants presented feasibility findings comparing a $540 million new Convention Center and 500-key headquarters hotel against a $93 million renovation/expansion. Council Members Nate Baker and Chelsea Cook questioned massive capital opportunity costs versus core housing, childcare, and infrastructure needs and demanded labor/living-wage protections, while Mayor Williams and Mayor Pro Tempore Middleton noted occupancy/prepared-food tax restrictions and potential convention revenue multipliers.

agenda_items.title: Resolution Endorsing NACTO Urban Street and Bikeway Design Guides
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Council Member Carl Rist and Council Member Nate Baker championed a resolution directing City use of NACTO urban street and bikeway safety standards ahead of NCDOT/AASHTO defaults. Mayor Williams, Mayor Pro Tempore Middleton, and Council Members Cook, Freeman, and Caballero raised concerns about legal liability, added costs on local developers, and mandatory phrasing, leading Council to refer the draft to the October 10 work session for softened language.

agenda_items.title: Settle October 7 Regular Meeting Agenda and Closed Sessions (Litigation & Personnel)
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Council voted unanimously to settle the October 7, 2024 regular meeting agenda, then passed two consecutive unanimous motions to enter closed session: first under NCGS 143-318.11(a)(3) regarding PFAS litigation (Tyco/BASF) and an unfiled claim, and second under NCGS 143-318.11(a)(6) for interim City Manager discussions and performance evaluations of City Manager Wanda Page and City Attorney Kimberly Rehberg.

votes.notes: Motion initiated at 03:08:10 and carried unanimously at 03:09:09.
votes.discussion_detail: Authorized closed session under NCGS 143-318.11(a)(3).

votes.item_title: Motion to Enter Closed Session — Personnel (Interim City Manager & Page/Rehberg Evaluations)
votes.notes: Motion initiated at 03:09:16 and carried unanimously at 03:09:56.
votes.discussion_detail: Authorized closed session under NCGS 143-318.11(a)(6).

disagreements.meeting_title: Durham City Council Work Session September 19, 2024 (Live Stream)
disagreements.issue: Durham Convention Center & 500-Key HQ Hotel Feasibility ($540M New vs. $93M Expansion)
disagreements.summary: Council divided over pursuing a $540 million new convention center and 500-key headquarters hotel, weighing hospitality tax limits and economic upside against public-spending priorities and labor protections.
disagreements.side_a_position: Question $540M public-private hospitality outlay and insist on strict community benefits, union neutrality, and core-service comparisons
side_a_arguments: Raised opportunity costs relative to affordable housing, childcare, and street/transit maintenance
Cook and Rist pressed for enforceable community benefit agreements, living wages, and union protections for hotel workers
disagreements.side_b_position: Continue evaluating downtown Convention Center competitiveness using restricted hospitality revenues
side_b_arguments: State law restricts occupancy and prepared-food tax proceeds to tourism-related projects rather than general operating services
Modernizing or replacing aging convention infrastructure prevents Durham from losing major regional events
disagreements.resolution: Informational study briefing; no funding commitment voted upon.

disagreements.meeting_title: Durham City Council Work Session September 19, 2024 (Live Stream)
disagreements.issue: Mandatory vs. Advisory Phrasing in NACTO Street & Bikeway Design Resolution (Item 22)
disagreements.summary: Council split between rapid adoption of NACTO multimodal design guides as binding policy versus softening resolution text to mitigate municipal tort liability and private development compliance costs.
disagreements.side_a_position: Adopt strong Council direction favoring NACTO urban street safety guides over auto-centric defaults
side_a_arguments: NACTO designs save pedestrian and cyclist lives and implement Durham's Vision Zero and bike/walk goals
City policy should visibly prioritize multimodal safety instead of deferring to highway-style standards
disagreements.side_b_position: Revise and soften binding language before adoption to address legal liability and practical implementation impacts
side_b_arguments: Concerned that mandatory directives create legal exposure when designs diverge from NCDOT/AASHTO standards
Sought clarity on compliance costs and administrative flexibility for City staff and developers
disagreements.resolution: Referred to the October 10, 2024 Work Session (03:07:08) for softer wording; revised version passed unanimously October 21.

meetings.title: Durham City Council September 16, 2024 (partial stream)
meetings.executive_summary: In the September 16, 2024 Regular City Council meeting (partial broadcast beginning mid-Consent Agenda), Council cast 15 formal votes including a Durham Housing Authority appointment, an FAA airport grant, three quasi-judicial permits for Lyons Farm Elementary School, and three large rezoning/annexation packages. While Hurley Road (12 units) and Farrington Road Multifamily (415 units with 5% at 60% AMI) passed 7-0, 5802 South Miami Blvd (432 units) passed 6-1 over DeDreana Freeman's dissent on its reduced 3.5% / 10-year affordable housing proffer.

agenda_items.title: Consent Agenda, Pulled Item 4 (DHA Board), and Supplemental Item 31 (FAA Airport Grant)
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Stream opens mid-Consent reading; Council adopted Consent 7-0, heard public comments from Ms. Lions and Naisha Lions before approving Item 4 (Durham Housing Authority appointment) 7-0, and approved Supplemental Item 31 (USDOT FAA Airport Improvement Program Grant Offer) 7-0.

agenda_items.title: Lyons Farm Elementary School Quasi-Judicial Permits (TSUP, MSUP & Major Site Plan D2400149)
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Quasi-judicial evidentiary hearing for DPS Lyons Farm Elementary School (M2400001) covering a Transportation Special Use Permit, Major Special Use Permit, and Major Site Plan Amendment.
agenda_items.vote_summary: TSUP, MSUP, and Site Plan all approved 7-0

agenda_items.title: 5802 South Miami Blvd Multifamily Annexation and Rezoning (432 Units)
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Public hearing for HM Partners LLC's 11.375-acre project reduced from 540 to 432 apartments with 28% tree preservation, 100-year stormwater, Green Building commitment, 15 affordable units (3.5%) at 60% AMI for 10 years, and a $50,000 DPS proffer added at the table. Freeman dissented over the small 3.5%/10-year affordability commitment.

agenda_items.title: Hurley Road / 830 Clayton Rd Annexation and Rezoning (1.03 Acres)
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Public hearing on Albert Fontenelle's 1.03-acre annexation and rezoning to RS-M (plus F/J-B) for up to 12 residential units after a 5-5 Planning Commission split.

agenda_items.title: Farrington Road Multifamily Annexation and Rezoning (415 Units)
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Public hearing for Northwood Raven LLC's 19.54-acre, 415-unit multifamily proposal committing 5% units at 60% AMI for 30 years, traffic calming, 4 additional EV charging spaces, Green Building standards, and an added $64,500 DPS contribution.

votes.item_title: Adopt Consent Agenda (Items 12-19, 21-22, and prior consent items excluding pulled Item 4, referred-back Item 20, and Supplemental Item 31)
votes.notes: Partial livestream started at 00:00:01 mid-way through reading Consent Agenda items.
votes.discussion_detail: The archived broadcast of the September 16, 2024 City Council meeting began mid-way through the reading of the Consent Agenda around Item 12, noting that Item 4 was pulled, Item 20 was referred back, and Supplemental Item 31 would be taken separately. With no additional items pulled from the remainder of the consent slate, Council moved and seconded adoption of the Consent Agenda. The motion passed unanimously 7-0 on the electronic board at 00:03:50.

votes.item_title: Item 4 (Pulled): Appointment to Durham Housing Authority (DHA) Board of Commissioners
votes.notes: Public speakers Ms. Lions and Naisha Lions addressed Item 4 prior to vote.
votes.discussion_detail: Council took up pulled Item 4 regarding an appointment to the Durham Housing Authority Board of Commissioners. Public speakers Ms. Lions and Naisha Lions addressed the Council regarding tenant perspectives and housing authority oversight before members closed public commentary. No council member objected to confirming the appointment. Council approved Item 4 unanimously 7-0 at 00:11:46.

votes.item_title: Supplemental Item 31: USDOT FAA Airport Improvement Program Grant Offer
votes.discussion_detail: Council next considered Supplemental Item 31 authorizing acceptance of a US Department of Transportation Federal Aviation Administration Airport Improvement Program grant offer. Having been added to meet federal grant execution deadlines, the item drew no opposition or extended questioning from council members. The grant acceptance motion passed unanimously 7-0 at 00:13:03.

votes.item_title: Item 27: Lyons Farm Elementary School Transportation Special Use Permit (TSUP M2400001)
votes.notes: Quasi-judicial evidentiary proceeding for Durham Public Schools.
votes.discussion_detail: Opening a quasi-judicial hearing for Durham Public Schools' Lyons Farm Elementary School expansion/site project (M2400001), Council heard sworn testimony from planning staff and school representatives on traffic circulation, queueing, and roadway mitigation measures. Council members examined bus and car-pool flow to verify statutory Transportation Special Use Permit criteria were satisfied. Finding substantial competent evidence in the record, Council unanimously approved the TSUP 7-0 at 00:40:27.

votes.item_title: Item 27: Lyons Farm Elementary School Major Special Use Permit (MSUP M2400001)
votes.notes: Quasi-judicial evidentiary proceeding.
votes.discussion_detail: Following the Transportation Special Use Permit vote in the same quasi-judicial record for Lyons Farm Elementary School (M2400001), Council addressed the required Major Special Use Permit findings covering compatibility, public safety, and adjacent property impacts. Based on the sworn evidence and site mitigation commitments presented, Council moved and seconded approval of the MSUP. The permit passed unanimously 7-0 at 00:43:15.

votes.item_title: Item 27: Lyons Farm Elementary School Major Site Plan Amendment (D2400149)
votes.discussion_detail: To complete the three-part quasi-judicial action for Lyons Farm Elementary School, Council considered Major Site Plan Amendment D2400149 incorporating the physical layout, buffers, and circulation plans tied to the approved TSUP and MSUP. With all evidentiary findings entered into the record and no opposing parties offering rebuttal, Council adopted the site plan amendment unanimously 7-0 at 00:43:51.

votes.item_title: Item 28: 5802 South Miami Blvd Multifamily Consolidated Annexation and Utility Extension Agreement (HM Partners LLC)
votes.notes: 432 multifamily units on 11.375 acres; 15 affordable units (3.5%) at 60% AMI for 10 years, 28% tree preservation, 100-yr storm, Green Bldg, +$50k DPS proffer added at table.
votes.discussion_detail: HM Partners LLC sought annexation and rezoning of 11.375 acres at 5802 South Miami Boulevard for a 432-unit multifamily complex (scaled down from 540 units to preserve 28% tree canopy alongside Green Building and 100-year stormwater commitments). During questioning, the applicant added a $50,000 Durham Public Schools contribution at the table, but DeDreana Freeman strongly criticized the developer's 3.5% affordable housing commitment (15 units at 60% AMI for only 10 years) as far below Council's typical 30-year standard and objected to how the compromise was framed. The majority credited the tree-save and density reduction near RTP jobs and passed the annexation 6-1 at 01:33:45 with Freeman dissenting.

votes.item_title: Item 28: 5802 South Miami Blvd UDO Zoning Map Amendment to PDR 37.978
votes.notes: Companion zoning map amendment for 432-unit multifamily project.
votes.discussion_detail: Immediately after annexing 5802 South Miami Boulevard, Council voted on the companion UDO zoning map amendment establishing Planned Development Residential 37.978 for the 432-unit project. Maintaining her objection to the weak 10-year, 3.5% affordability duration and unit share, DeDreana Freeman again voted Nay while the remaining six members voted in favor. The rezoning passed 6-1 at 01:34:21.

votes.item_title: Item 28: Consistency Statement under NCGS 160D-605 (5802 South Miami Blvd)
votes.discussion_detail: Council next voted on the statutory NCGS 160D-605 consistency statement for the 5802 South Miami Boulevard PDR 37.978 zoning map change. Despite her dissent on the project's affordability proffer, DeDreana Freeman joined her six colleagues on the formal Comprehensive Plan consistency finding. The statement passed unanimously 7-0 at 01:34:51.

votes.item_title: Item 29: Hurley Road / 830 Clayton Rd Consolidated Annexation and UEA (Albert Fontenelle)
votes.notes: 1.03 acres for up to 12 units; Planning Commission had tied 5-5.
votes.discussion_detail: Applicant Albert Fontenelle requested annexation and rezoning of 1.03 acres at Hurley Road / 830 Clayton Road to allow up to 12 townhome/multifamily units, advancing after a 5-5 split at the Planning Commission. Council members discussed neighborhood scale, access, and infill housing compatibility during the public hearing. Concluding that small-scale missing-middle infill fit the corridor, Council unanimously approved the annexation and utility extension agreement 7-0 at 02:00:27.

votes.item_title: Item 29: Hurley Road / 830 Clayton Rd UDO Zoning Map Amendment to RS-M + F/J-B
votes.discussion_detail: Following approval of the Hurley Road annexation, Council voted on rezoning the 1.03-acre parcel to Residential Suburban Multifamily (RS-M) with the Falls/Jordan Lake Protected Area (F/J-B) city watershed overlay. No additional questions were raised after the preceding hearing discussion. The zoning map amendment passed unanimously 7-0 at 02:01:07.

votes.item_title: Item 29: Consistency Statement under NCGS 160D-605 (Hurley Road / 830 Clayton Rd)
votes.discussion_detail: Council completed Item 29 by voting on the statutory consistency statement pursuant to NCGS 160D-605 for the Hurley Road RS-M rezoning. Council affirmed alignment with infill housing goals in the adopted Comprehensive Plan. The consistency statement passed unanimously 7-0 at 02:01:22.

votes.item_title: Item 30: Farrington Road Multifamily Consolidated Annexation and UEA (Northwood Raven LLC)
votes.notes: 19.54 acres, 415 units, 5% at 60% AMI for 30 yrs, traffic calming, +4 EV spaces, Green Bldg, +$64,500 DPS.
votes.discussion_detail: Northwood Raven LLC presented a 19.54-acre, 415-unit multifamily proposal along Farrington Road offering 5% affordable units at 60% AMI for 30 years, neighborhood traffic calming, four additional EV charging spaces, Green Building certification, and an added $64,500 Durham Public Schools contribution. Council members praised the 30-year affordability duration, multimodal/EV upgrades, and responsiveness compared with earlier cases. Council approved the annexation and utility extension agreement unanimously 7-0 at 02:28:52.

votes.item_title: Item 30: Farrington Road Multifamily UDO Zoning Map Amendment (PDR 21.229 + MTC I-40 + F/J-B)
votes.discussion_detail: Immediately following annexation of the 19.54-acre Farrington Road site, Council voted on the companion UDO zoning map amendment establishing Planned Development Residential 21.229 with the Major Transportation Corridor I-40 and Falls/Jordan-B watershed overlays. Having secured the developer's final proffers in the record, Council adopted the rezoning unanimously 7-0 at 02:29:46.

votes.item_title: Item 30: Consistency Statement under NCGS 160D-605 (Farrington Road Multifamily)
votes.discussion_detail: To finalize the Farrington Road Multifamily public hearing, Council considered the required NCGS 160D-605 consistency statement. Council affirmed that the mixed-income apartment development was reasonable and consistent with Durham's Comprehensive Plan along the I-40 corridor. The consistency statement passed unanimously 7-0 at 02:30:23.

disagreements.meeting_title: Durham City Council September 16, 2024 (partial stream)
disagreements.issue: 5802 South Miami Blvd Affordable Housing Duration and Percentage (Item 28)
disagreements.summary: DeDreana Freeman cast the sole dissenting vote on the 432-unit South Miami Boulevard project over its reduced 3.5% / 10-year affordable housing proffer.
disagreements.side_a_position: Approve the 432-unit rezoning with 15 units at 60% AMI for 10 years, 28% tree preservation, and $50,000 DPS proffer.
side_a_arguments: The developer reduced overall unit count from 540 to 432 to achieve 28% tree preservation and strong environmental/stormwater commitments.
Adding 432 homes near RTP plus $50,000 for schools and 15 affordable units yields net community benefit.
disagreements.side_b_position: Reject the rezoning because 3.5% affordable units for only 10 years falls well short of Durham's standard 30-year affordability expectations.
side_b_arguments: Ten years of affordability expires too quickly in a high-growth corridor, and 3.5% of units is disproportionately small for a 432-unit greenfield project.
Objected to how developer compromises between tree canopy and affordability were framed at the podium.
disagreements.resolution: Annexation and zoning passed 6-1 at 01:33:04 and 01:33:52.

meetings.title: Durham City Council September 16, 2024 (Full Meeting)
meetings.executive_summary: With all seven members present, the Durham City Council passed the Consent Agenda (7-0, referring Item 20 back and separating Items 4 and 31), confirmed a Durham Housing Authority Board appointment (Item 4, 7-0), and accepted an FAA Airport Improvement Program grant (Item 31, 7-0). Sitting in quasi-judicial capacity, Council unanimously granted a Transportation Special Use Permit, Major Special Use Permit, and Major Site Plan for Durham Public Schools' Lyons Farm Elementary School (7-0 across three votes). Council then approved three suburban growth rezonings: 5802 South Miami Boulevard (432 apartments under PDR 37.978, passing annexation and zoning 6-1 with DeDreana Freeman dissenting over low DPS proffers and absent affordable housing, while consistency passed 7-0), Early Road RSM/Fontanelle (7-0 across three votes), and Farrington Road Multifamily (415 units under PDR 21.229 with 5% affordability, 7-0 across three votes).

meetings.title: Durham City Council Work Session September 5, 2024
meetings.executive_summary: Chaired by Mayor Pro Tempore Mark-Anthony Middleton with Mayor Leonardo Williams and Council Member Chelsea Cook absent with excused absences, the five present Council members introduced an urban bow-hunting ordinance proposal, heard Citizens' Matters concerns ranging from leaf pickup and outdoor burning to railroad quiet zones, JFK Towers maintenance/safety, and well damage from development blasting on Junction Road. Briefings covered increasing GoDurham's FTA Disadvantaged Business Enterprise goal from 3% to 20% (Item 13), Tar River Land Conservancy watershed protection (Item 17), Durham's ~$5 million homelessness Continuum of Care system (Item 23, reporting 405 PIT count residents), FY24 Q4 financial results (Item 24), and GoDurham Access paratransit operations (Item 26). A presentation on Durham Public Schools enrollment capacity (Item 25, forecasting +5,000 students at ~$100,000 per seat) sparked Council pushback rejecting assertions that City residential rezonings caused crowding rather than state underfunding and delayed DPS capital planning, before Council voted 5-0 to settle the September 16 agenda.

agenda_items.title: Urban Bow Hunting Proposal and Citizens' Matters (Leaf Pickup, Quiet Zones, JFK Towers, Blasting)
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Council previewed a proposed urban bow-hunting ordinance and heard Citizens' Matters from Linda Sutton (leaf collection and outdoor burning bans), Zach Seroto (railroad quiet zones), Jeanette Alston (JFK Towers elevator/management failures and proximity to Northern High), and Katie Lundy Ross (requesting expert symposium and developer liability remedies for Junction Road blasting well damage).

agenda_items.title: FTA DBE Goal (20%), Watershed Easement, Homelessness CoC Update, FY24 Q4 Financials, and Paratransit Study
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Council reviewed raising GoDurham's FTA DBE target from 3% to 20% (Item 13) and a Tar River Land Conservancy watershed item (Item 17). Briefings also detailed Durham's ~$5M homelessness system (405 PIT individuals; 50/15/28 emergency/shelter/transitional bed allocations under Item 23), FY24 Q4 budget execution (Item 24), and GoDurham Access paratransit performance (Item 26).

agenda_items.title: Durham Public Schools (DPS) Enrollment Capacity & Capital Planning Briefing
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Staff and DPS presented capacity projections estimating 5,000 additional students and ~$100,000 per seat in construction costs. All five attending Council members criticized framing residential rezonings as the primary driver of school overcrowding, attributing shortfalls instead to state education funding constraints, charter/voucher shifts, and delayed DPS capital planning.

agenda_items.title: Settle Agenda for September 16, 2024 Regular City Council Meeting
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Following final pulled-item clarifications, the five present Council members settled the September 16, 2024 regular meeting agenda by unanimous voice vote.

disagreements.meeting_title: Durham City Council Work Session September 5, 2024
disagreements.issue: Attribution of DPS School Overcrowding to City Rezonings vs. State Funding and Capital Planning (Item 25)
disagreements.summary: During a briefing projecting +5,000 Durham Public Schools students at roughly $100,000 per seat, Council pushed back firmly against tying City housing approvals to school overcrowding.
disagreements.side_a_position: Reject linking City rezonings to school capacity deficits; attribute crowding to state funding gaps and DPS planning
side_a_arguments: North Carolina law bars cities from imposing mandatory adequate-public-facilities school impact moratoriums or full-cost fees
State underfunding, charter/voucher enrollment dynamics, and County/DPS bond timing—not housing growth alone—drive classroom shortages
Requested better joint seat-generation forecasting without pitting housing supply against public schools
disagreements.side_b_position: Staff/DPS capacity framing emphasizing rapid residential rezoning student-yield pressures (+5,000 projected seats)
side_b_arguments: High-volume new residential entitlements accelerate enrollment spikes beyond current school facility capital budgets (~$100,000 per seat)
disagreements.resolution: Informational briefing concluded with Council directing better intergovernmental data sharing ahead of future growth coordination.

meetings.title: Joint City County Planning Committee September 4, 2024
meetings.executive_summary: Chaired by Council Member Javiera Caballero alongside City Council Members Nate Baker and Mark-Anthony Middleton plus Durham County Commissioners, the September 4, 2024 JCCPC session held three major planning policy briefings with no formal committee votes. Senior Planner Carl Kolosna updated the committee on the Walltown / Northgate Mall Small Area Plan (59 June kickoff attendees, 201 comments, draft 19 policies, 68 acres), sparking a substantive exchange between Baker—who urged public-private support for community-led redevelopment—and Middleton, who cautioned that Walltown demographics have already gentrified (56% White / 38% Black kickoff survey split) and stressed honesty that small-area plans are non-binding. Senior Planner Kayla Seibel presented a revised Page-Miami Design District (formerly RTP South) transit-oriented rezoning proposal keeping Davis Park residential/mixed-use development plans intact while applying Compact Suburban Design districts on the east side and flagging a Family Fare gas station exclusion request for Planning Commission review. Planning staff Lisa Miller and Bo also outlined four engagement phases and Dr. Tawana Allen's Engagement Ambassadors program for the new UDO.

agenda_items.title: Walltown and Former Northgate Mall Small Area Plan Draft Policy Update
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Senior Planner Carl Kolosna reported on the June 29 Walltown kickoff (59 attendees, 201 comments, 68-acre Northgate site, 9 city-owned vacant lots, paper alleys, and flooding concerns) and release of 19 draft policies following Northwood's submitted-and-withdrawn rezoning application. Council Member Baker advocated aligning City/County tools behind the community vision, while Mayor Pro Tempore Middleton cautioned on gentrified participation demographics and clarified the advisory legal limits of a small area plan.

agenda_items.title: Page-Miami Design District (Formerly RTP South) Transit-Oriented Rezoning Proposal
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Senior Planner Kayla Seibel presented a revised rezoning map for the Page-Miami corridor after resident outreach, shifting from blanket Compact Suburban Design (CSD) to CSD Core and Support-1 east of the rail line near the relocated GoTriangle regional transit hub while retaining Davis Park's RC/RUM/mixed-use zoning and proposing Commercial Neighborhood (CN) for a vacant retail parcel. Committee members advised against carving out a Family Fare gas station from CSD Core to preserve long-term transit-oriented redevelopment.

agenda_items.title: New Unified Development Ordinance (UDO) Phased Community Engagement & Engagement Ambassadors
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Planning staff briefed JCCPC on Code Studio's technical modules and four phased engagement waves starting Fall 2024 across county libraries, office hours, and Dr. Tawana Allen's (TG Allen & Associates) Engagement Ambassadors program targeting 30+ focus groups. Council Member Baker asked about tying cross-street cross-sections from Public Works into Module 3, and Chair Caballero emphasized stronger outreach to refugee and non-English-speaking residents.

disagreements.meeting_title: Joint City County Planning Committee September 4, 2024
disagreements.issue: Walltown / Northgate Small Area Plan Advisory Limits and Community Demographic Representation
disagreements.summary: Committee members differed in emphasis regarding how forcefully the Walltown / Northgate Mall Small Area Plan can halt displacement and reflect legacy neighborhood voices versus acknowledging existing gentrification and legal constraints.
disagreements.side_a_position: Leverage City/County zoning, planning, and capital tools collaboratively to realize Walltown coalitions' Northgate Mall vision
side_a_arguments: Walltown Community Association and Northgate Mall Neighborhood Coalition have spent years building an equitable community framework
Collaborative iterative talks with Northwood and experienced mall redevelopers (such as Folger Pratt) can achieve affordable housing and open space
disagreements.side_b_position: Caution residents candidly that a small area plan is non-binding and recognize Walltown's ongoing demographic shift
side_b_arguments: Kickoff survey demographics (56% White vs. 38% Black) show gentrifiers already participate heavily in neighborhood forums
Residents must not be misled into thinking an advisory Small Area Plan provides statutory protection against redevelopment or rising costs
disagreements.resolution: Staff retained both public policy workshops and explicit disclosures regarding advisory legal scope ahead of October and December JCCPC reviews.

meetings.title: Durham City Council Sept 3 2024
meetings.executive_summary: Presiding as Mayor Pro Tem in Mayor Leonardo Williams's absence (traveling on city business), Mark-Anthony Middleton led the six present Council members through proclamations, consent business, an ARPA housing grant, and the Lee Valley annexation and rezoning public hearing. Council unanimously excused Chelsea Cook from the upcoming Thursday work session due to a family bereavement (6-0), approved the remaining consent agenda (6-0), and separately approved a $280,917.73 ARPA subrecipient grant agreement with the Durham Housing Authority (6-0) after Cook asked follow-up questions about eviction language. Following debate over Transit Opportunity Area (TOA) expectations, housing diversity, and sustainability proffers for the Lee Valley development (Green Hawk Operation Inc.), Council passed the annexation and utility extension agreement (4-1) and two UDO zoning map amendments (5-1) over Nate Baker's dissent, and adopted the statutory consistency statement unanimously (6-0).

agenda_items.title: Call to Order, Roll Call, Proclamation, Announcements, and Excused Absence Request
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Mayor Pro Tem Mark-Anthony Middleton called the meeting to order, noting Mayor Leonardo Williams was absent traveling on city business and had been granted an excused absence for August 5. Council presented a proclamation for Jack-N-Gill and Carol Robertson Day, heard DeDreana Freeman announce a follow-up community listening session on September 26 following the August 22 town hall, and heard Middleton announce the Bull City Future Fund (bullcityfuturefund.com) on behalf of the Mayor. Chelsea Cook requested an excused absence for the September 5 work session due to a death in her family.

agenda_items.title: Consent Agenda (Excluding Pulled Item 7)
agenda_items.discussion_summary: City Manager noted that additional information requested at the August 22 work session was attached to Item 7 (ARPA Agreement with Durham Housing Authority). Mayor Pro Tem Middleton read Consent Agenda items 1-7, 9-20, and 25—covering board/commission appointments, FAA Airport Improvement Program grants, DHA security equipment interlocal cooperation, software/IT contracts, Great Trails State Grant for the American Tobacco Trail, Sherwood Park playground contract, the Q2 2024 Crime Report, Digital Equity ARPA project, and a $1M Drinking Water State Revolving Fund lead service line loan—and pulled Item 7 for separate consideration.

agenda_items.title: ARPA Subrecipient Grant Agreement with Durham Housing Authority ($280,917.73)
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Pulled from the consent agenda, Council Member Chelsea Cook asked follow-up questions regarding contract language on potential evictions that had been discussed at the August 22 work session. Following her questions, Council moved and seconded authorization for the City Manager to execute the ARPA subrecipient grant agreement with the Durham Housing Authority in the amount of $280,917.73.

agenda_items.title: Consolidated Annexation and Zoning Map Change: Lee Valley (Green Hawk Operation Inc.)
agenda_items.discussion_summary: In the visible portion of the Lee Valley public hearing, Council members debated whether the project sufficiently advanced transit-oriented design (TOD) for a Transit Opportunity Area (TOA) on the Future Place Type Map despite the lack of current light rail or BRT corridors, and asked staff how a reserved RS-20 area could later accommodate commercial uses. Speakers also weighed whether the applicant had satisfied concerns raised during a prior April extension, housing diversity across the broader corridor, and improved affordability and sustainability proffers ahead of the upcoming UDO rewrite. After closing the public hearing at 01:50:37, Council approved annexation/utility extension, two UDO zoning amendments, and the consistency statement across four separate votes.
agenda_items.vote_summary: Annexation passed 4-1; two UDO zoning amendments passed 5-1 (Nate Baker voting no); consistency statement passed 6-0

votes.notes: Mayor Leonardo Williams absent (traveling on city business).
votes.discussion_detail: Chelsea Cook requested an excused absence for the upcoming Thursday work session due to a death in her family. Mayor Pro Tem Mark-Anthony Middleton entertained a motion and second, and the motion passed 6-0 with Mayor Leonardo Williams absent on city business.

votes.item_title: Item 7: Authorize City Manager to Execute ARPA Subrecipient Grant Agreement with Durham Housing Authority ($280,917.73)
votes.notes: Mayor Leonardo Williams absent; 6 seated members present.
votes.discussion_detail: Chelsea Cook asked brief follow-up questions regarding contract language on potential evictions tied to the August 22 work session discussion before Council voted unanimously to authorize the $280,917.73 ARPA grant agreement with DHA.

votes.item_title: Item 24 (Motion 1): Adopt Lee Valley Annexation Ordinance and Authorize Utility Extension Agreement with Green Hawk Operation Inc.
votes.notes: Clerk announced 4-1 with Nate Baker voting no (Mayor Williams absent; one of the six present members did not cast an aye/nay recorded in the 4-1 tally).
votes.discussion_detail: Following debate on Transit Opportunity Area alignment, reserve parcels, and proffers, Council approved the ordinance annexing Lee Valley into the City of Durham and authorizing a utility extension agreement with Green Hawk Operation Inc. by a 4-1 vote with Nate Baker dissenting.

votes.item_title: Item 24 (Motion 2): Adopt UDO Zoning Map Amendment Establishing Residential Compact with Development Plan (Lee Valley)
votes.notes: Mayor Williams absent; Clerk reported 5-1 with Nate Baker voting no.
votes.discussion_detail: Council adopted the UDO amendment taking property out of RS-20 (Falls/Jordan Lake Watershed Protection District B, Major Transportation Corridor I-40, county jurisdiction) and establishing Residential Compact with a development plan under city jurisdiction by a 5-1 vote.

votes.item_title: Item 24 (Motion 3): Adopt UDO Zoning Map Amendment Establishing RS-20 City Jurisdiction (Lee Valley Reserve Area)
votes.notes: Mayor Williams absent; Clerk reported 5-1 with Nate Baker voting no.
votes.discussion_detail: Council adopted the companion UDO amendment taking the remaining parcel out of RS-20 county jurisdiction and establishing RS-20 (Falls/Jordan Lake Watershed Protection District B) under city jurisdiction by a 5-1 vote.

votes.item_title: Item 24 (Motion 4): Adopt Consistency Statement Pursuant to N.C.G.S. 160D-605 (Lee Valley)
votes.notes: Mayor Williams absent; 6 seated members present.
votes.discussion_detail: Council unanimously adopted the statutory consistency statement required under N.C.G.S. 160D-605 for the Lee Valley zoning map amendments.

disagreements.meeting_title: Durham City Council Sept 3 2024
disagreements.issue: Lee Valley Consolidated Annexation, Transit-Oriented Design, and Proffer Sufficiency
disagreements.summary: Council split 4-1 on annexation/utility extension and 5-1 on the two Lee Valley rezoning ordinances, with Nate Baker dissenting over auto-oriented design in a designated Transit Opportunity Area while the majority accepted the project's affordability and sustainability proffers.
disagreements.side_a_position: Support annexation and rezoning based on improved affordability/sustainability proffers and met extension conditions.
side_a_arguments: The applicant satisfied conditions from the prior extension and added post-Planning Commission proffers, including affordability and sustainability commitments.
No active BRT or passenger rail corridor currently serves the site, and case-by-case gains should be taken rather than imposing ex-post-facto standards ahead of the UDO rewrite.
Housing diversity should be evaluated across the broader surrounding area rather than expecting every single parcel to contain every housing type.
disagreements.side_b_position: Oppose annexation and rezoning for falling short of Transit Opportunity Area design expectations.
side_b_arguments: The Future Place Type Map designates the site as a Transit Opportunity Area intended to transition Durham away from auto-centric development.
Additional transit-oriented design commitments and office/civic/commercial integration were needed despite staff guidance.
disagreements.resolution: Annexation passed 4-1 and both UDO rezoning motions passed 5-1 with Nate Baker voting no; consistency statement passed 6-0.

meetings.title: Durham City Council Work Session Aug 22 2024
meetings.executive_summary: Presiding as Mayor Pro Tem while Mayor Leonardo Williams remained at the Democratic National Convention in Chicago on an excused absence, Mark-Anthony Middleton led the August 22, 2024 City Council work session. Council heard an announcement previewing a NACTO street-design and Vision Zero resolution, met new Durham Police therapy dog Siren, and recognized Durham Emergency Communications and Police personnel for resolving a July 25 Amber Alert involving a youth in DSS custody. Council pulled four items (Items 7, 8, 9, and 12) from the upcoming September 3 agenda—including Chelsea Cook noting her recusal on Legal Aid's eviction diversion contract—reviewed the Q2 2024 Crime Report (noting a 25% drop in shooting incidents alongside increased fatalities and a 10-year high of 90 BLET applicants), received a City Attorney briefing on quasi-judicial hearing procedures, and unanimously settled the September 3 agenda (6-0).

agenda_items.title: Call to Order, Street Safety Announcements, and Police Therapy Dog Introduction
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Mayor Pro Tem Middleton called the work session to order, noting Mayor Williams's excused absence while attending the DNC in Chicago. A council member highlighted pedestrian and traffic violence alongside gun violence as Durham's top killers and announced plans to bring forward a resolution strengthening NACTO street design guidelines and Vision Zero efforts. Javiera Caballero welcomed students from Camp Destiny and Durham Police introduced therapy dog Siren, donated by Canine Responders Academy / Lab Pups.

agenda_items.title: DSS/DPD Amber Alert Recognition and City Manager Priority Items
agenda_items.discussion_summary: DSS Director Maggie Clapp recognized Durham Emergency Communications and Durham Police Department personnel (including the Organized Crime Division / Selective Enforcement Team) for safely recovering a youth in DSS custody following a July 25, 2024 Amber Alert. City Manager Wanda Page also presented Item 14 (Q2 2024 Crime Report presentation) and supplemental Item 25 (FAA Airport Improvement Program Grant). Council voted unanimously by voice vote to receive the City Manager's priority items.

agenda_items.title: Agenda Reading and Pulling of Items 7, 8, 9, and 12
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Mayor Pro Tem Middleton read Items 1 through 24 for the upcoming September 3 regular meeting into the record. Council members pulled Item 7 (ARPA Agreement with Durham Housing Authority), Item 8 (Legal Aid of North Carolina Eviction Diversion Program, on which Chelsea Cook stated she would recuse herself), Item 9 (Interlocal Cooperation Agreement with DHA for security equipment), and Item 12 (Great Trails State Grant for the American Tobacco Trail).

agenda_items.title: 2024 Second Quarter Crime Report Presentation
agenda_items.discussion_summary: In the visible portion of the Police Department presentation, Council questioned staff on filled staff positions compared to the prior year, a reported 25% decrease in shooting incidents from January through June juxtaposed with an increase in shooting fatalities, weapon calibers, and first-responder/hospital impacts. Police reported 90 Basic Law Enforcement Training (BLET) applicants through Q2—the highest level in 10 years—alongside growing interest from female applicants, which council discussion linked to recent officer pay raises.

agenda_items.title: City Attorney Briefing on Quasi-Judicial Hearing Procedures
agenda_items.discussion_summary: City Attorney's office staff briefed Council on statutory quasi-judicial evidentiary hearings (such as special use permits, variances, and certificates of appropriateness), explaining standing, hearsay limits, applicant affirmative consent to conditions, and Council's four disposition options (approve, approve with conditions, deny, or continue to a date certain). DeDreana Freeman raised concerns about neighborhood notice timelines leaving residents little time to retain counsel, and noted Durham Public Schools had shifted school building approvals from minor special use permits to rezoning to allow greater community input.

agenda_items.title: Settle September 3, 2024 Regular City Council Meeting Agenda
agenda_items.discussion_summary: City Manager presented the proposed September 3 agenda: Consent Items 1-7, 9-20, and 25, with Item 8 moved to General Business at Chelsea Cook's request so she could recuse herself solely from Item 8 without recusing from the entire Consent Agenda, plus GBA Public Hearings Items 22-24. Council approved the settled agenda unanimously by voice vote before adjourning at 3:00 p.m.

votes.notes: Mayor Leonardo Williams had an excused absence (DNC in Chicago).
votes.discussion_detail: After DSS Director Maggie Clapp recognized Emergency Communications and Police staff and the City Manager added the Q2 crime report presentation and supplemental FAA grant item, Council approved receiving the priority items by unanimous voice vote.

meetings.title: Durham City Council Aug 19 2024
meetings.executive_summary: Mayor Pro Tem Mark-Anthony Middleton presided over the August 19, 2024 regular City Council meeting while Mayor Leonardo Williams served as a DNC delegate in Chicago on an excused absence. Following proclamations on Breastfeeding Friendly initiatives and Women's Equality Day 2024, Council unanimously approved the Consent Agenda (excluding Item 7 on 505 West Chapel Hill Street, which the City Manager moved to General Business after it was placed on consent in error) and unanimously adopted the 2025 City Council meeting schedule. After deliberating on Item 7 (detailed in the standalone clip a9FTWJNGiF0), Council held a public hearing on Item 18, Duke's Central Campus Addition University College (UC) zoning map change. Several council members criticized the lack of specific development plans, clear master plan deliverables, and side-path timelines, resulting in unanimous consent to continue the hearing to October 7, 2024.

agenda_items.title: Call to Order, Roll Call, Proclamations, and Announcements
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Mayor Pro Tem Mark-Anthony Middleton called the meeting to order in Mayor Leonardo Williams's excused absence (attending the DNC in Chicago), with Middleton, Javiera Caballero, Chelsea Cook, DeDreana Freeman, and Carl Rist answering roll call (Nate Baker's name was called with no verbal response captured in the transcript). Council presented proclamations for Breastfeeding Friendly initiatives—highlighting efforts to narrow racial infant mortality disparities—and Women's Equality Day 2024 (August 26), and celebrated DCLT's Guthrie Village veteran housing and DHA's Commerce Street groundbreakings.

agenda_items.title: Consent Agenda Approval (Item 7 Moved to General Business)
agenda_items.discussion_summary: City Manager moved Item 7 (Update on the Redevelopment of 505 West Chapel Hill Street) from the Consent Agenda to General Business because it had been placed on consent in error, and the City Clerk noted DeDreana Freeman as alternate to HRC and HSAC. The remaining consent agenda—including Item 6 authorizing up to $29M in multifamily housing revenue bonds for 500 East Main, utility easements, solid waste engineering agreements, Southern Boundaries Park tennis court grant, and IT/fire RMS contracts—was approved unanimously.

agenda_items.title: 2025 City Council Meeting Schedule
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Council revisited whether to shift the July 24, 2025 work session due to the Mayor's expected international travel. Javiera Caballero noted that several members were uncertain of their schedules that far in advance, and Middleton confirmed the Council could amend the calendar later if needed before calling for a vote.

agenda_items.title: Update on the Redevelopment of 505 West Chapel Hill Street
agenda_items.discussion_summary: General Services staff member Stacy Poston introduced a revised second substantive motion reflecting work session feedback on the 505 West Chapel Hill Street redevelopment, prior to public comment and council debate (the remainder of Item 7 is truncated in this meeting digest and captured in full in clip a9FTWJNGiF0).

agenda_items.title: Public Hearing: Zoning Map Change — Duke Central Campus Addition
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Duke's counsel presented the Central Campus University College (UC) rezoning request (noting East Campus had been withdrawn and the Planning Commission recommended approval 8-1). Chelsea Cook objected that Duke had no specific development plans for parcels acquired over decades, while Javiera Caballero, Carl Rist, and DeDreana Freeman sought clearer master plan deliverables, sustainability and housing goals, and a timeline for a 10-foot transportation side path; Middleton cautioned against prosecuting broader disputes with Duke through this rezoning. With the applicant amenable, Council gave unanimous consent to continue the public hearing to October 7, 2024.
agenda_items.vote_summary: Continued to October 7, 2024 by unanimous consent

votes.item_title: Item 5: Adopt 2025 City Council Meeting Schedule
votes.notes: Mayor Leonardo Williams excused; Nate Baker did not answer roll call in the digest.
votes.discussion_detail: After agreeing to hold the current proposed 2025 calendar with the option to amend the July 24 work session date later, Council unanimously adopted the 2025 City Council meeting schedule.

votes.item_title: Item 18: Continue Public Hearing on Duke Central Campus Addition Zoning Map Change to October 7, 2024
votes.notes: Resolved by unanimous poll/consent ('thumbs up') with applicant agreement.
votes.discussion_detail: After council members raised unanswered questions regarding Duke's master plan, sustainability/housing commitments, and transportation side-path timing, Mayor Pro Tem Middleton polled the dais and recorded unanimous consent to keep the public hearing open and continue the case to October 7, 2024.

disagreements.meeting_title: Durham City Council Aug 19 2024
disagreements.issue: Duke Central Campus Addition University College (UC) Rezoning Without Specific Development Plan
disagreements.summary: Council members disagreed on whether to evaluate Duke's Central Campus UC rezoning without specific development plans and broader institutional commitments before deciding to continue the case to October 7, 2024.
disagreements.side_a_position: Delay/require clearer master plan, development intentions, sustainability, housing, and transportation timing commitments before voting.
side_a_arguments: Duke has no concrete development plans for parcels acquired over decades, leaving Council without control once broad UC zoning is granted.
The ordinance states a master plan shall be submitted, yet lacks clarity on what a master plan must contain compared to NCCU's publicly available plan.
Duke's transportation commitment for a 10-foot side path lacked a binding timing component, and community/council distrust of the county's largest private landowner warrants deeper due diligence.
disagreements.side_b_position: Evaluate the UC rezoning on standard land-use grounds without litigating broader disputes with Duke.
side_b_arguments: Council has previously approved rezonings without detailed development plans by relying on lists of prohibited uses, and UC zoning is designed to provide flexibility for universities.
Broader institutional conversations and grievances with Duke should be addressed in separate forums rather than prosecuted through this land-use case.
disagreements.resolution: Council polled unanimous consent at 03:26:22 to hold the public hearing open and continue the case to October 7, 2024.
